News.title: Drought declared across whole of Wales as conditions 'deteriorate'
News.content:
Richard Anthony, whose farm stretches over the Vale of Glamorgan and Bridgend county, said the ground on his land was as hard as a "rock" and had "no moisture at all".

The dry land has left Anthony unable to plant his crops, who added he had "never ever been in this situation" before.

"As soon as we've harvested the one crop, we plant in the next crop, but we can't do any of that now," he said. "I've never seen it as bad as this."

Our wheat deals are down between 20% and 30%. That is massive. we'll have to cope, we will survive, but the knock-on effect is huge."

Anthony said he is concerned that once the rain comes it will not stop, leaving him unable to plant next year's crops.

"It'll go from this to being too wet", he added.

National Farmers Union Cymru president Abi Reader has warned that the cost of the continuing dry and hot weather will have a financial impact on farmers.

"We're going to see costs for these farms rising, because they might be having to buy in extra feed for their livestock, or they might be spending a lot of money carting water," she said.

"We've been in this a long time now, and it's going to take a long time to recover, and absolutely everybody needs to remember that food security starts with water security," she added.

News.title: British Airways flight called mayday on approach to Heathrow
News.content:
A British Airways flight issued a "mayday" distress call on its approach to Heathrow Airport earlier this month, according to a statement from France's accident investigation authority.

The call was made on an Airbus A320 flying from Dusseldorf airport in Germany on 6 July following two stall warnings on the aircraft, before it landed without further incident.

The UK's Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) said it was "investigating a serious incident".

A British Airways spokesperson said the airline was assisting the AAIB with its investigation and was not legally able to comment further at this stage.

The French Air Safety Investigation Authority, the BEA, said that as the plane approached Heathrow, there was a data system failure which triggered a stall warning.

The crew then flew the aircraft in a different mode called "alternate law", which removes some automated flight protection systems. Another stall warning then occurred at 3,000 feet - which experts say was likely to have been just miles away from the airport.

The urgency call the crew had already made was upgraded to mayday, indicating imminent danger.

The BEA website attributed the statement to the AAIB, but the AAIB would not confirm it was from them.

They issued the following statement: "The AAIB is investigating a serious incident involving a commercial aircraft which occurred on 6 July on approach to Heathrow airport."

It said the investigation would be a correspondence investigation, meaning that no team would be sent to carry out field investigations.

Aviation safety investigator David Gleave said there are different forms of mayday calls, and to send an urgency message was "not unusual".

"You could have sick passengers on board who need urgent medical attentionâ¦ so it's up to the captains' discretion as to what they call, but its very unusual for it to be a significant failure on board the aeroplane."

News.title: MP Diane Abbott readmitted into Labour Party after suspension
News.content:
The long-serving MP Diane Abbott has been let back into the Labour Party, following a year-long suspension.

In a statement, a Labour spokesperson said Abbott had "apologised" following an independent process and that she would be readmitted into the parliamentary party, meaning she can sit as a Labour MP once again.

Abbott, who was suspended in 2025 following an antisemitism row, said she had been "issued with a formal warning".

East Kilbride and Strathaven MP Joani Reid has also been readmitted to the party. In March, she said she had "voluntarily" suspended herself after her husband was arrested on suspicion of spying for China.

Her husband David Taylor, was arrested along with two other men. All three have been released on police bail, which in May was extended until August.

Responding to her readmittance on Thursday evening, Reid she was "excited to play a full part in supporting our new prime minister".

She added: "I have never been part of a police investigation, as a suspect or as a witness, and I am pleased that this has now been recognised."

News.title: Anthropic says AI models hacked three firms during tests
News.content:
US tech company Anthropic says three of its artificial intelligence (AI) models hacked three organisations during tests, just days after its rival OpenAI said rogue AI agents had attacked the networks of other firms.

During a cybersecurity exercise, Anthropic's Claude AI model gained unauthorised access to systems by connecting to the internet from isolated test environments, it said on Thursday.

Anthropic said it discovered the incidents after reviewing more than 140,000 tests following OpenAI's disclosure on 21 July that its agents had hacked another AI company, Hugging Face.

Anthropic urged other AI labs to perform similar reviews to better understand the risks of their models' capabilities.

The San Francisco-based firm also said it has alerted the three companies that were hacked about the incidents.

Anthropic said in a statement, external that it is "approaching the fixes as if the responsibility were ours alone."

News.title: Archbishop of Canterbury committed to £100m slavery fund
News.content:
This is Dame Sarah's first pastoral visit to Africa since being installed as head of the Church of England at a ceremony in Canterbury Cathedral in March.

Reparative justice has been one of the themes running through the Ghana leg of this trip.

At Cape Coast Castle, which came under British control in the 1660s, Dame Sarah was shown dungeons where slaves were held, and the so-called "door of no return" through which they were forced on to ships.

The archbishop said: "You can't help but be deeply moved by the horrific conditions that people were kept in and the way that they were treated.

"It completely throws you off balance and brings home the evil that was transatlantic slavery."

Above the dungeons sits a chapel, which she said was a "stark illustration of the way the church was involved in the slave trade".

The Church of England has previously apologised for its associations with the slave trade.

Its missionary arm ran slave-farmed plantations in the Caribbean to fund the spread of Anglicanism, individual members of clergy were slave owners, and the Church received large donations from slave traders.

News.title: Palestine Action ban to be reviewed by Supreme Court
News.content:
The controversial ban under terrorism legislation of the protest group Palestine Action will be reviewed by the Supreme Court.

In a major blow to the Home Office, the court confirmed on Thursday that it had given the group's co-founder permission to appeal the ban which came into effect in July 2025.

While the full details of the reasons for the appeal are yet to be published, the BBC understands they relate to Huda Ammori's argument that the ban breaches human rights.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said in a statement the government would "robustly defend this appeal".

Officials at the court say the appeal will be expedited - which means it will be heard after the summer break. The eventual outcome of the case could have major implications for terrorism legislation in the UK.

The decision comes weeks after the end of the first major trial of members of the group which had caused more than Â£1m of damage to a defence firm near Bristol with an Israeli parent company. Four members of that break-in team were jailed, with one also sentenced for causing grievous bodily harm on a police officer who was hit with a sledgehammer.

Separately, more than 2,000 people are facing potential trial for protesting against the ban by declaring their support for a proscribed terrorism group in mass demonstrations.

The battle over the banning of Palestine Action has now gone on for more than year.

Former Home Secretary Yvette Cooper banned the group on advice from the police and security officials after an escalating spate of break-ins targeting Elbit, an Israeli-owned defence firm.

The High Court initially ruled that the ban was unlawful - but five judges on the Court of Appeal then overruled it, unanimously deciding the home secretary had acted lawfully and within her powers to proscribe Palestine Action.

That decision by the Court of Appeal will now be reviewed by the Supreme Court.

News.title: Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil
News.content:
Although the government has not made any announcements on the issue, Trump has praised what he perceives as a change of stance by the UK government.

In a social media post, published the day before Burnham became prime minister,, external Trump wrote: "The People of Aberdeen, in Scotland, are dancing in the streets because the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has stated that he will be opening up, all the way, the invaluable North Sea Oil!"

This week, when asked about his conversation with Burnham, Trump said: "He said he's going to open up North Sea oil.

"If he does that, you're going to be a wealthy country."

He later added: "You buy a lot of your energy, as you know, from the North Sea. You buy from Norway and Norway gets it from the North Sea... Norway's got trillions of dollars in the bank."

"Scotland has a better part of the North Sea."

Asked about Trump's comments, Burnham said: "I indicated in the phone call that we had a week last Monday that I would take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea, and that is my intention as we go forward from here."

In response, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Our country is burning. Crops are failing. Thousands have been killed by extreme heat.

"Allowing new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea will worsen the climate breakdown putting more lives at risk and doing untold damage to our economy.

"It's not too late for Burnham to do the right thing and commit to leaving dangerous fossil fuels in the ground."

The Conservatives and Reform have urged the government to approve more drilling in the North Sea, arguing it would reduce energy prices.

Last year, Tory Party leader Kemi Badenoch said it would be "absurd" for the UK to leave "vital resources untapped".

Some Labour MPs have expressed unease about more drilling, with Rachael Maskell urging the government to "follow the climate science because we have got a climate emergency".

Simon Francis, from the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: "No household struggling with their energy bills will see a penny come off by drilling more from the North Sea.

"Gas is sold at the global market prices, so whatever is pumped out is sold to the highest bidder, not handed to British billpayers at a discount."

Sir Keir's government had already made concessions, allowing "tie-backs" - production in unlicensed areas close to or connected to already licensed areas.

Currently, the debate over North Sea drilling has focused on two oil and gas fields - Rosebank and Jackdaw, located in Scotland.

In 2022 and 2023, regulators approved drilling at the sites, but that was overturned in 2025 following a legal challenge.

The legal process is ongoing, but the government will at some point have to decide whether to permit companies to produce oil in the two areas.

Other oil and gas licences have been approved in recent years but remain largely undeveloped.

If he wanted to encourage more drilling in the North Sea, Burnham could also opt to scrap the Energy Profits Levy, also known as the windfall tax.

The levy is due to be replaced in 2030 by another windfall tax, which operators prefer because it's only triggered when prices are high and falls back when they are low.

News.title: Greens review social media operation as Polanski row rumbles on
News.content:
The current row began after Polanski shared a single post on Instagram that contained a carousel of 20 pictures.

The re-post was shared to Polanski's 713,000 followers, because he accepted a request to tag him as a collaborator, which on the platform makes him a "co-author," placing it on his page and into his followers' feeds.

Polanski said he had not noticed the offending image among the others on the post.

According to him, he had accepted collaborator tags for eight other posts from the same event in Bristol alone.

Reform UK leader Farage claimed the t-shirt amounted to incitement to murder and his party reported it to the police.

Neither the Metropolitan Police nor Avon and Somerset Police say the incident meets the threshold for further action.

But the political row has continued with Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick calling Polanski a "nasty piece of work", at a news conference earlier on Thursday.

Inside the Green Party, there has been some criticism of Polanski's behaviour online.

He has attracted positive and negative attention for the rate at which he posts, comments, likes and replies across multiple platforms including X, Bluesky, Facebook and Instagram.

And this is not the first time a quick reaction has attracted controversy; last month he had to apologise to police after posting about their response to the Golders Green attack.

One senior party source said it was clear that due diligence had not been done on Polanski's social media output, and that moving forwards he needs "tight controls" to stay credible, while keeping a similar tone of engagement with his followers.

They pointed out that the speed and number of Polanski's interactions came with a "small upside" but a "colossal downside", and with the latest incident he had "shot himself in the foot at precisely the wrong time".

It comes as recent polling suggests the Green Party has lost ground to Labour, following Andy Burnham's election as Labour leader, and down from a peak earlier this year.

They added their concerns about a wider problem with the party's vetting on social media and of candidates, including around antisemitic posts in recent months.

Several candidates in recent elections have stood down over their social media activity, with two candidates arrested during May's local elections, and another suspended after being elected.

But Green Party peer and former deputy mayor of London Baroness Jones said the criticism of Polanski's Instagram re-post seemed to be "mainly from our opponents, not internal discussions".

She said that her party leader had "made a mistake", adding "we've all done it and got flak."

But she added: "His online presence is what makes him relatable".

Along with relatability, comes popularity: Polanski is the second-most followed UK leader on Instagram after Nigel Farage. The Greens surpassed other parties to become the most popular on the platform this year.

It is also seen as where a good portion of their voters spend time, as they are the most popular party among the under-30s, according to pollsters YouGov.

One party source said there had been discussions among councillors and activists about whether Polanski was "too online".

"Is he just too online? Is he doing it all himself? Where's the professionalisation here, given the level the party's now grown to, and what people expect of us?" they said.

"There's got to be more checks and balances" the source added.

News.title: Bank holds interest rates but says it is ready to raise them if Iran war escalates
News.content:
The Bank of England has kept interest rates unchanged for the fifth meeting in a row but has indicated it could raise them if the Iran war escalates.

It expects inflation - the rate at which prices rise - to pick up due to volatile oil and gas prices caused by the Middle East conflict, although the peak will be slightly lower than previously thought.

The Bank voted to hold interest rates at 3.75% at its latest meeting.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey warned the future of UK interest rates depended on whether the US led war against Iran continues.

While major uncertainties remain because of the war, the Bank predicts the UK economy will grow this year by more than previously forecast.

Bailey told the BBC: "If we get a continuation of this conflict going on and oil prices stay above $100 a barrel... the odds are that interest rates will have to go up higher."

But he also said if a ceasefire, and memorandum of understanding, is established and sticks that would make a difference.

"So it depends on how the events in the Middle East, frankly, unfold. And sadly, we all know this is highly unpredictable," Bailey said.

"What goes on in the Gulf is not, I'm afraid, under our control."

Three members of the Bank's nine-member rate-setting committee voted for a hike, one more than the previous meeting - with that member explicitly citing the collapse of the US-Iran memorandum of understanding for their vote to raise rates.

However, speaking at an earlier news conference, Bailey said the Bank was not currently moving towards raising interest rates.

"Please do not leave this room thinking that the Bank of England is edging towards a hike, because frankly, there's nothing in what I said, and I think any of us have said along those lines," he told reporters.

If the Iran war continues and oil prices hover around $100 a barrel, then a rate rise seems likely. But many in the markets expect tensions to subside in the coming weeks, ahead of crucial elections across the US in the autumn.

News.title: Virgin engineer died after explosion in fuel tank
News.content:
A Virgin Atlantic engineer died of a traumatic brain injury after an explosion as he worked inside a plane fuel tank, an inquest heard.

Aircraft technician Georgie Buxton, 23, was injured during the incident at Heathrow Airport on 11 June and underwent various surgeries to his head and neck. He died at St Mary's Hospital on 7 July.

Senior coroner Lydia Brown opened and suspended an inquest into his death at West London Coroners' Court on Thursday, as she is waiting to see if any criminal charges are brought.

A criminal investigation has been launched by the Metropolitan Police who are working with the Health and Safety Executive. The coroner said she had no details of any potential charges.

Buxton was one of two Virgin Airlines' technicians who were examining a fuel leak on a Boeing 787 900 on 11 June at about 08:45 BST.

A spokesman for Aviation Policing told the court: "Both technicians wore breathing apparatus to protect them from any residual fuel fumes whilst inside the fuel tank."

The spokesman said there was "a non-combustion explosion" while Buxton was inside the fuel tank.

He added: "Georgie Buxton took the impact of that explosion to his head and torso causing him to lose consciousness and suffer catastrophic injury."

A forensic post-mortem examination, carried out at the request of the police, found Buxton had suffered a traumatic brain injury â a craniofacial trauma.

News.title: Four people die after busiest day for small-boat crossings this year
News.content:
Four people died trying to cross the Channel overnight after the busiest day for small-boat crossings so far this year saw 752 arrivals in the UK.

One man died after a vessel capsized off France's northern coast late on Wednesday, local officials said, with a one-year-old child among those hurt.

Seven hours later, three people were found dead aboard a small boat after launching from Dunkirk overnight, some 100km (62 miles) up the coast.

French officials confirmed their deaths as the Home Office reported that Wednesday saw the highest number of crossings in a single day this year, with nine boats reaching the UK.

Local authorities in France said the first boat capsized off the coast at Hardelot around 23:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday.

The man is thought to have been in his 30s or 40s, officials added. Six other people including the child sustained minor injuries.

Local officials said the vessel was a "taxi" boat - which cruise along the coast and pick up their paying customers who are waiting in the sea.

Security officials "neutralised" the boat and an investigation into the incident has been launched.

The second boat launched from the Dunkirk area overnight was spotted near a breakwater off the coast at 06:00, the French coastguard said.

Search and rescue officials subsequently found three unconscious people aboard. Their deaths were later confirmed by emergency medical personnel.

A UK government spokesperson said: "Every death in the Channel is a tragedy and a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting vulnerable people for profit."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, speaking separately about small boat crossings on Thursday, said the UK had made "significant progress" on reducing the number of arrivals.

But, asked by reporters about US President Donald Trump's remark that the UK had a "huge immigration problem", Burnham said there was much still to do "to get those numbers right down".

News.title: Homes flooded and residents evacuated after quarry 'incident'
News.content:
Residents of a village on the outskirts of Cardiff were evacuated after flooding caused by a quarry "incident".

Roads have been shut in Gwaelod-y-Garth, with reports of water up to 5ft (1.5m) deep in some homes on Thursday afternoon.

Emergency services were called to the scene and people were advised to avoid the area.

The Breedon Group confirmed there had been an "incident in its quarry".

"Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities while engaging with the local community as we respond to the situation," the company said.

News.title: England on track for record heat-related deaths this year, UKHSA estimates
News.content:
England is on track this year for the highest number of heat-related deaths since records began, according to estimates by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

In a preliminary assessment, it said there were an estimated 2,877 heat-related deaths during the May and June heatwaves, almost double the figure for the whole of last year.

An estimated 753 deaths were associated with the 24-27 May heatwave and a further 2,124 with the one from 21-28 June. Definitive figures are expected in early 2027.

Both spells broke Met Office UK monthly temperature records, with 35.1C (95.2F) recorded at Kew Gardens on 26 May and 38.0C recorded at Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June.

The current record for heat-related deaths was set in 2022, when 2,985 deaths were recorded.

Report author Dr Ross Thompson, from the UKHSA, said "while the figures are interim, they suggest that, if we experience more periods of hot weather this summer, we could see the highest number of heat-associated deaths on record".

Thompson added: "These figures highlight the significant danger that very hot weather can pose to people's health.

"This is particularly true for those who are more vulnerable including older adults and people with underlying medical conditions."

He said "as the climate becomes warmer, we can expect periods of hot weather to become longer, more frequent and more extreme", adding that it is vital the country is prepared to deal with higher temperatures.

Earlier this week parts of the UK sweltered through another heatwave that peaked on Wednesday, with temperature reaching 35.2C in Writtle, Essex.

Cooler conditions and some rain are on the way for some on Thursday and into the weekend, but likely not in the driest areas.

The parties in the Israel-Hamas war have agreed to a “historic” framework paving the way to rebuild Gaza and remake its government, President Donald Trump announced on Thursday.

The deal includes the “COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza,” the president wrote on Truth Social.

Hamas communicated via mediators that it has agreed to the terms of the multi-step road map, U.S. and Board of Peace officials told The Independent.

The deal will eventually see the group hand security and political control to an international stabilization force of troops, a newly trained Palestinian police force and a transitional group of technocratic experts overseeing basic services, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the officials said.

The Israeli military, meanwhile, will pull back its troops from Gaza in phases, according to President Trump.

Israel and Hamas have agreed to a multi-part framework on the future of Gaza, which will see Hamas disarm and Israel withdraw its troops, according to President Trump ( AFP/Getty )

“One year ago there was a violent raging war, humanitarian crisis and hostages kept in brutal captivity,” he wrote in his post outlining the alleged agreement. “We have made historic progress and there is still much work to do.”

Each phase of the process will be verified by a committee that certifies compliance on all sides before additional changes can take place, the U.S. officials said.

Hamas member Ghazi Hammad told Al Jazeera that the group will follow through with disarming if Israel maintains its obligations.

“Israel will not interfere in the disarmament issue, and the national committee is the one that will carry out this task”, he said.

“Hamas remains steadfast in its national goals, represented by preserving the rights of the Palestinian people,” Hammad added.

As of Thursday evening, there were signs Israel may not have agreed to what the U.S. was describing.

An unnamed Israeli official told i24, an Israeli news channel, that Gaza had not been discussed during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s recent visit to Washington and that Israeli would not fully withdraw from Gaza until Hamas had fully disarmed and the Strip had been completely demilitarized.

The Independent has contacted Israel and its military for comment.

This is a breaking news story and will be updated with new information.

Palestine Action can appeal its terror ban at the Supreme Court, judges have ruled, setting up a final legal battle with the Home Office this autumn.

The Court of Appeal ruled last month that the group’s proscription under terrorism laws was lawful in a major win for the government.

Lady Chief Justice Baroness Carr said that Palestine Action’s ban was “a justified and proportionate interference with individual rights”, describing the group as one that “overtly promotes unlawful violence amounting to terrorism”.

Now three justices at the Supreme Court have granted Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori permission to appeal the ruling. The challenge will be heard this autumn.

The ban, which began on 5 July last year, made membership of, or support for, the direct action group a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison.

open image in gallery A protester is arrested outside Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Thursday ( Getty )

Palestine Action was banned by then-home secretary Yvette Cooper in July 2025 after members broke into RAF Brize Norton and vandalised jets to protest the war in Gaza.

A five-judge panel at the Court of Appeal found that Ms Cooper’s decision struck a “fair balance” between the need to safeguard national security and disrupting individuals’ rights to freedom of expression and assembly.

After the judgment, Ms Ammori said the decision was “one of the most extreme attacks on free speech and the right to protest in modern British history”.

Before the case reached the Court of Appeal, High Court judges had found that the ban was in fact unlawful, arguing that only a small number of Palestine Action’s activities amounted to terrorism, and that the group’s acts had not crossed the high bar to make it a terrorist organisation.

This week, the Metropolitan Police warned protesters campaigning in front of Westminster Magistrates’ Court that expressing support for Palestine Action is a terrorism offence.

open image in gallery Huda Ammori said she would continue her legal fight to the European Court of Human Rights if necessary ( Peace Pledge Union/YouTube )

Some 77 people were arrested at the protest in central London on Thursday, police said.

Hundreds gathered outside the magistrates’ court where more than 2,000 cases related to supporting the group had been due to be heard. But their cases have been adjourned to October, to await the outcome of the Supreme Court appeal.

Responding to the news that her case will head to the UK’s highest court, Ms Ammori said on Thursday’s arrests “further evidences our case that the proscription of Palestine Action has become a vehicle for a far broader crackdown on expressions of solidarity with the Palestinian people”.

She added: “We will continue to fight this proscription all the way to the Supreme Court and, if necessary, to the European Court of Human Rights to overturn what has become one of the most extreme attacks on free speech and the right to protest in modern British history”.

News.title: Fired worker charged with making fake profile on TikTok of his boss and making sexual comments
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A Michigan man who allegedly used a fake TikTok account to try to get revenge on his former boss is now facing felony charges.

An Indiana man was blindsided when he was called by his company's HR department and told he was going to be fired over inappropriate sexual comments he allegedly made on social media. In reality, someone had impersonated him and left the comments using his name and likeness, according to Fox 59.

The suspect, 32-year-old Tyler Larsen, allegedly created the account that used the victim's photo and real name, and then began posting sexual remarks on the videos of juvenile girls dancing, according to police.

In May, the victim was fired.

Doug Kouns, a former FBI agent and founder of Veracity IIR, told Fox 59 that it's easy for people to create an account on social media and impersonate others.

A man in Indiana lost his job after a former employee who he fired allegedly created a fake TikTok account using his name and photo and posted inappropriate sexual messages on videos of young girls dancing ( Getty )

In this case, police managed to work with the internet service provider to track down the origin point of the fake TikTok account. Investigators discovered the account allegedly belonged to Larsen.

The victim had a personal connection to Larsen. Before the incident, Larsen worked under the victim, and the victim told police he had to fire Larsen in January. Larsen has now been charged with felony identity deception.

The victim was rehired by his workplace in mid-June once the deception came to light.

Social media impersonation isn't just a threat for individuals, but also poses a risk to businesses and other organizations.

Fake profiles on social media have become the leading cybersecurity threat facing organizations in 2026, according to the Corporate Service Company's 2026 cybersecurity outlook report.

The report notes that the advancement of deepfake images and AI-powered image generators has made it substantially easier for cybercriminals to impersonate executives and employees.

But anyone with access to a person's digital images online — like those posted on Instagram or Facebook — can use them to create a fake profile.

Seattle’s police chief has resigned amid criticism of the city’s response to a fatal shootout at a food festival last weekend, Mayor Katie Wilson announced on Thursday.

The departure of Chief Shon Barnes followed hours of intense speculation about whether he would step down, as some of his supporters claimed he had rebuffed Mayor Wilson’s request for his resignation.

Mayor Wilson confirmed the appointment of Deputy Chief Andre Sayles as interim chief, a law enforcement veteran with more than two decades of experience. Chief Barnes told The Seattle Times on Thursday that whether he remains chief is "up to the mayor," adding that he was off for the day and spending time with family.

A police department spokesperson told The Associated Press they did not have any information to share about the situation.

open image in gallery Barnes was out of town at a law enforcement conference when gunfire erupted last weekend at the Bite of Seattle ( AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson )

Barnes was out of town at a law enforcement conference when gunfire erupted last weekend at the Bite of Seattle, an annual three-day festival that draws hundreds of food and retail vendors and performers. Three people, including one suspect, were killed, and four people were wounded. One of the injured was a 2-year-old boy.

Dozens of officers were at the event, and at least one saw a 15-year-old suspect firing into a crowd and quickly persuaded him to surrender, according to court documents. Police are still searching for at least one other person.

Both the Seattle Police Department and Wilson have faced criticism for slow and confusing communication in the shooting's aftermath.

After an initial social media post announcing that there had been a shooting with multiple victims, it took nearly five hours for police to provide any additional information to the public, including whether there was any ongoing threat. In the meantime, Wilson announced that two people had been taken into custody, a statement she later retracted.

Assistant Seattle Police Chief Tyrone Davis finally provided an update around 11 p.m. Sunday night during news conference that was also attended by the mayor, Gov. Bob Ferguson and U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal.

Barnes is the second Black police chief in Seattle.

Several Black community organizations, including the Seattle NAACP and the Urban League of Metropolitan Seattle, rallied to try to save his job Thursday. In an open letter to the mayor's office, they credited him with improving relations between the department and the community, helping reduce gun violence and strengthening the department's operations.

“This is the wrong decision at the wrong time and would disrupt Seattle’s progress in public safety,” the letter said. “The tragic fatal shooting at the Bite of Seattle was heartbreaking for our city, but Chief Barnes should not be made a scapegoat for the complex challenges of public safety.”

open image in gallery Barnes is the second Black police chief in Seattle ( David Ryder/Getty Images )

Civil rights lawyer James Bible was with a small group of Black leaders who met with Wilson early Thursday. Wilson didn’t “tip her hand” regarding whether she’ll fire Barnes but appeared to be considering their argument in favor of keeping him on the job, he said.

“I’m hopeful that she will take a step back and make a different decision for now and then create criteria for any future decisions,” Bible said.

Barnes was appointed by Seattle's previous mayor, Bruce Harrell, in December 2024 after serving as chief of the Madison, Wisconsin, police department.

When Wilson — a democratic socialist who once supported defunding police — won the mayor's race last year, she kept Barnes on as chief. That was a signal to the city's business establishment and community groups that she did not intend to take a radically different approach to public safety.

Wilson came into office with no prior elected or management experience, but with a reputation as someone who thought deeply about social and policy issues. A lingering question was how decisively she would act as mayor.

“She looks weak and vacillating,” Seattle political consultant Sandeep Kaushik said Thursday. “There’s almost 24 hours now where it’s not clear whether the police chief is still the police chief.”

Barnes has faced some criticism for spending time in Chicago, where his family lives. Sgt. Patrick Michaud, a department spokesperson, said Thursday that Barnes has made four trips to Chicago this year and spent in total about 18 days traveling there. Barnes also has traveled to several police executive and recruitment conferences.

Barnes was named as the chief of police in Seattle five days after he was thrust into the national spotlight because of a shooting at a religious school in Wisconsin that killed a teacher and student. At the time, Harrell said Barnes had demonstrated “impressive leadership capabilities” during an investigation into the shooting.

The tension between the mayor and police chief comes as Seattle heads into another big festival weekend. Seafair Weekend Festival 2026 — a boating event, air show and festival — starts Friday.

The last person known to have seen Navajo elder Ella Mae Begay alive has been accused of burglary in an unrelated incident, raising questions about whether he will be sent back to federal prison in Begay's disappearance.

Preston Tolth is the only person ever charged and convicted in connection with the 2021 disappearance of Begay, a weaver and grandmother of nine from a remote community on the Navajo Nation who has never been found. He acknowledged stealing her truck, beating her and leaving her on the side of the road.

Her case has become emblematic of the heartache felt across Indian Country when loved ones go missing or are killed. Begay's photo appears at marches. Her name is regularly invoked at rallies calling attention to the crisis.

Phoenix police arrested Tolth, 27, on Tuesday after getting a call about a home break-in. Officers found him about a block away, wearing clothing that matched the description of the suspect and carrying a pocket knife, according to court records.

Tolth was released from federal prison in June, five years to the day Begay vanished and two years earlier than his sentence was scheduled to end. The Bureau of Prisons cited a federal statue that counts time served after the commission of a crime but before sentencing, including on unrelated charges, in releasing him early.

Tolth was sent to a transitional housing facility in Phoenix. Under the terms of his plea agreement in federal court, he was not to commit any additional crimes while on supervised release. He also was barred from possessing dangerous weapons.

He faces a single charge of burglary in Maricopa County. Court records did not have an attorney listed for him, and his public defender in the federal case did not respond to an emailed request for comment Thursday.

Esther Winne, a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Arizona, said the office is aware of his arrest.

“There is a process for handling violations,” Winne said in an email Tuesday, declining further comment.

Gerald Foxworth, an employee at Phoenix Oasis where Tolth was staying, said Tolth returned to the facility drunk on July 4 in violation of program rules. Tolth left on his own after refusing to be transported to a medical center, Foxworth said, and the facility informed Tolth's probation officer.

The U.S. Marshals Service had an active warrant out for Tolth’s arrest when he was picked up by Phoenix police.

The Associated Press left phone and email messages with Tolth's probation officer Thursday requesting comment.

Begay's family said they were unaware Tolth left transitional housing. His arrest is the latest frustration in a case they say has offered little in the way of justice or closure. The eldest of Begay's three children, Gerald Begay, said he is relieved no one was harmed in the break-in.

“(Federal officials) made the decision to release this person. Now he’s out here hurting people,” Begay said. “This could have ended far worse.”

___

This story is published through the Global Indigenous Reporting Network at The Associated Press.

New Mexico's foster care system is facing legal action after allegedly compelling a 15-year-old American citizen to walk across the border into Mexico alone to reunite with his estranged mother.

Attorney General Raúl Torrez has filed a civil lawsuit against the Children, Youth and Families Department (CYFD), demanding the child's return and seeking to block similar future reunifications without court approval. The complaint states staff drove the minor to El Paso, Texas, on July 6, instructing him to cross the border bridge alone to find his mother, a Mexican national deported earlier this year on drug charges.

"The State of New Mexico cannot claim to protect children while abandoning one of its own at an international border," Torrez said in a news release.

After crossing into Mexico, the child could not immediately find his mother and ran back across traffic to re-enter the U.S.

open image in gallery After crossing into Mexico, the child could not immediately find his mother and ran back across traffic to re-enter the US ( Herika Martinez / AFP via Getty Images )

At that time, U.S. Customs and Border Protection urged New Mexico's child welfare agency to drive the child back to New Mexico, the attorney general's complaint says. But the documents state staff refused and allegedly said the child was now a “Texas problem” before leaving him at the border.

“The most important thing is that the child is safe and living with his mother, who CYFD has been in frequent contact with,” said Jake Thompson, a CYFD spokesperson in a statement Wednesday. “CYFD is reviewing the complaint and the order and will respond to them in court.”

After the border incident, the 15-year-old was left with the Texas Department of Family and Protective Services, the complaint states. Despite efforts to communicate with CYFD, Texas officials were allegedly forced to return the child to his mother in Mexico weeks later, according to the complaint. Email and phone messages to the Texas welfare agency were not returned Thursday.

Torrez said the boy remains in Mexico with his mother despite multiple attempts to reenter the U.S. Torrez called the case part of a broader pattern of neglect within the state’s foster care system and demanded CYFD staff do what they could to repatriate the teenager.

New Mexico's child welfare agency says boy was never at risk

In a statement, CYFD denied the child’s safety was ever at risk and said his mother had requested he be reunited with her in Mexico. They said staff conducted two virtual home visits, concluding the situation was safe for him.

CYFD’s Office of Advocacy includes immigration specialists, which help children reunite with family members in other countries, according to its website.

“There is nothing in New Mexico state law that prohibits reuniting a child with a parent in another country, assuming it is done safely,” said Cristen Conley, director at the Corinne Wolfe Center for Child and Family Justice at the University of New Mexico.

Michael Coleman, a spokesperson for New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, said the office, which is responsible for overseeing CYFD, has been in regular contact with the agency throughout the case.

“New Mexico and Texas authorities, and a New Mexico judge, independently concluded that the child should be with his mother,” Coleman said in a statement. “The Attorney General’s office is now asking for the child to be returned to New Mexico. The filing does not state where the child will live or who will take care of him if that happens.”

Case highlights foster system's pattern of failures, attorney general says

In April, the New Mexico Department of Justice released a 200-page report detailing what it alleged were systemic failures in the welfare agency that meant children were returned to dangerous environments while department staff prioritized reunification over safety. The case also comes as the Trump administration seeks to deport immigrant children by accessing data from the Office of Refugee Resettlement and attempting to bypass previous court rulings.

After the border incident, the teenager contacted the Office of the Child Advocate, an independent government watchdog that monitors the child welfare system, which eventually referred the case to the New Mexico Department of Justice.

The child's parents are two Mexican nationals, but he had been living with his siblings and godmother in the U.S. and hadn't had contact with either parent in years, according to the attorney general's complaint.

According to the complaint, the godmother attempted to send him to Mexico to live with family earlier this summer, but he ran away and ended up at a New Mexico hospital near the border. When he was ready to be discharged in June, the hospital refused to release him to his godmother because she was not the official guardian and instead contacted CYFD. He eventually was placed in foster care, the complaint reads.

Boy has a heart condition requiring daily medication

Torrez's office alleges that CYFD didn't conduct proper risk assessments of the child's mother and instructed a minor to cross an international border on foot without an adult. Documents also say the child has a heart condition that requires daily medication, but CYFD staff didn't make a sufficient attempt to ensure continued medical care following the reunification.

In a statement, CYFD said the boy had been living in an informal guardianship with a couple in New Mexico identified as godparents. The godparents petitioned the court in June to end their informal guardianship, leaving the boy without a legal guardian in the U.S. CYFD also said that the child’s siblings have since relocated with their godparents across the border and the siblings now live with their mother as well.

English mayors will be allowed to keep a share of the taxes collected in their area, Andy Burnham has said as part of his pledge to “take power out of Westminster and carry it into every postcode in the country”.

The prime minister’s plans to let mayors keep a slice of income tax and business rates come as part of his bid to incentivise regional leaders to promote economic growth in different parts of the UK.

However, the plan falls short of the suggestion that he would allow mayors to raise taxes themselves by devolving control over income tax, as it has been handed to the Scottish and Welsh parliaments.

Details of the reforms are expected to be announced in a white paper, published when chancellor John Healey presents his first Budget in the autumn.

But Mr Burnham, who was mayor of Greater Manchester for about nine years, said the policy would be designed so that “every local leader will have the power and resources to improve public transport, build homes and create jobs”.

The rate of income tax which billpayers face will not change as a direct result of the reforms, according to the government.

Andy Burnham continues his devolution drive ( PA )

Ministers will retain an equalisation system, so areas where less tax is collected continue to receive financial support.

Mr Burnham said: “I said we’d take power out of Westminster and carry it into every postcode in the country.

“Today, we make good on that promise.

“Under our plans, more of the taxes raised in a community will stay in that community. Soon, every local leader will have the power and resources to improve public transport, build homes and create jobs.

“I know what it’s like to be ignored by politicians in Westminster. I’m not going to make that same mistake now I’m PM.

“The whole of government will now pull together behind the people and places that desperately need our support.

“This is how we’ll bring back hope and bring power home to you.”

Several parts of England have a mayor, including Greater Manchester, the Liverpool City Region, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, and South Yorkshire, including Rotherham and Sheffield.

They have powers over issues such as transport, skills and infrastructure planning.

Mr Burnham hosted several of the local leaders at his inaugural No 10 North meeting in Manchester last Friday, when he told them: “What I’m trying to do here is make the UK one team where we’re all pulling behind you because your place is where growth happens or it doesn’t happen.”

Voters in parts of the country will elect mayors for the first time over the coming years, including in Greater Essex and Hampshire and the Solent.

Mr Healey said: “The people who best understand what skills employers want, what transport an area needs and where investment can make the biggest difference are those who live there.

“For the first time we’re giving mayors a share of income tax so communities directly benefit when their economy grows – passing power out of Westminster and driving growth in every postcode.

“This is the way we start to build new hope and advance the working people of this country.”

Housing, communities and local government secretary Angela Rayner said the announcement would put “an end to the begging-bowl culture of the past”, instead giving locally elected leaders “the tools they need to drive the change that communities have been crying out for”.

News.title: Mackenzie Shirilla is now arguing that her trial for killing two friends in crash violated her constitutional rights
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Mackenzie Shirilla, who is serving a life sentence for intentionally crashing a vehicle at high-speed into a brick wall and killing two passengers, is arguing in new court filings that her original trial and imprisonment violated her federal constitutional rights.

Shirilla, 22, filed a federal habeas corpus petition on Tuesday in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio. The filing asks a federal judge to set aside her murder conviction and grant a new trial.

In the petition, Shirilla’s new defense lawyers contend that her previous attorneys rendered ineffective assistance, that critical evidence was withheld from the court and that the case was improperly transferred from juvenile court to adult court, as reported by Fox 8 News.

Shirilla was convicted of murder in August 2023 following a bench trial in Cuyahoga County. Prosecutors established that in July 2022, Shirilla — who was 17 at the time — accelerated her vehicle to 100 mph down a dead-end street in a Strongsville business park before crashing into a brick wall.

The collision killed Shirilla’s boyfriend, Dominic Russo, and their friend, Davion Flanagan. A judge sentenced Shirilla to 15 years to life in prison.

open image in gallery Mackenzie Shirilla, the 22-year-old serving a life sentence for intentionally crashing a vehicle and killing two passengers, is arguing that her original trial and imprisonment violated her federal constitutional rights ( WKYC )

The new court filing outlines several key constitutional challenges surrounding her prosecution.

Her new attorneys argue there was insufficient evidence to establish probable cause that Shirilla acted “purposely or knowingly,” which is a legal requirement to transfer a minor to adult court, contending that excessive speed alone does not prove reckless intent. The petition also asserts that police improperly persuaded the coroner’s office to alter the official manner of death from accident to homicide without obtaining required court oversight.

Additionally, the filing claims Shirilla was denied her Sixth Amendment right to confront witnesses because a deputy medical examiner testified at trial instead of the pathologists who performed the autopsies.

Shirilla’s new defense team criticized her trial counsel for failing to object to that testimony and for omitting key evidence, including text messages suggesting Russo instigated a dispute shortly before the crash, proof that Shirilla had traveled to the area to collect a produce order and medical records indicating a pre-existing condition that could cause sudden loss of consciousness.

open image in gallery The wrecked car driven by Mackenzie Shirilla on the day she killed her boyfriend, Dominic Russo, and their friend Davion Flanagan, in July 2022 ( WKYC )

Shirilla’s previous direct appeals and post-conviction filings in state court were unsuccessful, including an application for relief that was dismissed after being submitted one day late. Her attorneys argue in the federal filing that state courts misinterpreted the statute governing those filing deadlines.

According to state records, Shirilla currently has two pending state-level filings — one requesting the Eighth District Court of Appeals to reopen her appeal based on trial counsel performance, and another asking the Ohio Supreme Court to reconsider her post-conviction relief petition.

The federal case has been assigned to U.S. District Judge John Adams. No hearing dates have been scheduled.

Shirilla remains incarcerated at the Ohio Reformatory for Women in Marysville. Prison records show she will first become eligible for a parole hearing in September 2037.

The Independent has contacted Marein & Bradley, the law firm representing Shirilla, for comment.

News.title: UK economy to flatline, warns Bank of England
News.content:
Britain’s economy is set to almost grind to a halt for the rest of the year, the Bank of England has warned.

Growth will drop to just 0.1pc per quarter, the Bank predicted, slowing sharply after a strong start to 2026.

Higher petrol prices and energy bills, a weak jobs market and rising mortgage costs are all draining confidence and spending power from the economy.

Inflation, which slowed to a 15-month low of 2.6pc in June, is also expected to rise again to 3.2pc later this year, the Bank warned.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s Governor, said inflation had “fallen faster than we’d expected” but warned that war in the Middle East would lead to a fresh spike.

He added that growth would “weaken slightly further in the near term as the effects of the conflict weigh further on demand”.

The Bank also predicted that unemployment will rise back above 5pc in the coming months, limiting workers’ ability to ask for higher wages to cope with rising living costs.

It presents a challenging backdrop for Andy Burnham and his Chancellor, John Healey, who have pledged to help voters struggling with the cost of living.

The forecasts came as policymakers led by Mr Bailey held interest rates at 3.75pc.

Although three members of the nine-strong Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted for higher rates, up from two at the previous meeting, the Governor dismissed suggestions the Bank is moving towards higher interest rates.

The public should “not… [think] the Bank of England is edging towards a hike,” Mr Bailey said.

“Frankly there is nothing I have said, or any of us have said, along those lines. We took a decision today to leave the Bank Rate unchanged and that is the relevant conclusion.”

Clare Lombardelli, a Deputy Governor, said voting to keep rates at 3.75pc “was not a close judgement”, calling the decision “pretty clear” given slowing inflation in the domestic economy.

Officials are monitoring the economy for any signs that increases in oil, gas and petrol prices caused by the war in Iran are creeping into higher costs and wages in the wider economy.

Mr Bailey said: “The possibility of repeated resumptions of conflict, combined with lower than usual European gas stock levels and a fall in global refining output, mean that risks to energy prices lie to the upside.”

He added: “Reassuringly, there are few signs so far that second-round effects are generating more broad-based inflationary pressures.”

Companies are struggling to pass higher costs on to their customers because of the economy’s weakness, he added.

Workers are typically securing only modest pay rises as the weak jobs market leaves them in a poor position to push for bigger salaries.

Mr Bailey stressed there are still major risks to the outlook given the war and promised to “monitor the situation carefully” and was “ready to adjust our stance”.

“It is our job to ensure that inflation gets back to the 2pc target and stays there, and that is what we will do,” he said.

Borrowing costs dropped in financial markets after the decision.

The Government’s two-year borrowing cost fell from 4.44pc to 4.34pc, the sharpest fall in a month.

The FTSE 250 index of mid-sized UK companies rose 0.8pc to a record high of 24,184.10.

Traders still believe the Bank will raise interest rates twice within a year.

However, Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said rate rises “remain more a threat than a reality”.

He said there was evidence of disinflation in the economy and interest rates could be “cut to 3pc in 2027”, adding: “That’s very different to market pricing for rates to be close to 4.5pc in 2027.”

News.title: Arsonists torch more Ebola clinics as misinformation spirals in DRC
News.content:
Two more Ebola treatment facilities have reportedly been burned down in recent days as health officials struggle to overcome violent public mistrust of medical teams.

At least a dozen facilities have now been attacked since Congo declared its Ebola outbreak amid fear, misinformation and suspicion of outside authorities.

The outbreak is the fastest growing on record and officials said the virus had now killed more than 1,500 people.

The official death toll from the outbreak centred on the north eastern Ituri province of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has risen by 500 in only a week.

Sources told the Telegraph the large jump in deaths was largely caused by a “data harmonisation exercise” between different regions, and the new deaths may not have all happened in the past week.

However, the daily confirmed toll has also continued to climb sharply with the latest government update reporting 50 people dying in the previous 24 hours.

Airfinity, a health analytics firm, said the outbreak “continues to outpace detection and the response” and there is a high chance of it spreading further inside DRC.

News.title: Race for vaccine against new Ebola strain gets $8.5m boost
News.content:
The “most promising” vaccine to tackle the Ebola strain behind an explosive outbreak in the Congo has been given an $8.5 million boost, as researchers race to develop an effective shot.

So far at least 3,360 people have been infected and 1,487 people have died in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), in an epidemic triggered by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola.

But unlike past outbreaks of the more common Zaire strain, there are currently no approved vaccines to tackle Bundibugyo.

On Thursday, the Coalition of Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (Cepi) revealed up to $8.5 million of funding for the only single-dose inoculation, which was described as the “most promising vaccine candidate” by the World Health Organization (WHO) in an analysis in May.

It is being developed by researchers at Hilleman Laboratories – a unique partnership between the pharmaceutical giant Merck and the British philanthropic powerhouse Wellcome, which is headquartered in Singapore.

The vaccine candidate is a Bundibugyo version of the Ervebo shot, which was created by Merck (MSD in Europe) and has already been approved for Ebola Zaire.

It uses a rVSV platform, where a modified version of VSV virus is used to train the immune system to react to target pathogens – in this instance, the Bundibugyo species replaces Zaire.

News.title: AMR chatbot could prevent drug-resistant infections in African hospitals
News.content:
A phone-based chatbot advising medics how to prescribe antibiotics has helped raise the quality of care in African hospitals and should stop bugs developing dangerous resistance, developers say.

Staff at four hospitals across Zambia and Kenya have been using two digital tools in a pilot project to try to address one of the world’s biggest health threats.

Anti-microbial resistance (AMR) is caused by germs evolving so that medicines such as antibiotics designed to kill them no longer work.

The menace is linked to nearly five million deaths each year and makes it increasingly difficult to treat infections. The annual death toll could nearly double in the next 25 years, according to some forecasts.

The rise in AMR is being significantly driven by the misuse and overuse of antimicrobials in human medicine and in agriculture.

Using antibiotics when they are not necessary, using the wrong ones, or getting the dosage wrong, all add to the chances that bugs will develop resistance.

With a shortage of new drugs in the development pipeline, one push to defeat AMR has been to get medics to stick to existing prescription, dosage and treatment advice.

The Antibiotic Stewardship Programme through Innovation, Research, and Education (ASPIRE) is trying to give them guidance using technology they already have in their pockets.

News.title: Tottenham new boys score in shoot-out win over Sydney FC
News.content:
Tonali was brought on as a half-time substitute, before Robertson took the captain’s armband from Archie Gray after he was introduced in the 65th minute.

The former Liverpool left-back delivered three dangerous crosses which went unconverted, something of a theme for a Spurs team who failed to make the most of long spells of dominance.

James Maddison and Mateus Fernandes were not in the match-day squad, while Pedro Porro, Marcos Senesi, Cristian Romero, Micky van de Ven and Jean Paul van Hecke have yet to join the group after the World Cup.

There was another impressive showing from 17-year-old prospect Luca Williams-Barnett, who is pushing for first-team opportunities this upcoming season.

Penalties followed the final whistle, with Spurs scoring all four of their spot kicks. Goalkeeper Martin Dubravka, signed on a free transfer this summer, saved one and Sydney FC’s Josh Lacey hit the post to give Spurs the spoils 4-2.

News.title: Recovery aids and building muscle: Welsh weightlifter Laura Hughes answers your questions
News.content:
Laura Hughes first discovered weightlifting while training at her local Crossfit gym, making the transition from amateur gym-goer to competitive lifting.

Now a member of the Welsh national weightlifting squad, the 33-year-old holds the Welsh record for both the snatch and the clean and jerk (the two official competitive lifts in weightlifting) and is currently third overall in the women’s Welsh rankings. Hughes won bronze at this year’s Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, following on from her third place at the 2018 Games in Australia.

We caught up with her for our Readers Ask series, where industry specialists answer questions from our Telegraph Recommended Reader Panel.

Who inspired you to get into weightlifting?

Olamilekan, South East

Originally, it was lots of different people, particularly general gym goers who were doing weightlifting at my gym. As I’ve grown as an athlete and become more competitive, I’ve had other inspirations.

Most notably, coming into [the Commonwealth Games], it has to be Gareth [Evans], our coach. Looking back at his performance in 2018 when he won his gold medal is so inspiring. [English lifter] Emily Godley was another competitor in 2018. She won the gold medal in my category and I just remember thinking that she was on fire that day.

What are the best exercises for you to build muscle mass?

Norman, Wales

We spend a lot of time doing our main lifts, so snatches, clean and jerks, but we also do lots of pulls and squats. I spend a lot of time doing accessory work to make sure that my body stays healthy, especially being an older athlete. I’ve put on quite a lot of muscle in this last block just from going heavier and pushing my limits with my main lifts.

What advice would you give to people who want to improve their strength?

David, North West

The most important thing is consistency. As long as you’re doing something, do it regularly, even if it’s twice a week. Don’t be afraid of picking up some dumbbells. If you’ve got somebody that can teach you how to lift weights properly, that’s going to be the best option. Do it safely, do it consistently, and don’t be afraid to try new strength exercises.

News.title: Explosive mpox outbreak causes 3,000 cases in Madagascar
News.content:
More than 3,000 cases of mpox have been recorded in Madagascar after the virus spread from a single port city to some of the country’s busiest coastal hubs.

A total of 3,022 cases and 20 deaths have been recorded as of this week, with cases in Toamasina and Taolagnaro accounting for more than half of all diagnoses.

The outbreak has been linked to Clade 1b mpox, a strain that emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare a global public health emergency at the time.

“The main factor driving the continued spread of the disease is human mobility, seeding new outbreaks in areas where the virus has not circulated before,” Professor Carlos Maluquer de Motes of the University of Surrey told The Telegraph.

“Under-reporting is likely, with the real number of cases exceeding what is being reported.”

News.title: Chelsea in 10-goal thriller as ‘Alonso ball’ brings risk and reward
News.content:
Chelsea’s first match under the management of Xabi Alonso was a 10-goal thriller in Australia, as the Premier League side eventually showed their class in a 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers.

Star striker João Pedro, who was controversially left out of Brazil’s World Cup squad, scored a nine-minute hat-trick after coming off the bench with half an hour of the friendly remaining.

Alonso had selected a youthful team for the first hour before bringing nine senior players, including João Pedro, into the side in the second half. According to Transfermarkt, Chelsea’s squad is valued at over £1.3bn while their opponents a more modest £5.86m.

Teenage signing Dastan Satpayev, midfielder Dario Essugo and winger Jamie Gittens also found the net for Chelsea, who were defensively vulnerable for long spells for the game.

Here are five things Telegraph Sport learned from Alonso’s first match.

João Pedro picks up where he left off

João Pedro scored 13 goals in the second half of last season and his impressive performances resulted in the 24-year-old being named Chelsea’s player of the campaign. It was something of a surprise, then, when he was left out of Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil squad this summer.

The good news for Chelsea is that João Pedro’s absence from the World Cup has given him plenty of time to recover ahead of the new campaign, and he looked thrillingly sharp in his second-half performance against Western Sydney Wanderers. The difference in class between João Pedro and Liam Delap, the man he replaced, was clear for all to see.

Two of the Brazilian’s three goals were classy, composed finishes — and he also created a goal for Gittens after surging past three defenders on the left wing. João Pedro looks like he means business.

Sports.title: Transfer news LIVE: Liverpool talks planned, Vinicius Jr Arsenal latest, Bruno Guimaraes admission
Sports.content:
Vinicius Junior has been linked with a sensational move to Arsenal this summer.

The latest transfer news from Arsenal, Manchester United, Liverpool and more as they look to improve their teams ahead of the Premier League season

Welcome to Mirror Football's transfer news live blog on Thursday, July 30th.

The summer transfer window will slam shut in just over a month's time with business strarting to ramp up in preparation for the new campaign. Morgan Rogers, Sandro Tonali and Elliot Anderson have all moved clubs is mega-money deals, in excess of the £100m mark, and that could be just the beginning.

Arsenal remain keen on signing Real Madrid star Vinicius Junior, whose future at Real Madrid is unclear heading into the final 12 months of his contract, and the Gunners are willing to move for the Brazilian if the opportunity arises.

Mikel Arteta's side are prepared to offer the 26-year-old star the biggest deal in the club's history, but also have their eye on improving other areas of the pitch. They remain keen on signing Newcastle United captain Bruno Guimaraes, and there is ample drama on that front with the Magpies' denying any talk of negotations between the two clubs.

Elsewhere, Liverpool are reportedly planning on holding talks with Paris-Saint Germain in an attempt to sign French international Bradley Barcola. Andoni Iraola's side are in the hunt for a successort for Mohamed Salah and have made the PSG star their number one transfer target.

Manchester United remain hopeful of adding another midfielder to their ranks ahead of their return to the Champions League, having already signed Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans. There's also the small matter of Marcus Rashford's future at the club needing resolved.

Follow all of the transfer news, rumours and updates below:

Sports.title: Ex-Newcastle owner Amanda Staveley in talks to buy West Ham stake
Sports.content:
Ex-Newcastle owner Amanda Staveley in talks to buy West Ham stake

Amanda Staveley and her husband, Mehrdad Ghodoussi, sold their stake in Newcastle United two years ago but have set their sights on a return to football with West Ham

View 2 Images A consortium led by Amanda Staveley has held talks over buying a stake in West Ham (Image: Nigel French/PA Wire)

A consortium led by Amanda Staveley, the former co-owner of Newcastle United, is said to be 'close' to acquiring a 25 per cent stake in West Ham.

‌



The Hammers were relegated from the Premier League last season and will now ply their trade in the Championship but that has not deterred interest from Staveley and her husband, Mehrdad Ghodoussi, in buying into the east London club following their departure from Newcastle two years ago.

‌



PCP Capital Partners, Staveley and Ghodoussi's firm, have held talks over purchasing the shares previously held by the late David Gold.

‌



The Times claim that a deal for Staveley's consortium to acquire the 25 per cent stake from Gold's daughter, Vanessa, is close following talks.

Chelsea, Sunderland and Nottingham Forest caught out as Premier League gambling ban bites READ MORE :

Arsenal close in on £80m Bruno Guimaraes transfer in major breakthrough for Mikel Arteta READ MORE :

Not only that, the report notes that if Staveley and Co are successful in their attempt to purchase a minority stake in the club then it could be followed by them presenting an offer for the shares owned by David Sullivan, which would give them majority control of the club.

Sullivan resigned as West Ham chairman last month in the wake of historic sexual allegations. A BBC Panorama investigation alleged that Mr Sullivan had preyed on women for sex. He has strenuously denied the allegations and said he will be launching legal action against the BBC.

‌



Staveley's consortium is said to be backed by investors from the United States and the Far East who had initially considered bidding for one of West Ham's bitter rivals, Tottenham.

However, the consortium has designs on transforming West Ham's fortunes following relegation and there are plans to invest heavily in the playing squad.

View 2 Images Staveley was a pivotal figure behind Newcastle's Saudi-backed takeover (Image: Getty Images)

‌



There are also ambitions to purchase the club's much maligned home ground, the London Stadium; talks have even already been held with officials connected to the London mayor’s office.

Thought Staveley's consortium hope to buy into the club, pre-emption rights means that West Ham's other major shareholder, Daniel Kretinsky, has first option to purchase the shares ahead of external parties.

He and Vanessa Gold had previously released a joint statement in June saying the Czech billionaire, who owns a 27 per cent stake in the club, had agreed a deal to purchase some of Gold's shares to increase his standing to "approximately 43 per cent".

Sports.title: UEFA have one problem in toppling Gianni Infantino from power at FIFA over World Cup plan
Sports.content:
UEFA have one problem in toppling Gianni Infantino from power at FIFA over World Cup plan

Gianni Infantino has seen his controversial plans backfire, with UEFA and CONCACAF rejecting the proposal, and now his future as FIFA president hangs in the balance

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino faces an uncertain future at FIFA after Aleksander Ceferin's UEFA challenged him (Image: Harry Murphy/UEFA via Getty Images)

Gianni Infantino's position as FIFA president is under threat after his plan to sell off the World Cup triggered a tremendous backlash - but a viable challenger to his throne is yet to emerge.

‌



European football's governing body UEFA met virtually on Thursday and, after a fiery meeting, fired out a powerful and damning statement which stated their willingness to boycott future FIFA tournaments.

‌



UEFA called Infantino's secretive behaviour around the proposal to invite third-party investment in tournaments "irresponsible and indefensible". And although it didn't name him, it accused Infantino of "a profound failure of leadership" and of seeing his first duty as "to maximise financial return".

‌



Infantino's attempts to effectively buy off FIFA members by offering $40m (£30m) if they back his plan have backfired spectacularly, with CONCACAF - North and Central America's governing body - following UEFA's lead later on Thursday. CONCACAF said it rejected the proposal, criticising the "lack of due process" at FIFA around the plans.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Gianni Infantino in trouble as new statement released after UEFA fury over World Cup plans READ MORE :

England and UEFA nations WILL BOYCOTT World Cup in protest over Gianni Infantino sale plan READ MORE :

UEFA and CONCACAF uniting in defiance of Infantino would appear to stop the plans dead in their tracks, while also throwing the Swiss bureaucrat's future as FIFA president into doubt.

‌



Just 13 days ago the Guardian reported that more than 200 of FIFA's 211 members had formally endorsed Infantino for re-election for a fourth term, having first taken control in 2016. He was set to run unchallenged and extend his reign at FIFA congress in March.

However, his barefaced attempts to sell off football in pursuit of enrichment, which appeared designed to buy support, may have torpedoed his efforts.

The only thing currently missing is a credible challenger. Paris Saint-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi had garnered some support, but a source has said he has "absolutely no ambition, no intention, nor any interest in this role at FIFA".

‌



View 3 Images Nasser al-Khelaifi reportedly doesn't want to challenge Gianni Infantino (Image: LOU BENOIST/AFP via Getty Images)

He leads the European Football Clubs umbrella group, so already holds plenty of power of his own, having helped steady the ship after the failed European Super League coup in 2021.

UEFA chief Aleksander Ceferin has emerged as the biggest thorn in Infantino's side, having previously led the fightback against his proposal to stage the World Cup every two years. But the Slovenian reportedly also lacks the desire to mount a leadership challenge, unlike Infantino doesn't crave the limelight, and is happy at UEFA.

‌



Legia Warsaw president Dariusz Mioduski has been backed by the Belgian, Spanish, Norwegian, German and Swedish associations, according to a report from talkSPORT earlier this month. Meanwhile, CONCACAF president Victor Montagliani and Confederation of African Football (CAF) Patrice Motsepe may lack the desire to run against Infantino.

There is time for things to change, however with contenders given until November 18 to attract supporters and put forward their names.

View 3 Images Aleksander Ceferin is leading the backlash against Gianni Infantino (Image: Alexander Hassenstein, Getty Images)

‌



The fiery nature of UEFA's statement suggests they could be seeking regime change at FIFA. "We unanimously and unequivocally reject FIFA’s proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other FIFA competitions to private investors," it reads.

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football’s greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.

"It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game. This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA’s duty as the custodian of world football."

Article continues below

Time will tell if that "failure of leadership" leads to Infantino's downfall.
