Sports.title: Q&A: Why are UEFA boycotting FIFA tournaments and can it stop Infantino?
Sports.content:
UEFA announced on Thursday that it will boycott FIFA tournaments until plans from president Gianni Infantino to sell off stakes in the World Cup are ended.

It came after an emergency meeting of the confederation's 55 members, and could have seismic implications for world football and Infantino's plans.

Here, Sky Sports News' chief correspondent Kaveh Solhekol answers the immediate questions - and what the future could hold...

What happened at the UEFA meeting?

The emergency virtual meeting of UEFA's members lasted two hours. Everyone at the meeting spoke out against Infantino's sell-off plan, including FA chair and FIFA vice president Debbie Hewitt and FA chief executive Mark Bullingham.

All 55 associations voted for the UEFA action, which would include those from England, Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.

A number of them have released individual statements affirming the action, including the English FA, who said: "We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view. We oppose FIFA's plans. The FIFA World Cup belongs to football and always will."

In a further blow to Infantino, CONCACAF also rejected the idea of the proposals. They too convened a meeting of their 41 member associations, with a statement expressing 'deep concerns' surrounding 'the absence of any review or approval by the relevant FIFA governance bodies'.

It went on to include a series of action points in relation to Infantino's plans - but did not mention any plans of a boycott, as UEFA decided to. It is the first time a confederation has done so for a FIFA tournament.

Upcoming FIFA Tournaments UEFA threatening to boycott: FIFA Under 20 Women’s World Cup (Poland) - Sep 2026

FIFA Under 17 Women’s World Cup (Morocco) - Oct 2026

FIFA Under 17 World Cup (Qatar) - Nov/Dec 2026

FIFA Women’s Champions Cup (Miami) - Jan 2027

FIFA Women’s World Cup (Brazil) - Jun/Jul 2027

Why is UEFA doing this?

This is UEFA saying to Infantino: 'enough is enough. We're not going to let you do this. And if you go ahead and do this, even if you think you have the votes to proceed with these controversial proposals, we will not play in any of your future tournaments'.

The next big tournament is the Women's World Cup next summer in Brazil, so as things stand, no European countries would play in that tournament.

The next World Cup 2030 is Spain, Portugal and Morocco - European countries would not play in that tournament.

Image: UEFA - headed by Aleksander Ceferin - are boycotting FIFA tournaments after president Gianni Infantino plans to seek private investment

This is UEFA showing that they are united and totally and utterly oppose Infantino's proposal to sell off a stake in the World Cup.

If this develops into a serious split between UEFA and FIFA - which I don't think it will - you could also have the potential on the horizon where UEFA think 'we already do a great job of running the Champions League, we do a great job of running the Euros, why don't we set up our own version of the World Cup, and we can invite Argentina, Brazil, the best sides in Africa, the best sides in Asia, to play in that as well'.

Could this put a stop to Infantino's plans?

It would mean the end of the proposals because if I'm an investor looking at buying a 20 per cent stake in FIFA's tournaments, why would I invest in tournaments that don't have European countries?

Look at the World Cup that we've just had. Six of the eight quarter-finalists were from Europe. Three of the semi-finalists were from Europe. The winners were from Europe.

Why would anybody invest in Infantino's madcap scheme when it wouldn't have teams like Spain, France, England, Italy or Germany? The proposal is dead in the water.

Image: UEFA member Spain won the World Cup, with three of the final four teams being from Europe

We don't know what Infantino is going to do next, because he's sitting in his ivory tower in Zurich being interviewed by people he employs, trying to sell this project.

But if I was an investor reading this news about how UEFA have responded, I would be thinking 'maybe I need to invest in something else, because Gianni hasn't been able to deliver what he promised he was going to deliver'.

What happens next?

First things first - Infantino will have some serious explaining to do.

Prospective investors and bankers will be calling him to find out why he has not been able to deliver Europe. FIFA Council members, heads of confederations and federations will be asking why he plotted to sell off a stake in the World Cup behind their backs.

In terms of the boycott, the first test for UEFA and the FA senior teams will come in October, during the Women's World Cup qualifier play-offs.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gary Neville, Andy Burnham, the FA and more react to Gianni Infantino's World Cup sale plan

England face Greece during the October international break, and there will be 15 other matches taking place. Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Republic of Ireland are also scheduled to take part in the first round of the play-offs.

The two-legged ties will take place on October 9 and 13, with the winners from each match going into round two, which take place in November and December.

Sarina Wiegman and her staff are preparing for their two-legged tie against Greece as normal, Sky Sports News understands.

It's currently the same for the Women's U20 World Cup; however, the timing couldn't be much worse for European nations.

The tournament is due to start on September 5 in Poland and concludes on September 27. Poland, England, France, Italy, Portugal and Spain are the European nations taking part.

Where do the other confederations stand?

There are six confederations in world football. What we know is that UEFA are absolutely not in favour of this, and will do whatever it takes to stop it.

We know CONCACAF, who run football in North and Central America, seem to be against it as well. They released a statement on Wednesday saying 'we're deeply concerned, we're disappointed that this was all done in secret'. This was followed up with more condemnation after Thursday's meeting.

Image: The USA was one of the recent co-hosts of the World Cup and play under CONCACAF

We've had the Asian Football Confederation - who are normally rock solidly behind Infantino - come out and say 'we're deeply concerned as well. Why weren't we consulted?'

So Infantino is losing support from confederations, but I still think there are plenty of football associations around the world - there's 211 of them - who will say 'Infantino has quadrupled the amount of money we get from FIFA, and he's now coming along and saying in January we can have an extra $20m (£14.9m) and going forward we can have triple as much money as we're getting'.

But it doesn't matter if they sign up to it or not, because without UEFA and European countries, you cannot have a proper World Cup.

'Infantino has made himself more unpopular than Blatter'

What I don't understand about Infantino is: why does he make himself such a controversial figure?

He's already the most powerful person in world football. He's the president of FIFA; they just had a great World Cup - according to them it was the greatest World Cup ever - so he should be at the height of his powers and be popular.

Instead, he's made himself even more unpopular than Sepp Blatter. There are people in the world of football who now pine for the days when Blatter was the FIFA president.

What is he [Infantino] doing? Why is he getting into bed with Donald Trump and his family, why is he trying to sell stakes in the World Cup, why not just do your day job and run world football properly, instead of being such a controversial figure, thinking that you're a president, an oligarch, a statesman, when at the end of the day, all you are is a custodian of world football.

Sports.title: Doyle: Raider can blitz King George rivals
Sports.content:
Sky Sports Racing’s ambassador Hollie Doyle previews the best of the action on Day Four of the Goodwood Festival with the Group Two King George Qatar Stakes headlining the action.

Fast five the key to King George favourite

Five furlongs down the hill is tailor-made for Karl Burke's lightning-fast Night Raider who can bounce back from his defeat at Royal Ascot in Friday's feature at The Goodwood Festival, the King George Qatar Stakes (3.35).

Ascot was just too stiff a test for him, but the Temple Stakes winner can show his class from a decent attacking draw in stall 13, despite having to concede a three-pound penalty for that Group Two blitz at Haydock.

Aspect Island, who was a close second in Listed company at York recently, looks a Group race winner in the making and can give another good account of himself for James Owen and Billy Loughnane. Third in the Breeders' Cup Juvenile Turf Sprint last autumn, he is another who should enjoy this pure speed test.

New York can become a headline act

Talk Of New York can produce a headline performance for William Buick in the Group Three HKJC World Pool Thoroughbred Stakes (2.25) on Friday.

Godolphin's son of Wootton Bassett caught my eye in the Heron Stakes at Sandown before running a big figure in the St James's Palace Stakes at the Royal Meeting, despite refusing to settle. Indeed, he was less than two lengths behind Wednesday's brilliant Sussex Stakes winner Bow Echo.

Saber Strike has 9lbs to find with Charlie Appleby's colt on these terms but has always been well-regarded by William Haggas and the team. His third in the Group Three Criterion at York reads well and the combination of first-time blinkers and this idiosyncratic track should keep him interested.

Golden chance for Spencer in feature Handicap

The Coral Golden Mile (3.00) on Friday promises to be quite a spectacle with 20 runners thundering down the hill, including David Menuisier's Tribal Chief.

Everything points to a big run from the five-year-old with Jamie Spencer doing the steering. Jamie is a master on hold-up horses like him. He caught my eye in defeat in big handicaps at Ascot and Sandown and looks ready to enjoy his day in the sun at a track at which he has already won.

I am also hoping my husband Tom (Marquand's) mount Scoville can build on an encouraging run in the Royal Hunt Cup - his first following a wind operation. He was up there to be shot at at Ascot but may have to be ridden differently from his wide draw this time.

Believe in King stayer in Friday marathon

I am a big fan of Alan King's stayer Believitanducan who can extend his winning sequence to four this year in the marathon Coral Goodwood Handicap (1.50) on Friday.

The improving five-year-old can make light work of a five-pound rise for his win in the Northumberland Vase at Newcastle last month. He stays all day so won't mind the extra half mile and is another plum ride for William Buick.

Valiancy blotted his copybook in the Copper Horse at Royal Ascot behind Alan King's Daiquiri Bay but looked hugely progressive before that and shouldn't be written off too soon. He is a worthy favourite but must give Believitanducan all of 10lbs.

At a bigger price, keep an eye on Irish raider Alphonse Le Grande who wasn't far behind my selection at Gosforth Park and races off the same mark he won off in that controversial Cesarewitch two years ago. I won the Vase on him at Newcastle in 2024 and know what a tough, thorough stayer he is on his day.

Step up in trip ideal for Hannon sprinter

Jaijai looks well drawn and well weighted in the six-furlong Hawes and Curtis Nursery Handicap (4.45) on Friday. Richard Hannon's course winner probably found five-furlongs at Windsor too easy a test last time but can prove a tougher proposition back up in trip.

Innichen is a typically tough Jack Channon handicapper who is another to keep an eye on. He is up eight-pounds in a hotter race than the one he won at Nottingham, but Tom (Marquand) knows him well and it wouldn't surprise me to see him continue that upward curve despite a questionable draw.

I'll be back on Saturday with my thoughts on the final day of a memorable Qatar Goodwood Festival, including the Stewards' Cup.

Sports.title: Uefa agrees to boycott Fifa competitions if World Cup sell-off plans proceed
Sports.content:
European countries have agreed to boycott all Fifa competitions if Gianni Infantino pushes forward with his proposals to sell chunks of the World Cup to US-based private investment.

In an extraordinary development all 55 Uefa members resolved not to participate in future World Cups or other Fifa-run events, saying in a statement that they “unanimously and unequivocally reject” the proposals. An emergency meeting that lasted just short of two hours ended with a united front despite earlier fears that smaller countries, attracted by the money on offer through Infantino’s scheme, would be swayed in favour.

European FAs are expected to write to Fifa this week with a formal notification of their threat to boycott future tournaments unless the planned World Cup sell-off is withdrawn.

It means Infantino faces an uphill battle to push his plan forward. Countries had been given until 19 September to sign up but there will now be significant pressure to drastically revise his scheme or withdraw it completely. While the majority of European FAs had submitted letters of support in favour of his re-election next March, such a decisive line in the sand from Uefa weakens his position dramatically.

Uefa’s statement confirmed the decision. “As a result of today’s discussion, no Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership,” it read.

Thursday’s meeting was introduced by the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, with executive committee members and Uefa’s Fifa council representatives also addressing delegates. Those early speeches are understood to have set the tone, with around 20 further FA heads taking the floor and multiple sources describing an atmosphere of “unity”. Among those to offer their view was Debbie Hewitt, the president of the FA, who one attendee said gave a “very tough” exposition in favour of a boycott.

That was backed up in a statement by an FA spokesperson that read: “We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view. We oppose Fifa’s plans – the Fifa World Cup belongs to football and always will.”

Along the lines spelled out by Uefa, at senior level the proposed boycott would begin with next year’s Women’s World Cup, while the first age-group Fifa tournament to be boycotted is likely to be the Under-20 Women’s World Cup. It is due to take place in Poland from 5 September with six of the 24 competitors, including England, due to represent Uefa countries.

England’s women’s team also have a two-legged World Cup qualifying playoff tie against Greece in October, which would be a major test of the FA’s resolve if Fifa refuse to back down.

The European governing body invited other confederations to follow their lead. Uefa are understood to be confident that a number of Asian countries, in particular, are similarly minded. Infantino’s strongholds traditionally lie outside Europe and a collapse in support elsewhere could have severe consequences for the Fifa president.

“National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football’s greatest competitions or bear the consequences,” Uefa said. “This is not a ‘democratic decision’, but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.”

Sources within European football believe Uefa’s decision increases the chances of a Europe-backed candidate running against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, which he had been expected to sail through without opposition.

The North, Central American and Caribbean confederation, Concacaf, also unanimously rejected Fifa’s proposal after an emergency meeting chaired by the president, Victor Montagliani, who is seen as a potential successor to Infantino, but stopped short of following Uefa’s lead by announcing a boycott.

Despite this, it is understood that the majority of Concacaf’s 41 members are losing confidence in Infantino’s leadership of Fifa, raising the possibility that his own position could be in serious doubt for the first time since he took office in 2016.

A number of European national associations are understood to have held talks with their respective governments over the matter, many of whom have backed a boycott in private.

The new UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, was the first politician to criticise Fifa’s plan on Tuesday evening, writing on X that the World Cup “was never anyone’s to sell”.

“This is a principled decision that we strongly support. Football belongs to the fans, not billionaire investors. Enough is enough. It’s time to take a stand to protect our game.”

Sports.title: Not so black and white: how Eddie Howe lost control at Newcastle in one summer | Louise Taylor
Sports.content:
Last September, David Hopkinson, just installed as Newcastle’s chief executive, perched on a stool at a downstairs corner table in Shearer’s Bar at St James’ Park and between sips of zero alcohol lager, likened Eddie Howe to Bruce Springsteen. According to Hopkinson, Newcastle’s manager was “the Boss” and “the talent”. He conjured up an imaginary scene involving Springsteen asking for M&M’s before a concert and being duly supplied with a dressing room overflowing with the brightly coloured confectionery. The same principle, he said, would apply to “Eddie”, who would e furnished with “whatever he wants”.

Six months later, things had changed. In late March, Hopkinson sat around a heavy wooden table in a St James’ Park boardroom and, between sips of coffee, said he did not “have a stance on the manager’s future”. What he could tell assembled reporters was that a recent home defeat by Sunderland “hurt”. It “resonated” and was being taken “seriously”. Given that Newcastle had just lost a Champions League tie 8-3 to Barcelona on aggregate and were en route to finishing 12th in the Premier League, Howe admitted to “sleepless nights” before a summit with the club’s majority Saudi Arabian ownership at Matfen Hall hotel in Northumberland the following month.

The 48-year-old, who only a year earlier had choreographed Newcastle’s Carabao Cup triumph, securing their first domestic trophy since 1955, would win that particular battle. Thanks to a convincing, typically articulate presentation detailing his future tactical plans, Howe was allowed by the visitors from Riyadh to remain in the job he had occupied since November 2021. Even then, however, he suspected he was losing a war that had begun long before Hopkinson’s installation.

It was an often subliminal conflict about power and control that started when Amanda Staveley, the club’s former co-owner, was ousted in the summer of 2024. Howe had been very much Staveley’s appointment and, given that she was then responsible for running the club on a daily basis, he was permitted considerable say in buying and selling players.

During his time in charge of Bournemouth, Howe exerted significant control over all spheres of the organisation, his unwillingness to delegate even extending to proof reading the match programme. In an era when sporting directors rather than managers invariably call the ultimate shots in the Premier League Howe, unusually, enjoyed similar authority at Newcastle. With Andy Howe, his nephew, occupying a senior recruitment role and invitations to visit the team’s training ground issued at Eddie’s discretion, Howe’s word was law.

That regimen initially served him well. When Paul Mitchell, who succeeded Dan Ashworth as sporting director, suggested alterations to transfer policy and playing style, Howe made his displeasure plain. Within a year Mitchell left. It was June 2025 and with the League Cup won three months earlier the manager had never seemed more secure. Yet that exit of a second sporting director arguably prefaced Howe’s ownfall.

View image in fullscreen Alexander Isak celebrates scoring the second goal in the Carabao Cup final against Liverpool at Wembley in March 2025. Three months later he asked to leave the club. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters

Admittedly, it was not his fault Alexander Isak forced a £125m move to Liverpool last summer, but Howe was heavily involved in Newcastle signing £240m of largely underachieving talent in a forlorn attempt to compensate for the Sweden striker’s defection. If neither the £69m Nick Woltemade nor the £55m Yoane Wissa were suitable replacements for Isak, Jacob Ramsey and Anthony Elanga often underwhelmed. Only the central defender Malick Thiaw impressed.

Moreover, it had not gone unnoticed in Riyadh that Howe’s unwillingness to sell players exacerbated the ownership’s financial problems at a time when Newcastle’s comparatively low commercial revenues made it a struggle to remain within football’s spending rules. In May, the club entered a Uefa settlement agreement after breaching European investment rules last season. It dictates they must balance the books very carefully for the next three years and explains why their latest sporting director, Ross Wilson, sold Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali to Barcelona and Tottenham respectively this summer. Howe was reluctant to lose the pair and became dismayed at the prospect of seeing another key individual in Bruno Guimarães depart for Arsenal.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Wilson, who arrived from Nottingham Forest in October, has presided over a marked policy pivot involving signing young players possessing high resale potential. So far this close season Newcastle have acquired four promising yet inexperienced newcomers aged 20 or under in Ewen Jaouen, Bazoumana Touré, Aladji Bamba and Sean Steur. Hopkinson has boasted that Newcastle are aiming to be one “of the best clubs in the world” by 2030 but Howe is not the only one to have detected a disconnect between such lofty expectations and a bold experiment with youth that could easily go badly wrong. Well aware he had remained at Bournemouth a season too long before being sacked in 2020, it seems Howe decided it would be better to jump rather than be pushed, and leave on amicable terms.

In five years on Tyneside, he improved some players almost beyond recognition – Joelinton and Jacob Murphy in particular – and choreographed an often thrilling brand of football during two Champions League campaigns. At their high tempo, hard-pressing best, Newcastle were gloriously entertaining, but Howe’s team became frequently poor in possession and adept at forfeiting leads. Pace and athleticism seemed prioritised ahead of vision and incision. Like their workaholic manager, Newcastle increasingly resembled a team that had forgotten how to relax and read the game’s nuances.

Howe is gifted enough, intelligent enough and young enough to reach the highest echelons of coaching but first he needs to rest, reassess and, perhaps, remember why he once fell in love with Arsenal’s football during their Cesc Fàbregas-inspired tiki-taka phase. The irony of his Newcastle tenure is that a manager obsessed with off-field control came undone partly by its absence on the pitch.

It is a paradox Howe may reflect on as he sits at his treasured piano and creates some new mood music of his own.

Sports.title: Maxence Lacroix joins ‘beautiful club’ Chelsea as John Stones seals Inter deal
Sports.content:
Maxence Lacroix has joined Chelsea from Crystal Palace to become the club’s fifth signing of the summer. The France international, who won the FA Cup and Conference League with Palace, was the Blues’ main defensive target of the window.

Lacroix, 26, signs a six-year deal with Xabi Alonso’s side. “I am really happy to be part of this beautiful club,” said Lacroix, who played three times for France at the World Cup, including in their 6-4 bronze medal match defeat by England.

“Everyone knows the legend of Chelsea, its tradition of winning, and to be a part of that is a proud moment. I think it’s the best move for me because it’s the best club in the world. When I spoke with the manager, I saw that we have the same direction and desire for this club.

“We want to win. When you see the quality of the players here, everything we have around the club, it’s something that we can achieve. The ambition is to lift trophies, and I can’t wait to contribute.”

Chelsea had been looking to add experience to their back line having missed out on Rennes’ Jérémy Jacquet in January, with the player opting to join Liverpool. Levi Colwill, who is considered to be a key part of the club’s long-term plans, missed almost all of last season with an anterior cruciate ligament injury, with Wesley Fofana and Trevoh Chalobah forming the central-defensive partnership for much of the campaign.

After a dismal season that saw the club finish 10th, the club’s hierarchy has acknowledged a change in recruitment policy is needed, with a refocusing away from young, inexperienced players towards ones that can help the team compete for the title.

Lacroix, who made 55 appearances last season for Palace, has been one of the league’s most consistent defenders since moving to Selhurst Park from Wolfsburg in 2024.

The Blues confirmed the club-record arrival of Aston Villa forward Morgan Rogers last week, and have also added Atalanta defender Marco Palestra, striker Emmanuel Emegha from Strasbourg and Sporting Lisbon’s Geovany Quenda.

Chelsea also look set to sign Brighton’s Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson after his contract with Brentford was terminated.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

John Stones has joined Inter on a two-year contract, the Serie A club have announced.

The England centre-back was a free agent after leaving Manchester City and had attracted interest from clubs across Europe.

The 32-year-old ended his 10-year stay at City in June. He made 295 appearances for the club after joining from Everton for £47.5m in 2016 and won six Premier League titles, three FA Cups and a Champions League title.

Sports.title: Premier League agrees proposal to share an extra £1.5bn with EFL clubs
Sports.content:
The Premier League has agreed on a proposal to reset financial distribution within English football’s top four divisions, one that would lead to an extra £1.5bn being shared across the pyramid over the next decade.

Clubs voted unanimously to support the so-called “new deal for football” at a meeting on Thursday, after discussions with the EFL. The offer will now be presented to the EFL’s board for consideration.

According to details originally published by Sky News, the Premier League’s offer would run for 10 years and result in an additional £1.5bn being shared with EFL clubs on top of the £1.6bn currently distributed to clubs and communities every three years. Some of the money would be put into discrete funds – a “lifeboat” fund for clubs in immediate crisis and one that is directed exclusively at infrastructure.

To cover the extra costs, Premier League clubs have reportedly agreed to raise the transfer levy applied to all top-flight deals from 4% to 6%. The Guardian reported this week that Manchester City were initially opposed to increasing the levy.

The Premier League said in a statement that its clubs had “unanimously voted to approve a funded proposal for a new strategic partnership with the EFL”. It said it would now “look forward to continuing discussions with the EFL on progressing this proposal” and remain “committed to finding a football-led solution”.

The EFL has yet to officially receive the offer but acknowledged “constructive” discussions with the Premier League and said its board would “review the full detail of the proposal, including its potential benefits, implications and alignment with the long-term interests of our 72 clubs, ahead of further dialogue with the Premier League”.

This is the first time that Premier League clubs have officially agreed a proposal that could be put to the EFL since they were first asked to give more money to the rest of the pyramid five years ago. The Covid pandemic had revealed the precarious nature of finances at many EFL clubs and in 2022 the then sports minister Nigel Huddleston said the British public were already “out of patience” over a failure to reach an improved settlement.

The belief that the Premier League’s riches could be shared more effectively across the game helped lead in part to the creation of the Independent Football Regulator, which came into being last year. The regulator has played no direct part in the negotiations, but has a “backstop” power to force a settlement if none is agreed.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

While there is cautious optimism that a deal can now finally be agreed, it is not a guarantee that the EFL will accept the Premier League’s offer, with sources suggesting it sees the proposal as being very similar to one that was mooted in 2023 but ultimately never approved by Premier League clubs. Both sides say they remain committed to ongoing dialogue.

Sports.title: FA raises minimum ban for racism and other forms of discrimination to 10 matches
Sports.content:
The FA is to increase the minimum punishment for discriminatory behaviour to 10 matches, in an attempt to counteract behaviour it says “continues to be a challenge across the game”.

The changes will come into force at the start of the new season and will apply to players and other football participants who are found guilty of an “aggravated breach” of the FA’s disciplinary rules on improper conduct, effectively actions that included discriminatory behaviour against any protected characteristics. Currently the minimum suspension for such a breach is six matches.

Across the 2025-26 season 10 individuals were found guilty of aggravated breaches, with their punishments, decided by independent Regulatory Commissions, ranging from six to nine matches. Under the new rules a punishment of fewer than 10 matches will only be allowed if sufficient mitigating factors have been presented, and the individual themselves has pleaded guilty to the charge.

Among the cases heard involved the Preston’s Milutin Osmajic, in which the Montenegrin was found to have made racist remarks to the Burnley player Hannibal Mejbri during a Championship match. Osmajic, who denied making the remarks, was served with a nine-match ban and given a minimum fine of £20,000. There has been growing concern that the behaviour of players in the professional game has trickled down the pyramid, creating greater problems in the grassroots game.

“We are committed to delivering a game free from discrimination. While significant progress has been made in recent years, discriminatory conduct continues to be a challenge across the game,” the FA said in a statement. “Enhanced measures are necessary to tackle this abhorrent conduct, and our updated sanction guidelines will now require regulatory commissions to impose a standard suspension of at least 10 matches in these circumstances.”

The new rules do afford commissions some flexibility. Cases that involve aggravated breaches “in writing only or via any communication device” – ie comments made online – could receive a punishment as low as three matches in the event of mitigating factors being accepted. If, however, an individual found to have breached the rules then commits a second offence, bans of over a year could be applied.

Sports.title: Scottish Premiership returns with McInnes adding new twist to Old Firm rivalry
Sports.content:
Only residents of cloud cuckoo land can hold the firm belief that Scottish football will emerge promptly from a summer of discontent. The onset of a new domestic season, ordinarily a cause for excitement, instead gives reason to ponder the grim realities of what came before.

That it is unsurprising there has been no detailed explanation or plan from the Scottish Football Association following a lamentable World Cup does not prevent the scenario from being so deflating.

Mike Mulraney, the president, was last seen peeking out from the crowd behind Gianni Infantino and the US president at Trump Tower. Ian Maxwell, the Scottish FA’s chief executive, bemoaned “hysterical commentary” around his country’s World Cup performance during a brief media appearance after Steve Clarke had resigned. These executives had all but spurted with laughter when it was suggested handing Clarke a four-year contract immediately before Scotland set sail for the United States was perhaps a needless dalliance with risk.

Perhaps Mulraney and Maxwell are too engrossed in the sourcing of Clarke’s replacement to speak out on the overall state of the national sport. It is only fair to give them the opportunity to appoint a coach who can oversee much-needed transition in a geriatric Scotland squad.

The nation’s leading clubs have been moot on a big picture they wilfully ignore but that was exposed at a World Cup. The problem is that lingering and legitimate anger over Scotland’s showing on the biggest stage – despite all rationale behind it – mirrors so much broader sentiment as the Premiership returns. This has scope to be a troublesome, toxic campaign.

Celtic’s supporters remain irate at the custodians of their club, whom they perceive as complacent and out of touch. In Derek McInnes, Rangers have a new manager who is deeply unpopular on the other side of the city. Nobody should underestimate the lingering resentment that exists among followers of Hearts over the way the campaign of 2025-26 concluded.

The most reprehensible element of that arrived on 11 June, when the Scottish Professional Football League published the outcome of a disciplinary process into the pitch invasion that forced the ending of Celtic’s title-clinching clash against the Edinburgh club.

View image in fullscreen Celtic fans run on to the pitch after their team went 3-1 up against Hearts in the title-deciding game. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Snuggled in alongside wrist tickles for Hamilton Academical, Inverness and Stenhousemuir was a meagre fine for Celtic and a suspended, paltry ticket reduction. Rangers fans, who need little encouragement to rail against officialdom, were subdued until McInnes was slapped with a touchline ban for comments made against a refereeing decision.

Rangers have criticised elements of an independent report into the chaos which followed their March Scottish Cup loss to Celtic. Motherwell are speaking with lawyers due to objection to a Scottish FA fine for a video posted on social media.

A 2-0 European qualifying first-leg defeat in Kosovo last week was rightly sufficient to send Hibs fanatics into the internet’s version of orbit. Such results stopped being a shock long ago.

Certain clubs do actually have reasons to be cheerful. Celtic’s signing of Kasper Høgh for a club record fee not only demonstrated the kind of fiscal muscle-flexing that supporters wish happened more often but provided the most intriguing transfer arrival of the close season. Scepticism exists over the ability of players to perform outside the perennially successful environment of Bodø/Glimt.

Without such doubts and at a fee which even many Championship clubs would think little of, Høgh would have moved long ago. The 25-year-old, though, has a physical profile and direct style that should succeed in Scotland.

Celtic’s challenge is to replace existing first-team performers – Arne Engels and Alistair Johnston the prime examples – should irresistible bids arrive without posting the kind of net profit that makes balance sheets look more important than trophies. Fans have rightly welcomed the Høgh signing but need more.

Rangers, in contrast to their oldest foes, have burned through extraordinary amounts of cash in recent years while generally watching others lift trophies. This has fuelled rage in and reputational damage from the stands, which an American ownership has curiously opted not to challenge.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

In McInnes, Rangers – who kick off the season at Dundee United on Friday – have a manager whose knowledge of club and culture looks better placed than most before him in recent years to lay gloves on Celtic. Vanja Dragojevic looks a smart midfield signing from Partizan Belgrade. Rangers need attacking spark yet it should be no surprise that McInnes’s first act was to implement a stronger core. He lacks nothing in motivation or work ethic in the job he has always craved. This version of Rangers should be much improved. Yet on the simple basis of course and distance specialism, Celtic remain the title favourites.

View image in fullscreen Motherwell’s recent success offers a template for other top-flight clubs to follow. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Nobody linked to Hearts should have been expected by now to fully process the circumstances in which they came within minutes of a first title win in 66 years, only for that dream to be snatched away. McInnes’s departure for Rangers, the completely new style implemented by Wouter Vrancken and a palpable raising of expectations all contribute to a period of upheaval.

Hearts’ tilt at glory came earlier than anyone could anticipate. The club remains on the minds of people who previously had no interest in the Scottish game. A comprehensive Champions League qualifying defeat by Sturm Graz showed the scale of work Vrancken has ahead of him. Patience, however, would be wise.

Motherwell’s work with and post the management of Jens Berthel Askou proved those below the Premiership’s biggest fish needn’t only cling on for dear life. The football was superb, the attendance figures boosted and a broader market was impressed. Motherwell’s sales of Elijah Just and Elliot Watt for multimillion pound fees completely justify a club model that thinks outside the box.

St Mirren have clear aspirations of introducing more young players and a more alluring brand of football. Kilmarnock displayed that at the end of last season under Neil McCann. Aberdeen will surely be a stronger force this time under Stephen Robinson.

Only one artificial pitch remains in Scotland’s top flight, which provides cause for celebration.

Football remains a Scottish obsession. It is also undeniably a sick patient. The dawning of a fresh season should appeal only if there is a glimpse of fresh thinking.

Sports.title: Fifa’s sales pitch revealed: more tournaments, more debt … but no mention of women’s game
Sports.content:
Fifa’s sales pitch to persuade members to approve the sale of the World Cup’s commercial rights clearly states that its plans for financial growth will be achieved by staging more tournaments, having higher ticket prices and debt financing.

A 25-page sales deck titled “Fifa Forward Enterprise Member Materials”, that has been seen by the Guardian, makes the case for the creation of a new company to run Fifa’s commercial operations, 20% of which would be sold to Joshua Kushner, a US investor who is the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

The prospectus has been produced by JP Morgan, the US bank that was also behind the failed European Super League breakaway five years ago.

In addition to the previously reported $20m (£15m) sign-up payment Fifa has offered to all 211 member associations, which could be made available as soon as January, the document projects that the four-year Fifa Forward payments would increase to $24m for each member by the 2035-39 cycle.

JP Morgan makes clear in the sales deck that such growth will come from “a growing tournament portfolio”, “third party sources of capital and debt financing”, and prioritising “high yield” partnerships and events.

There is also a reference to more than doubling the number of global tournaments held each year, from 200 to 450, which if followed through would put a huge strain on player workload.

Staging the World Cup more frequently would be the most obvious way of raising revenue, with Gianni Infantino having previously proposed making it a biennial tournament five years ago.

The bank also raises the prospect of TV coverage of the biggest events such as the World Cup being sold to subscription channels or streamers, by referring to a lan to “expand and optimize media rights monetization”.

JP Morgan claims that Fifa is “undermonetized” but significantly makes comparisons with other sports leagues with the revenue figures based on club or franchise earnings, rather than with comparable governing bodies.

Fifa’s stated annual revenue of $3.6bn therefore compares unfavourably with the NFL’s compared revenue of $21.2bn, Major League Baseball’s $13.1bn and the NBA’s $12.5bn.

The document was sent to all 211 member associations on Wednesday night and immediately provoked a strong reaction.

One senior figure queried why Fifa, which has cash reserves of around $4bn and accumulated revenues of $15bn over the current four-year cycle, would need to take on debt.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Another highlighted the odd comparison of a world governing body with private, member-run leagues, while JP Morgan’s proposed timeline for completing the deal was also questioned.

According to the document “Investors will be given access to a term sheet and select materials” in August before a vote of Fifa members has taken place.

Significantly there is little mention of the investor group elsewhere in the prospectus, with no reference to its identity, projected returns or exit terms.

There is one more major omission in the document, as there is not a single mention of women’s football anywhere across the 25 pages.

Fifa was approached for comment.

Sports.title: Harvey Elliott revels in ‘second chance’ at Liverpool and has no regrets over Aston Villa loan
Sports.content:
Harvey Elliott believes he has been given “a second chance” at Liverpool and denied his ill-fated loan to Aston Villa was a lost year in his career.

Elliott joined Villa on a season-long loan last September with an obligation for them to buy the midfielder for £35m once he made 10 appearances for the club. However, Elliott featured only nine times, playing 277 minutes in total, with Unai Emery and Villa unconvinced over completing the deal. Having made an 89th-minute substitute appearance for Liverpool at Newcastle in August, the 23-year-old was unable to sign for a third club in a single season.

Elliott has featured in both of Liverpool’s pre-season wins under Andoni Iraola in the United States. While non-committal about his long-term future – Sunday’s opponents Leeds have been linked – Elliott spoke positively about his time at Villa, the first time he has discussed last season’s issues, and claimed he could yet feature in Iraola’s plans.

“Everyone knows how much I love the club so the feeling never goes of putting the shirt back on, representing the club, and fulfilling your childhood dream,” said Elliott, a boyhood Liverpool fan. “But truthfully, yes [I felt it would never happen again], because I wanted a new challenge. I wanted to explore something, come out of my comfort zone, and I thought that would take me on as a player. Unfortunately, it didn’t work out, but the way I see it is it’s kind of a second chance, especially with the gaffer and new coaching staff coming in.

“It’s another chance to impress and hopefully get in their good books. But whatever happened last season, I wish Villa nothing but the very best. I had a lot of love for them and they treated me very well. I’m here now, and I’m trying to cement my spot in the team or within the squad.”

Quick Guide Joe Gomez facing month on sidelines Show Liverpool defender Joe Gomez is expected to miss the start of the new Premier League season with a muscle injury, Andoni Iraola has confirmed. Gomez went down injured after only eight minutes of Liverpool’s first pre-season friendly against Sunderland in Nashville on Saturday. The defender is facing a month on the sidelines – and Liverpool open their league campaign at Newcastle on 23 August – increasing Iraola's concerns about the depth of his defensive options. “Joe has a muscle injury,” said the new Liverpool head coach on Thursday. “It was quite clear since he complained straight away so he will be some weeks off. It’s difficult to say [how long] – normally one month. If it goes very good, then a little bit less. If it goes bad then a bit more but it’s a muscle injury. It’s not massive. I think it will be impossible to have him for the start of the season because we are not so far but it shouldn’t be a lot more.” With Virgil van Dijk starting pre-season training back on Merseyside this week, Giovanni Leoni recovering from an ACL injury and new signing Jérémy Jacquet yet to feature in the US after a shoulder problem, Iraola has been forced to field young and makeshift central defensive partnerships against Sunderland and Wrexham. Two 18-year-olds, Mor Talla Ndiaye and Ifeanyi Ndukwe, and full-back Luke Chambers occupied the positions in the wins in Nashville and New York. Iraola said: “You’ve seen in these games that we are pretty thin in the centre-back position. The only centre-backs we have are Mor and Ifeanyi who are 18, just arrived at the club, and are doing incredibly well. I’m happy that the team has shown composure and solidity at the back and it speaks very well about them." Jacquet could make his first Liverpool appearance against Leeds in Chicago on Sunday, the final game of the club’s US tour. Florian Wirtz may also feature and Iraola has confirmed where he wants to deploy the £116m signing next season. “I see Flo probably more in that position behind the striker,” Iraola said. “I know he has played on the left sometimes but we're going to start with him as the No 10. He's quite complete as a player and I'd like to add a few more things. In the first days of training it's clear that he's in a good place mentally.” Andy Hunter Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Elliott insists he harbours “no hard feelings” towards Villa. The Liverpool player was named player of the tournament at the European Under-21s Championship in the summer of 2025 and was touted as a possible member of Thomas Tuchel’s World Cup squad before his career stalled in the Midlands. But he insists: “I wouldn’t say it was a lost year because, at the end of it, I won the Europa League. To have that on my CV is incredible, especially with Villa. I saw with my own eyes how much it meant for them and I wouldn’t say it’s a lost year when you achieved something like that, because that’s selfish.

“It was a situation I couldn’t control. It was just a case of accepting it, and just trying to get my head clear and get myself in the best position to come back here, and I tried as hard as I could. I still feel like I can get better and I’m working as hard as I can to do that.”

Elliott admits Emery discussed his reasoning several times and that enabled him to handle the frustration of being sidelined for the majority of the season. “He explained very, very clearly and a fair few times. The whole club were very apologetic about the situation and, ultimately, it was a situation that I couldn’t control,” Elliott said. “But I knew 100% what the case was. It was like, ‘Ok, I can get over it, I know what the situation is now’.

“It was just about me handling it and showing my professionalism. I’m not that kind of guy who wanted to kick up a fuss and cause problems, because no one really deserves that. It’s just part of football and it was a learning curve for me and an opportunity that I hope I don’t experience again. But it’s a situation where I know I’ve been able to get through it.

“I’m really happy to be back and putting a Liverpool shirt on again. Playing at Liverpool, there’s no better feeling.”

Sports.title: Curtis Jones calmed down by Liverpool teammate after furious row with Dominik Szoboszlai in unseen footage
Sports.content:
Curtis Jones calmed down by Liverpool teammate after furious row with Dominik Szoboszlai in unseen footage

Tempers flared between Curtis Jones and Dominik Szoboszlai following Liverpool's latest pre-season friendly.

The Reds clinched a 1-0 win over Wrexham as part of their USA tour on Wednesday night.

3 Jones and Szoboszlai clashed on the pitch after Liverpool's win over Wrexham Credit: X / @anythingLFC_

Andoni Iraola's side saw off their Championship opponents at Yankee Stadium in New York City thanks to Rio Ngumoha's deflected second-half strike.

However, their victory has been somewhat overshadowed by an apparent row involving Jones and Szoboszlai.

Teammates clash

New footage has since emerged of the pair clashing on the pitch at full time.

Their back-and-forth exchange eventually came to an end after teammates and coaching staff stepped in.

The video, which was filmed from the crowd at Yankee Stadium, shows an animated exchange between the pair.

After Jones had embraced Iraola, he could be seen trading words with Szoboszlai as he walked past his teammate.

Visibly agitated by Jones' reaction, the Hungary international turned back to continue their back-and-forth.

The tense exchange continued for around two minutes with both players waving their arms and pointing across the pitch.

They even pointed their fingers into each others' chests as tempers threatened to boil over.

Fellow Liverpool stars Kostas Tsimikas and Jeremie Frimpong eventually approached to attempt to cool the pair down.

3 New footage shows the team-mates furiously exchanging words on the pitch Credit: X / @anythingLFC_

Although Jones was initially guided away by Frimpong, he continued to gesticulate before walking back towards Szoboszlai.

A member of the Liverpool coaching team then stepped in to speak to Szoboszlai.

Jones had been a second half substitute for Liverpool against Wrexham, having been introduced at half-time.

Meanwhile, Szoboszlai started as captain, playing a total of 76 minutes before replaced, with 30 of those alongside Jones.

The pair have also made 97 competitive appearances alongside each other for the Reds since Szoboszlai joined the club in 2023.

Liverpool will face Leeds United in Chicago on Sunday in the final match of their pre-season tour of the USA.

3 Frimpong and members of the coaching staff were forced to intervene and cool the pair down Credit: X / @anythingLFC_

They are then scheduled to take on both Monaco and Como at Anfield prior to the start of the new Premier League season.

Jones' future

The incident comes amid speculation surrounding Jones' Liverpool future.

He has been the subject of growing interest throughout the summer, namely from Italian giants Inter Milan.

The Serie A champions have seen two approaches rejected since the end of last season.

Liverpool will not allow Jones to leave the club unless their £34million valuation is met, talkSPORT understands.

Jones has entered the final 12 months of his current contract, which expires next summer.

Sports.title: Newcastle star could jump ship to Saudi Arabia amid Eddie Howe chaos
Sports.content:
Joelinton reportedly told Newcastle United he wants to leave the club earlier this summer.

The midfielder's desire to depart St. James' Park has emerged amid of the ongoing managerial uncertainty at the club.



3 Joelinton could be set to follow Eddie Howe out of the Newcastle exit door Credit: Getty

talkSPORT understands Eddie Howe is set to leave the Magpies after almost five years in charge.

The 48-year-old has decided to step down having won the Carabao Cup and twice securing Champions League qualification.

Al Ahli boss Matthias Jaissle is expected to be named as his successor.



Newcastle have agreed terms with the German coach and are set to pay his £8.5million release clause.

Joelinton future

Howe could soon be followed out of the door by Joelinton if the 29-year-old gets his wish.



According to the Daily Mail, the Brazil international told Newcastle he wants to move to Saudi Arabia.

He informed the club of his intentions in the weeks following the end of last season.



It is said to have occurred after Anthony Gordon had moved to Barcelona as well as during the process of selling Sandro Tonali to Tottenham Hotspur.

However, a potential offer from the Saudi Pro League for Joelinton has yet to materialise.

The fan favourite currently has two years remaining on his Newcastle contract.

3 Joelinton has reportedly told Newcastle he wants to move to Saudi Arabia Credit: Getty



Initially signed as a striker from Hoffenheim in 2019, Joelinton has made 263 appearances for the club.

Of those, 42 came last season across all competitions as the Magpies competed both domestically and in Europe.

The upcoming campaign will not feature continental competition after Newcastle failed to qualify last term.

Howe's side finished four points adrift of a Conference League berth in 12th place.



Joelinton has scored 35 goals for Newcastle as well as providing a further 23 assists.

He is yet to feature so far in pre-season, though, due to a thigh injury.

3 Howe is set to step down as Newcastle boss after almost five years in charge Credit: Getty

The club have been targeting a return to action in time for the start of the new season, however.



Newcastle host Liverpool in their Premier League opener on Sunday, August 23.

Sports.title: League One Leicester to sign Premier League player in major coup
Sports.content:
League One Leicester to sign Premier League player in major coup

Add us as preferred source

Leicester City are set to sign Brighton winger Tommy Watson on loan, talkSPORT understands.

The England youth international is closing in on a move to the King Power Stadium which has been driven by Foxes boss Russel Martin.

3 Leicester are set to complete the loan signing of Brighton winger Watson Credit: Getty

Watson joined the Seagulls for £10million from Sunderland last summer, signing a four-year deal with the club.

His arrival came after he had scored the winning goal in the Championship play-off final for his boyhood club.

However, the 20-year-old has since made just ten appearances for Brighton.

In those matches, he has scored once and provided three assists.

Watson spent the second half of last season on loan at Championship promotion chasers Millwall.

He went on to make 12 appearances for Alex Neil's side, who were beaten in the play-off semi-finals by Hull City.

Having returned to the Amex this summer, though, Watson is on the verge of being loaned out once again.

Leicester are set to win the race for his signature despite their relegation to League One.

Leicester coup

New manager Martin is understood to have been key to securing Watson's arrival on loan.

The 40-year-old replaced Gary Rowett in the dugout earlier this summer, signing a three-year deal with the Foxes.

3 Watson spent the second half of last season on loan at promotion-chasing Millwall Credit: Getty

It is Martin's first managerial role since leaving Scottish giants Rangers in October.

He previously guided Southampton to promotion from the Championship via the play-offs in 2024.

Leicester are currently preparing for only their second-ever season in the third-tier of English football.

The Foxes were relegated to League One last term for the first time since 2009.

Their only previous campaign at the level saw them win promotion as champions.

Martin's side begin the new season away to Notts County on Saturday, August 15.

3 Martin is understood to have driven the Foxes' move to sign Watson Credit: Getty

Foxes transfer business

Watson's imminent arrival will make him Leicester's fourth signing of the summer.

Conor Chaplin and Alex McCarthy have both been signed on free transfers following their releases from Ipswich Town and Southampton, respectively.

Meanwhile, England youth international Christian McFarlane has joined on a season-long loan from Manchester City.

As for departures, Abdul Fatawu, Bilal El Khannouss, Jeremy Monga and Harry Winks have been sold.

Victor Kristiansen has also departed on loan to join Panathinaikos.

Meanwhile, Patson Daka, Ricardo Pereira, Jordan Ayew, Jannik Vestergaard, Jamaal Lascelles, Wanya Marcal, Asmir Begovic and Silko Thomas have left on free transfers.

Sports.title: Ex-Newcastle owner Amanda Staveley plots bid for 25.1 per cent stake in EFL club
Sports.content:
Ex-Newcastle owner Amanda Staveley plots bid for 25.1 per cent stake in EFL club

Amanda Staveley is reportedly in talks to buy a stake in West Ham United.

The former Newcastle United director is looking to purchase a 25.1 per cent share in the Championship club.



3 Staveley is reportedly in talks to buy a 25.1 per cent stake in West Ham Credit: Getty

Staveley helped oversee the Saudi Public Investment Fund's takeover of Newcastle in 2021.

She remained at the club as a director, having owned a 10 per cent share alongside her husband Mehrdad Ghodoussi.

As well as her involvement at Newcastle, the 53-year-old is also a director of PCP Capital Partners and acted for Sheikh Mansour when he bought Manchester City in 2008.



The pair left St. James' Park in July 2024, though, but Staveley could now be set to return to English football.

Staveley's West Ham talks

According to Sky News, she is interested in buying shares in the Hammers.



The 25.1 per cent stake she could purchase includes shares owned by the Gold family.

Although talks are ongoing, any potential deal is said to be complicated by pre-emption rights.



West Ham's existing investors have first refusal before any shares change hands.

Vanessa Gold, the daughter of former Hammers chairman David, currently owns a nine per cent share in the club.

She is also the current chairwoman, having inherited her father's shares following his death in 2023.

3 Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky is currently the Hammers' largest shareholder Credit: Getty



Czech billionaire businessman Daniel Kretinsky bought 16 per cent of the shares in the club from Gold in June.

The deal took Kretinsky's share of the Hammers to 43 per cent, making him the club's largest shareholder.

Gold's father first bought a 50 per cent share alongside David Sullivan in 2010.

Sullivan, who still owns around a 38.8 per cent stake, stepped down as chairman last month.



New season looms

West Ham are currently preparing for their first season outside the Premier League since the 2011/12 campaign.

Their relegation in May ended the club's 14-year stay in the division.

3 West Ham are set to embark on their first Championship season since 2011/12 Credit: Getty

Meanwhile, the upcoming season will be only their second outside the top-flight in the laat 21 years.



Nuno Espirito Santo's side face Portsmouth in the Carabao Cup first round on August 8 before beginning their league campaign away to Burnley eight days later.

Sports.title: Inter Milan win race to sign John Stones ahead of Arsenal and Chelsea
Sports.content:
Inter Milan win race to sign John Stones ahead of Arsenal and Chelsea

Inter Milan have completed the signing of John Stones on a two-year contract.

The Italian giants announced the deal to sign the England and former Manchester City centre-back on Thursday.



3 Stones boosted his future prospects after an impressive World Cup with England Credit: Getty

Stones was without a club, having left Man City following the expiry of his contract in June.

Arsenal, Chelsea and Juventus were also interested in the defender, however, the Premier League clubs have lost the race.

Liverpool were urged to make an approach for him too but didn't pursue him.



Instead, the Englishman joins Inter as they look to build on their recent glory.

Inter clinched the Serie A title for the second time in three years last term, once again qualifying for the Champions League.



They have been looking to strengthen their back line, having already held talks with Tottenham captain Cristian Romero.

Inter may have expected to face stiffer competition from Arsenal, who could need a new centre-back to fill in for the injured William Saliba, but the Gunners look like they won't sign Stones.



Recent revival

Stones had plenty of options to pick from this summer, having put himself in the shop window at the World Cup.

He made five appearances for England on their run to the semi-finals, as the Three Lions ultimately went on to finish third.

The defender left Man City in June, following ten years with the club having signed from Everton in 2016.

3 Stones bid an emotional farewell to Manchester City after playing a reduced role in his final season at the Etihad Credit: Getty



3 He won six Premier League titles during ten years at City Credit: Getty

During that time, he won 19 trophies including six Premier League titles, the Champions League and the Club World Cup.

However, he played a bit-part role in his final season at the Etihad Stadium, featuring just nine times in the Premier League.

Only five of these were starts, as the Citizens finished second to Arsenal in the title race.



Stones' league outings contributed to a total of 18 appearances across all competitions, with injuries reducing his involvement.

Head over to talkSPORT BET for all the latest transfer odds ahead of the key moves this summer

Sports.title: Outgoing chief make bold claim MLS will surpass $4.7bn Premier League as most valuable in world
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi's watch will be over by the time the next MLS TV rights deal is up but outgoing commissioner Don Garber has grand designs.

Outgoing chief make bold claim MLS will surpass $4.7bn Premier League as most valuable in world

Major League Soccer has set its eyes on world domination.

The 2026 World Cup was a massive commercial hit, even if Mauricio Pochettino's USMNT suffered a humiliating defeat against Belgium.

4 Soccer is on the rise in the United States Credit: Getty



Lionel Messi getting a second trophy would have been the icing on the cake, but the tournament gripped the U.S. market for over a month.

Now, it is time to make sure the impact sticks around -- just like the 1994 edition which gave birth to MLS.

Outgoing Commissioner Don Garber thinks U.S. soccer can surpass European and South American leagues one day.

"We proved that we are a soccer nation over the last month," he told Front Office Sports ahead of the World Cup final. "We proved that we can build the most valuable commercial market in the world [for soccer]."



Inter Miami, Los Angeles FC, LA Galaxy, Atlanta United and New York City FC boast valuations of over $1 billion per Forbes.

That compares to some mid-table English Premier League teams, although falls some way short of $7.2 billion giant Manchester United.



The EPL's TV and central commercial rights are worth almost $4.7 billion annually -- well ahead of any rival.

MLS is confident of closing the gap, however, with a post-World Cup surge in ticket sales.



Messi's arrival in 2023 was a massive boost, but the 39-year-old probably won't be around when TV rights next come up for auction.

Apple TV currently pays around $250 million annually in a deal which runs until 2029.

4 Garber is ready to hand over his duties Credit: Getty

4 Fans have been snapping up tickets Credit: Getty



ESPN claims that MLS bosses hope to agree a package worth $400-500 million next time, which would be around the same as the current U.S. EPL rights agreement.

MLS ownership is close to appointing Garber's replacement with LAFC co-managing owner Larry Berg and former Fox Sports executive David Nathanson the final candidates.

They are expected to make final presentations to owners in days before the decision is made.

Don Garber won't rule out MLS promotion and relegation

Garber has served since 1999, with Doug Logan the only other man to have held the position since the league was founded in 1993.



He leaves the league in a stronger position than he inherited with San Diego paying a $500 million fee to take the number of teams to 30 in 2023 and a purpose-built stadium boom taking place.

Garber thinks another increase could take some time and thinks 32 franchises may be the limit.

4 Spain prevented Messi's fairytale ending Credit: Getty

"For a lot of different reasons -- schedule makeup and the like -- I don't see us going beyond 32, and I'm not sure 32 is coming anytime soon," Garber said. "It's about making what we have bigger, better, stronger and capturing this cultural moment."



His successor will take over amid debate over whether soccer chiefs should ditch the U.S. sports model and adopt promotion and relegation.

Garber has overseen a transition to a European calendar and admitted that more changes could be on the cards.

“I will say this now that I wouldn’t have said five years ago, I never thought we’d change our calendar and we did," he said. "I never thought we’d have 30 teams and we do.

"I never thought we’d have 29 stadiums, and we will. I never thought we’d ever talk about promotion, relegation.



"There is a time where if it makes sense for Major League Soccer to be what we want it to be, we need to have promotion/relegation, we’ll do it. If it doesn’t make sense, we won’t.”

Sports.title: ‘100 per cent’ – Eddie Howe tipped for huge managerial role after Newcastle exit
Sports.content:
‘100 per cent’ – Eddie Howe tipped for huge managerial role after Newcastle exit

Eddie Howe has been backed to one day manage England following his Newcastle United departure.

The Magpies boss is set to leave St. James' Park after almost five years in charge.

4 Howe has been backed to become England manager in the future Credit: AFP

Howe has decided to step down as manager just 24 days before the start of the new Premier League season.

Although his exit has not yet been officially confirmed, Matthias Jaissle is expected to replace him in the dugout.

talkSPORT understands Newcastle are in advanced talks to appoint the Al Ahli manager as their new boss.

The Magpies begin the season at home to Liverpool on Sunday, August 23.

Howe reaction

Following the news of Howe's imminent exit, Martin Tyler heaped praise on the former Bournemouth boss live on talkSPORT.

Reacting to his departure, he told Olly Clink and Charlie Baker: "I hope it’s for proper reasons. I know he had a bit of ill health last year and one wonders whether that had some impact on his decision.

"I hope it didn’t. I hope it’s a straight football decision. It’s been a complicated time in the club, I don’t need to tell you that.

"When players seem to be leaving, when you can’t do too much about them and other aspects of the football club.

"It is a tough part of management now that this raft of sporting directors, directors of football, call them what you will, call the shots.

4 Howe leaves Newcastle after just under five years as manager Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

"And I think it’s perhaps too much against what you really believe is best for the club and the best thing is to shake hands and move away.

"But he’s a wonderful man Eddie, he’s very hard-working to start with managerial talents. He’s first in, last out in terms of the training ground and I think he’ll deserve a break from it.

"Whether he wanted a break, you’d have to ask him. I can only wish him well because to work with as a broadcaster, he’s special."

Howe had been in charge of Newcastle since November 2021.

During his tenure, he has twice guided the club to Champions League qualification.

Meanwhile, their Carabao Cup triumph in 2025 ended a 70-year wait for a major domestic trophy.

4 Howe ended Newcastle's 70-year wait for a major domestic trophy in 2025 Credit: EPA

England job

Tyler has also tipped Howe to move into international management with England.

Asked if the 48-year-old is a future Three Lions boss, he added: "100 per cent, yes and I think maybe it has to come at a certain age.

"Thomas Tuchel’s not of that age and, I mean Thomas came close and he should be respected for that.

"I think people have forgotten that third place, away from 1966, is the best England have ever done in a World Cup.

"It was like, ‘oh, we got so close,’ but to finish third meant something and what a way to do it actually."

Thomas Tuchel's side finished third in North America this summer, their best performance since winning the World Cup in 1966.

4 The FA have backed Tuchel to continue as England manager through to Euro 2028 Credit: PA

Despite beating France in the third-place play-off, though, Tuchel has faced criticism for the manner of England's semi-final loss to Argentina.

His tactical approach after taking the lead has come under fire, with their opponents scoring twice late on after the Three Lions had brought on additional defenders.

However, the FA have backed their current boss, who is under contract until the end of Euro 2028.

Tuchel signed a two-year extension on his previous deal in February.

Sports.title: England legend demands unprecedented Argentina punishment from ‘greedy’ FIFA
Sports.content:
England legend Stuart Pearce wants to see heavy punishments handed out to Argentina after they were charged for numerous breaches by FIFA.

FIFA have charged Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina with assault. Thiago Almada has been done for unsporting behaviour as well.

4 Argentina as a nation and a few players are in deep trouble Credit: AFP

As a nation, Argentina face several very serious charges. These include racism and discrimination by their supporters.

They have also been charged with using sport to promote a non-sporting political message.

This relates to the use of the banner after their win over England in the World Cup semi-finals in which they claimed that the Falkland Islands were Argentine territory.

The banner read 'Las Malvinas son Argentinas', which translates as 'The Falklands are Argentine'.

The final charge is to do with breaching order of security, directly relating to delayed kick-offs.

And speaking on Breakfast with Andy Goldstein and Angelina Kelly, Pearce said: "What do you think they are going to do to the Argentinian players?

"Bear in mind, they upgraded Jarell Quansah's suspension and a six-game suspension to a Qatari [Assim Madibo].

"So, a player, after the game has finished, throwing punches...

"If you set a precedent for banning a player for six games for an accidental tackle, which I think is ludicrous because he wasn't a well-known player.

"Then bans for Ronaldo were quashed."

4 Argentina are almost certain to be found guilty of the breach relating to the Falklands banner Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

Pearce goes in on FIFA

It wasn't just Argentina in Pearce's sights this morning as he took aim at FIFA as well.

Gianni Infantino plans to sell off the World Cup and has offered each nation up to $40million to ensure they voted for it by the middle of September.

Since, UEFA have revealed that every single one of their nations would boycott the FIFA's competitions should Infantino's plan come to fruition.

The FA are one of the associations to back these plans, so if they go ahead, England won't be at the World Cup and no English team would be at the Club World Cup either.

Pearce was speaking before the UEFA statement dropped, but he feels that fans and players would be harmed by these plans.

He said: "I am really dubious of any idea that comes out of them. Any idea, I mistrust.

4 Infantino's plans have been met with widespread rejection Credit: Getty

"Greed seems to be at the centre of everything, and not the fans.

"But I then feel sorry for the players if you end up boycotting it. What about the generation of footballers that never get to play in a World Cup because of that?"

What next?

talkSPORT exclusively understands that UEFA are set to be joined by other football federations in proposing a FIFA boycott.

Infantino's plan is to potentially merge FIFA's commercial and operational arms merged into one private-equity firm.

They involve selling stakes of the World Cup to private investors, with Donald Trump said to be involved in discussions.

4 Plans to sell off the World Cup are set to be decided by the middle of September Credit: AFP

The 57-year-old plans to run for FIFA president again, but talkSPORT understands that UEFA are trying to find a candidate.

One name who had significant support in UEFA circles was Paris Saint-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi.

However, those close to Al-Khelaifi insist he had no aspirations to stand, nor give up his roles at PSG and beIN Sports.

A spokesperson for Al-Khelaifi said: "Mr. Al-Khelaifi has absolutely no ambition, no intention and no interest in the FIFA role and all this media noise, and instead will continue to quietly and constructively support all the institutions of world and European football."

UEFA's statement

The UEFA statement against Infantino's plans is damning.

They said: "UEFA and its national associations will not participate in FIFA competitions.

"UEFA and its 55 member associations stand as one. We unanimously and unequivocally reject FIFA’s proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other FIFA competitions to private investors.

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football’s greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.

"It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game. This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA’s duty as the custodian of world football.

"National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football’s greatest competitions or bear the consequences. This is not a “democratic decision”, but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.

"But our opposition goes far beyond process.

"The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever. Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure. From that moment onwards, every decision on the international calendar, every decision on competition formats and every decision shaping the future of football is no longer driven by what best serves the game, but by what best serves shareholders.

"This model has no place in world football. Football’s future cannot be dictated by the expectations of those whose first duty is to maximise financial return. Nor can the interests of national associations, leagues, clubs, players and supporters become subordinate to investor returns. Football cannot mortgage its future for financial gain.

"Europe’s position is clear. We will never lend this model our legitimacy. No one has the moral authority to sell what they merely hold in trust for the next generation.

"As a result of today’s discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership.

"Nobody should be in any doubt: UEFA and its national associations will oppose these plans with absolute determination.

"There are moments when institutions are judged not by what they are prepared to accept, but by what they refuse to compromise. This is one of those moments.

"Some things are simply too important to sell. The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale."

Sports.title: Roy Keane and Micah Richards like you've never seen them before! Sky pundits dress up for campaign ahead of new Premier League season
Sports.content:
Roy Keane and Micah Richards like you've never seen them before! Sky pundits dress up for campaign ahead of new Premier League season

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Sky Sports favourites Roy Keane and Micah Richards have undergone a makeover for a new Sky Bet campaign – as Victorian gentlemen.

The former Manchester United captain and Manchester City star have become known for their on-screen chemistry, but now they have been taken back to a different era, featuring some impressive facial hair.

Footage shared by Sky in a teaser shows the duo walking down in the stands at a football ground, suited and booted with coffee in hands.

The outfits are completed by waistcoats and some classic hats.

Another image features the two in the car park, a bit more casual with Keane losing the hat. They are, though, using an old-fashioned football.

Roy Keane (left) and Micah Richards (right) have donned some new outfits for a new Sky promotional campaign

The duo took to the car park to show off their football skills - with a classic ball

League action will then start the weekend after, with the Premier League starting when Arsenal take on Coventry on August 21.
