Cyber attacks on several local water systems in the US state of Minnesota carry telltale signs of a hacker group affiliated with Iran, US media reports say.

About 30 water systems were attacked Sunday and Monday, local time, using methods that have pointed investigators to a Tehran-backed group, according to the reports which cite a security firm and US investigators.

Australian hospitals on high alert after hack Hospitals across the nation are on alert after an Iranian cyber militia linked to the Islamic regime hacked a US multinational that supplies critical equipment to Australia.

The operation disrupted the water supply in the small town of Braham, in the greater Minneapolis area, for about two hours before service was restored.

According to cybersecurity firm Tenable, the method used in the attack "is consistent with" the CyberAv3ngers cybercriminal group, which the US government accuses of operating under Tehran's control.

US authorities also suspect Iranian hackers, although they have not formally established responsibility at this stage.

On July 22, just days before the attack, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued an advisory warning of an offensive by Iran-affiliated organisations against online control systems for infrastructure in the United States.

"Iranian cyber actors continue to target US critical infrastructure, and the FBI is committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing costs on those responsible," said Assistant Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI's Cyber Division.

" Cybersecurity threats are a serious concern for our nation's drinking water and wastewater systems. "

The FBI did not immediately respond to AFP's request for comment.

A new war front

In March, the Handala Hack group — also said to be operating under the Iranian government — claimed responsibility for cyber attacks against two US companies: medical equipment supplier Stryker and digital payments platform Verifone.

Stryker confirmed the incident, while Verifone denied that it had occurred.

Women grieve at a funeral for school strike victims, who were mostly girls aged seven to 12. (Reuters: WANA/Amirhossein Khorgooei/ISNA)

The hackers described their actions as retaliation for the bombing of an elementary school in Minab, southern Iran, on the first day of the US-Israeli offensive against the Islamic republic on February 28.

According to the findings of an internal US military investigation revealed by the New York Times, the strike, which killed more than 150 people, appears to have resulted from incorrect coordinates used while targeting an adjacent military base.

AFP

World.title: Breaking: Trump touts deal to disarm Hamas in Gaza talks breakthrough
World.content:
US President Donald Trump says Cairo talks between mediators and Hamas leaders have reached a breakthrough on Gaza that will lead to Hamas disarming and Israel withdrawing.

"HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas," Mr Trump posted on social media.

He said the plan would be carried out in phases and eventually lead to Israeli forces leaving Gaza.

A Board of Peace official said it would supervise the reconstruction of Gaza and Hamas would hand over weapons to a "national committee for the administration of Gaza".

Earlier today, sources close to the talks told Reuters news agency that progress was made but it was uncertain if the agreement would hold, as an Israeli official had said the proposed terms were not satisfactory.

"This agreement is a critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government that will work closely with the Board of Peace to help the Palestinian people," Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social.

"At the same time, Israel will have the security it deserves, with Gaza no longer used as a base for terror attacks."

A US official told Reuters Israel did not agree and "Trump will be disappointed".

The Israeli embassy in Washington and Hamas did not immediately respond to requests for comment about Mr Trump's post.

Israeli strikes killed at least six Palestinians in Gaza on Thursday, local time, including two children, medics said.

Agreement based on reciprocal steps over trust: Diplomat

A Hamas official said the group was preparing a "positive and good" response, but did not say whether it had agreed to fully disarm, which has been a key sticking point in talks over the past four months.

Hamas wants Israel to commit to ending attacks on Gaza and withdrawing its forces.

Sources close to Hamas said the group was willing to "confine and store" heavy weapons under a Palestinian body, but not hand them over to Israel.

It is not yet clear what will happen with light or personal weapons or if the new Hamas stance would be accepted by Israel or the Board of Peace.

A diplomat close to the Cairo talks said the plan includes the elimination of tunnels, arms stockpiles and weapons production facilities, adding that by the end of the process there would be no remaining militant infrastructure in Gaza.

The diplomat described the agreement's road map as based on reciprocal steps, rather than trust.

The reality on the ground in Gaza remains a long way from such an agreement.

The Israeli military has continued to expand its occupation, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu saying Israel intends to expand its control to 70 per cent of the enclave.

It remains unclear if Israeli troops will withdraw.

World.title: Breaking: Anthropic's Claude AI model hacks three companies during safety tests
World.content:
Artificial intelligence firm Anthropic says its Claude AI model hacked the systems of three external organisations during testing, ​days after ‌rival company OpenAI revealed a rogue agent had gone on a days-long ‌hacking spree at ⁠AI firm Hugging Face.

Claude gained ‌unauthorised ​access to ‌the other companies' systems during cybersecurity evaluations, after a misconfiguration allowed the models to reach the ​internet ‌from testing environments that were supposed to be ⁠isolated, Anthropic ‌said in a statement.

The company said ‌it identified the incidents after ‌reviewing 141,006 cybersecurity evaluation runs, a process ‌it ​launched following ⁠OpenAI's disclosures.

"Claude compromised the impacted organisations' infrastructure using basic techniques, such as exploiting weak passwords ⁠and unauthenticated endpoints," it said.

Reuters

World.title: England hires NZ's Fleming to coach men's Test side, Root as captain
World.content:
English cricket has turned to another New Zealander to coach the men's Test team, hiring former Kiwi star Stephen Fleming, while batting great Joe Root has been reappointed as captain.

Fleming replaced his former teammate Brendon McCullum, who was fired after losing the Ashes series in Australia 4-1 over the winter and, last month, losing at home to New Zealand 2-1.

England now has an all-New Zealand coaching set-up, with McCullum remaining in charge of the one-day and Twenty20 teams.

Fleming will not take charge until after Pakistan's three-Test tour, which begins on August 19 in Leeds. McCullum's former assistant, Marcus Trescothick, will be the interim England coach for that series.

Root was previously the permanent Test captain from 2017-22 in a national record 65 Tests. He won a record 27 of those matches but has won only one of his past 18 in charge.

The 35-year-old Root formally replaces Ben Stokes, who retired suddenly from international cricket after the New Zealand series in June. Stokes had endorsed his vice-captain, Harry Brook, as the next captain.

McCullum sacked as Test coach The architect of England's controversial Bazball approach to Test cricket is given his marching orders after a disappointing string of results.

Fleming said he was excited to work with Root and Brook, adding: "I know what it feels like to have the weight of leadership and international cricket take their toll."

Fleming was New Zealand's longest-serving captain across 80 Tests and he won 28 of them. He played for three English county teams and won a league title with Nottinghamshire in 2005.

"English cricket gave that to me and it is a privilege to have this chance to give something back," he said in a statement.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The England and Wales Cricket Board said it was allowing Fleming to spend time with family as he stepped down from his role at the Chennai Super Kings only this month.

Fleming led Chennai to a record five titles and 10 finals in the Indian Premier League. He also coached sister franchises in South Africa and the United States.

He will prepare England for three Tests in South Africa in December-January.

Fleming has only seven Tests in charge to ready England for the home Ashes series next year.

AP

World.title: Quick hits: Tongan dance moves bring joy, David Beckham hits the velodrome
World.content:
A para athletics race will be run again amid much drama, a Tongan weightlifter thrills the crowd with his dancing, and Nigeria wins the fashion stakes at the velodrome.

Here are the quick hits from day seven of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Para athletics race to be re-run

Eliza Ault-Connell was knocked out of the women's 1500m T54 final. (Getty Images: PA Images/Martin Rickett)

After a dramatic crash that took out two athletes, a disqualification that reordered the medal spots, and a subsequent protest, para athletics officials ordered a re-race of the women's 1,500m T54 final.

The race was thrown into chaos early on when Australian Eliza Ault-Connell went down heavily in a nasty crash, with Mauritian world champion Noemi Alphonse also knocked out of contention.

Canadian Nandini Sharma, who went on to finish second across the line, was disqualified for causing the crash.

After having that medal taken off her, Australia's Mikaela Dingley was promoted into the bronze medal position.

However, Australia and Mauritius protested the decision and, after Athletics Canada's appeal was dismissed, authorities decided to re-run the race, with some commentators saying it should have been stopped at the time of the crash.

Sharma will not be able to take to the start, with Canada saying it was "disappointed" in the decision.

"Having considered the multiple appeals that were submitted, the Jury has decided that the disqualification will stand," the statement read.

"While Athletics Canada is disappointed with this decision, we accept the process and look forward to Nandini competing again in the T53/54 400m race."

The re-race will be held on Friday 7:24pm AEST.

2. World record falls

Tara Neyland broke her own C4 4,000m Individual Pursuit world record. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Australian para cyclist Tara Neyland laid down a stunning time to top qualifying in the women's C4-C5 4,000m individual pursuit qualifying, setting a world record.

Her factored time was 4:45.796, achieved at an average speed of 49.716km/h.

Neyland later returned to the track to win gold in the final.

The 32-year-old is already a three-time world champion on the track and a two-time world champion on the road.

The women's individual pursuit distance officially moved from 3,000m to 4,000m on January 1, 2025, so competing at this distance is still relatively new.

Which perhaps accounts for England's Morgan Newbury breaking the world record in the C5 classification qualification period.

3. Tonga's dancing weightlifter

Josh Uikilifi treated spectators to his best dance moves. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

If weightlifting medals were handed out for post-lift moves, Tonga's Joshua Uikilifi would have topped the podium.

Uikilifi had the SEC Armadillo crowd eating out of the palm of his hand as he competed in the men's 110kg classification.

He treated spectators to some spectacular dance moves after each successful lift.

Uikilifi produced a total of 331kg to finish fourth behind Fiji's Taniela Rainibogi, who won gold with a Games record of 378kg.

4. Nigerian para cyclists turn heads

The Nigerians were the best dressed at the velodrome on day seven. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Australia dominated the medals on the opening day at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome, but it was Nigeria which turned heads.

The Nigerian para cyclists hit the track in eye-catching uniforms, reportedly inspired by the kit worn by the national men's football team at the 2018 FIFA World Cup.

Oyindamola Abdullahi Tijani and pilot Okeyah Bethel looked magnificent as they contested the men's tandem B 1,000m time trial.

They deservedly got the seal of approval across social media platforms.

For the record, Tijani and Bethel finished fifth in the final.

Scotland's Neil Fachie (pilot: Aaron Pope) won gold ahead of James Ball (Matthew Rotherham) of Wales.

Australia's Kane Perris (Luke Zaccaria) took bronze.

5. Ronaldo and Beckham in the velodrome

If you thought the only sightings of David Beckham and Ronaldo at a major global sporting event were going to be in North America this year, then we have news for you.

Yes, that's right, David Beckham and Ronaldo were at the Sir Chris Hoy velodrome in Glasgow, a stone's throw away from the footballing theatre of Celtic Park.

Well, David Beckham Elkatohchoongo and Ronaldo Singh Laitonjam were there, joining Rojit Singh Yanglem in India's team sprint squad.

"My father was a footballer in the national team, and he was a huge fan of David Beckham," Elkatohchoongo told AFP in 2023 at the Asian Games.

"When I was born in the hospital, they told my mum: if it's a boy, then it's David Beckham."

Laitonjam was also named after a footballer, not actually Ronaldo but Ronaldinho.

His father had, according to AFP, made a bet with his work colleagues that the Brazilian would score against England in the 2002 World Cup match they were watching.

The Barcelona legend promptly did, and minutes later Laitonjam senior received a phone call telling him that his wife was in labour.

"Just as the ball went in the goal, I must have started making an appearance," Laitonjam told The Hindu newspaper.

"I think my dad won some money that day. That's probably why I got that name. He felt I was very lucky for him."

David and Ronaldo could not add the necessary star power to the Indian team their namesakes may have demanded, though, finishing seventh and last in qualifying.

World.title: Migrants from Morocco pour into Spanish border territory
World.content:
Spanish military units are being deployed to reinforce police in the city of Ceuta after migrants in Morocco broke through fences, overwhelming the local force.

Spanish state television TVE reported that 2,000 to 3,000 people crossed. Reuters was not immediately able to confirm that report.

Ceuta is an autonomous city of Spain, on the North African coast, and has been the scene of previous mass migration events in recent years.

Video footage showed hundreds of migrants swimming or floating on inner tubes from the Moroccan side, and others breaking through a gate on land and running into the city.

Migrants run and cheer as they cross on foot into Ceuta from Morocco. (Reuters: Faro TV)

"It was very tough. The police tried to stop us. But our will and determination allowed us to come here," migrant Jadid Zacaria, his hair and shirt still wet from the ocean, said in an interview as migrants streamed through a border gate nearby.

Nine people were found dead, local authorities said, adding to a toll of 60 migrants who have died attempting to cross into Ceuta in recent months.

The Spanish government said 200 specialised police officers and 60 troops had arrived from the Spanish mainland to reinforce the enclave's regular forces.

The scene was reminiscent of 2021, when about 10,000 people from Morocco and sub-Saharan Africa, many of them minors, entered the enclave of 85,000 people in days.

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez will travel to Ceuta today with Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska for meetings with security forces and local authorities, his office said.

Morocco's Interior Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

'Entering from the sea'

Earlier, a Guardia Civil spokesperson said migrants were "massively entering from the sea" around the Tarajal breakwater, a border seawall that migrants can swim around to enter Ceuta.

The spokesperson could not estimate the number of migrants but said police were overwhelmed.

Many local shops were shuttered.

Enrique Serrano, who runs a women's clothing store in central Ceuta, said business owners were organising self-defence because they believed police resources would be insufficient.

Migrants cross into the North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco by attempting to swim, according to Spain's Guardia Civil. (Reuters)

"I'm not opening this afternoon because the situation is extremely tense … The first thing I have to do is protect my business and my family," he said.

Ceuta and Melilla — another Spanish autonomous city located in North Africa — have the European Union's only land borders with Africa.

Both cities periodically experience surges in attempted crossings by migrants seeking to reach Europe.

Local government seeks state of emergency

Spain's Socialist government stands out in Europe for its pro-migrant stance, and it has recently launched a program to provide legal status for some 500,000 undocumented migrants, triggering an influx of applications double that number.

Right-wing parties criticised the drive, arguing it would attract more migrants to Spain, and were quick to blame Mr Sanchez for allowing the situation in Ceuta to reach crisis proportions.

Conservative opposition People's Party leader Alberto Nuñez Feijoo said in a post on X: "The situation in Ceuta is desperate. The government cannot look the other way… because we are facing a national security crisis."

Spanish military stands guard at the border after thousands of migrants reportedly crossed into Ceuta. (Reuters: Fabian Bimmer)

Ceuta Mayor Juan Jesus Vivas had urged the national government to declare an emergency over the mass arrivals.

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said on X that the images from Ceuta showed that Mr Sanchez's migration policy was "misguided".

A source told Reuters that Italy was exploring reintroducing border controls for people travelling from Spain to Italy, which normally falls in the European Union's passport-free Schengen zone.

'An explosion'

Earlier this month, Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants intercepted at sea while attempting to reach Ceuta or Melilla could not be summarily returned under the enclaves' special "border rejection" regime, which allows authorities to immediately send back people caught crossing the border fences.

Spain's government said it was the "exploitation by mafias and criminal organisations" of this ruling that had triggered the migrant surge, not its bid to give legal status to some undocumented migrants.

"It has been a slow trickle since the Supreme Court's ruling, but today has been an explosion," the Guardia Civil spokesperson told Reuters.

The Interior Ministry said it was working closely with Morocco to address the surge in irregular arrivals, having prevented thousands of migrants from illegally entering Ceuta in recent days.

Migrant rights activist Zakaria Zarroqui said people were still flocking to the adjacent Moroccan city of Fnideq in an attempt to cross into Ceuta and the situation was still out of control.

Mauricio Valiente, director of the Spanish Commission for Refugees, which has lawyers working in Ceuta, said the migrants crossing into the enclave were of Moroccan and sub-Saharan origin, including families.

Reuters

Strike action that stopped Brisbane’s ferry network on Friday has concluded, with CityCats gradually churning back into service from 10am.

CityCats stopped running at whichever stop they were closest to at 8am. Julius Dennis

World.title: Labor ignored internal report revealing toll of scrapping Baby Boomer health rebate
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAged care Labor ignored internal report revealing toll of scrapping Baby Boomer health rebate Brittany Busch July 31, 2026 — 10:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Labor was warned that scrapping the private health rebate for over-65s meant some pensioners would have to cut back on spending or go without cover, according to documents released to the Coalition under freedom of information laws. Opposition health and aged care spokeswoman Anne Ruston said on Friday the documents revealed that the Department of Health had used fictional case studies to demonstrate the effects of Labor’s budget change on older Australians, showing that some would rein in already strained budgets and others would drop their private health insurance altogether. Coalition aged care spokeswoman Anne Ruston vowed to fight the changes. Alex Ellinghausen Labor announced in April it would scrap the Howard-era bonus for seniors as it wrangles with the $47 billion aged care sector plagued by workforce and resource challenges. Health and Ageing Minister Mark Butler said the change would free up funding for under-pressure aged care services. Ruston has vowed to fight the changes in the Senate, saying older Australians on fixed retirement incomes were the least able to respond to price shocks such as the hundreds of dollars extra per year they can expect to pay without the rebate.



Older Australians receive a rebate up to 8 per cent higher than younger people on a similar income. Related Article Aged care Labor’s reforms harm the people they’re supposed to help: aged care watchdog The upper house, where the Coalition, Greens and crossbenchers can join forces to block government legislation, has proven a minefield for Labor on aged care reform. The government has twice in the past year caved to Senate pressure, first agreeing to fast-track the release of 20,000 home care packages and then to guarantee a new layer of human oversight for the algorithm that assesses care package needs. “We will do everything we can in the parliament to block these changes and have called for a Senate inquiry to pursue the truth about who will be most affected by this new tax,” Ruston said in a statement. “Mark Butler has badly underestimated the damage his own policy will do.” Ruston also pointed to polling commissioned by Private Healthcare Australia that showed more than a third of over-65s with private health said they were more likely to drop their cover without the premium rebate.



Treasury has forecast only 44,000 of the 3 million over-65s with private health insurance would be pushed into the public health system because of the changes. Responding to reports first published by News Ltd, Butler on Friday said he was confident in the department modelling and took a swipe at the Queensland, NSW and Tasmanian governments, which have rebelled against the change and argued it would increase the burden carried by their state health services. “I’m a little surprised, frankly, that the state governments have swallowed the rather self-serving modelling that the insurance industry itself is putting out there,” he told Seven’s Sunrise program. Butler said every dollar saved on the premium rebate would go back into supporting older Australians in other ways, such as funding more aged care beds. Health and Ageing Minister Mark Butler is overseeing sweeping reforms to aged care and the NDIS. Alex Ellinghausen



“We’ve put an eye-watering amount of extra money into aged care over the last few years to get it out of the position that the royal commission described it, out of neglect. And to fund the extra demand that’s coming from the ageing and the Baby Boomer generation … that sometimes involves difficult decisions in a budget,” he said. Butler said older Australians would still get a rebate on private health insurance, but it would be based on their income like everyone else. “Two households next to each other, for example, on $50,000, one of them over 65, the other household in their 40s or in their 50s with kids, they’ll now both receive the same subsidy from ... taxpayers to pay for their private health insurance.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: ASX jumps after Wall Street rally; HSBC sells $36b Australian home loan portfolio to US giant
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX jumps after Wall Street rally; HSBC sells $36b Australian home loan portfolio to US giant Stan Choe Updated July 31, 2026 — 10:04am ,first published July 31, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has jumped at the open after a monster day for Microsoft’s stock led a powerful rebound on Wall Street, while computer-chip companies regained some of their sharp recent losses. The S&P/ASX 200 surged 85.8 points, or 1 per cent, to 9053.5 in early trade. The bourse lost 0.8 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.35¢. Technology stocks continue to drive the direction of Wall Street. Bloomberg Global bank HSBC is selling its $36 billion Australian home loan portfolio to private equity giant Blackstone, and it will wind down the rest of its local retail banking business over the next 18 months. The banking group on Friday said it was quitting retail banking in Australia to focus on banking commercial and corporate clients, as part of a simplification push. Overnight, the S&P 500 rallied 1.7 per cent and more than recovered its drop from the day before, which was its worst in seven weeks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 613 points, or 1.2 per cent. The Nasdaq composite, which is full of artificial-intelligence stocks, rallied 2.8 per cent a day after it fell 9.8 per cent below its record set last month.



On Wall Street, Microsoft led the way and leaped 15.5 per cent for its best day in nearly 18 years after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Growth was strong for its Azure cloud business, and CEO Satya Nadella said it reflects how customers are using Microsoft to move into AI. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates As the Fed sits tight on interest rates, investors take action Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Perhaps just as importantly for Wall Street, Microsoft did not announce a big increase in how much it plans to spend on AI investments, something that several other Big Tech rivals have done. Worries are high that such spending is eating into companies’ cash flows and may not ultimately be worth it if AI does not produce as much productivity and profits as promised. Apple released its results after the closing bell, with sales and profits beating Wall Street expectations, fuelled by its customers snapping up iPhones and MacBooks amid price increases across the consumer electronics sector. Driving Apple’s results was a 21.7 per cent increase in iPhone sales to $US54.25 billion ($77.2 billion), above analyst estimates of $US53.86 billion, according to LSEG data. Those iPhone sales were Apple’s best-ever for a third quarter, when phone sales typically begin to slow as customers anticipate new models during the fall. Apple shares are 3.3 per cent lower in after-hours trade.



Amazon said it will be increasing this year’s capital spending on technology, mostly artificial intelligence, by an additional 10 per cent after the tech and e-commerce giant delivered strong profits and net sales during for fiscal second quarter, helped by surging growth in its prominent cloud computing unit. Amazon shares surged 9.4 per cent in after-hours trade. The company said that sales in its cloud computing unit called AWS rose 37 per cent during the April-June period, faster than the 28 per cent clip in the previous quarter and marking the fastest rate of growth in 18 quarters. CEO and President Andy Jassy disclosed to investors on the call that Amazon now expects capital spending to total $US220 billion, which also includes outlays on robots, semiconductors and satellites. That’s up from the $US200 billion investment plan that was announced in February and well above the $US128 billion in capital spending for all of last year Meta Platforms fell 8 per cent. The parent company of Facebook and Instagram reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though it made slightly more in revenue than expected. It also raised the lower end of its forecasted range for spending on investments this year. Companies involved in the making of the computer memory and processors that such “hyperscalers” are buying to power their AI efforts rose, recovering some of the big losses they’ve taken on worries their stock prices shot too high in the euphoria around AI.



Micron Technology jumped 18.4 per cent, for example, to trim its loss for the week to 5 per cent. It was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500 after Microsoft. Lam Research, a supplier to the semiconductor industry, soared 18 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Chip giant Advanced Micro Devices rallied 13 per cent. On the losing end of Wall Street was Jersey Mike’s Subs. The sandwich chain’s stock fell 6 per cent in its first day of trading on the New York Stock Exchange. In the bond market, longer-term Treasury yields held steadier following their sharp accelerations Wednesday. They had jumped after the chairman of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, gave few clues about what the central bank will do with interest rates to combat the painfully high inflation that continues to hurt the country. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they can also slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury was 4.67 per cent, the same as late Wednesday. The 30-year Treasury yield ticked up to 5.22 per cent from 5.20 per cent, a day after it shot up from 5.09 per cent. Those yields move with investors’ expectations for inflation and economic growth in upcoming years. Warsh reaffirmed on Wednesday the Fed wants to get inflation back to 2 per cent, even though the central bank decided not to raise interest rates despite inflation remaining higher than that. He also implied the bond market may already be doing some of the Fed’s work to restrain inflation, and he pointed to how yields have climbed since the central bank’s last meeting six weeks earlier. That leaves investors questioning whether the Fed is prepared to act if inflation worsens, or whether it is relying on financial markets to achieve the same outcome, according to Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management. “If investors conclude that the latter is true, the credibility of the Fed’s inflation-fighting commitment could come under increasing scrutiny. Arguably, it already is.” President Donald Trump, who nominated Warsh to lead the Fed, has lobbied for lower interest rates even though they could cause inflation to accelerate.



Reports released Thursday suggested the US economy’s growth slowed by more during the spring than economists expected. A measure of Inflation, meanwhile, remained worse last month than the Federal Reserve’s target, but it slowed from May’s level. Related Article Opinion

Home loans Buckle up for the banks’ mortgage war! Home loans have fallen off a cliff Elizabeth Knight Business columnist In the oil market, prices eased. Brent crude, the international standard, fell 1.4 per cent to settle at $US86.88 per barrel. It had swung as low as $US72 early this month and as high as $US102 last week on uncertainty about whether the United States and Iran could reach a deal to allow oil tankers to move freely again from the Middle East to customers worldwide. In stock markets worldwide, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.2 per cent, and France’s CAC 40 rose 0.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves.



Seoul’s market has been at the centre of AI’s huge swings because it’s dominated by two tech titans, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. After more than doubling through this year’s first six months, the Kospi has plunged 34 per cent so far in July. Its drop on Thursday came as Samsung Electronics dipped 0.7 per cent. The tech giant reported a record profit for the spring and said demand for its chips continues to outpace supply, but its earnings nevertheless fell shy of analysts’ high expectations. World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic has revealed its Claude models broke into the live systems of three organisations during cybersecurity testing, days after rival OpenAI disclosed a similar issue.

The company said a misconfiguration left its testing environments connected to the internet, despite Claude being told in its prompt that it was in a sealed simulation. Believing the real companies it found were part of the exercise, Claude compromised them using basic techniques including weak passwords and unauthenticated endpoints.

On June 13, Anthropic suspended worldwide access to its two most powerful AI models. Bloomberg

More to come.

World.title: Trump says Hamas will disarm under deal for Gaza to get new government
World.content:
Breaking WorldMiddle EastIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Trump says Hamas will disarm under deal for Gaza to get new government Nidal al-Mughrabi and Bo Erickson Updated July 31, 2026 — 9:45am ,first published 9:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cairo/washington: US President Donald Trump said Cairo talks between mediators and Hamas leaders had led to a “historic agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas” in what he described as structured phases. Sources close to the talks told Reuters earlier on Thursday that progress had been made, but it was uncertain if the agreement would hold, as an Israeli official had said the proposed terms were not satisfactory. US President Donald Trump at the White House on Thursday. AP Photo/Alex Brandon “This agreement is a critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government that will work closely with the Board of Peace to help the Palestinian people,” Trump said in a social media post late on Thursday (Washington time) as he thanked mediators Egypt, Qatar and Turkey. “At the same time, Israel will have the security it deserves, with Gaza no longer used as a base for terror attacks.”



The Israeli embassy in Washington and Hamas did not immediately respond to requests for comment about Trump’s post. Earlier, Israeli strikes killed at least six Palestinians in Gaza on Thursday, including two children, medics said. Palestinians inspect damage on Thursday, a day after an Israeli airstrike hit Gaza City. Bloomberg A Hamas official and a diplomat close to the Cairo talks said the progress would be tested by Israel’s response and whether this allowed a broad accord to be reached. However, the Israeli official earlier on Thursday, who declined to be identified, said Israel had rejected a proposal. “Israel demands the complete disarmament of Hamas, including the removal of weapons from Gaza and the complete demilitarisation of the Strip as a precondition for any process,” the official said.



“The 15-point document in question does not provide a satisfactory response to these demands and Israel conveyed its objections.” Hamas leaders are holding talks with mediators from Egypt, Qatar and Turkey on the second phase of Trump’s Gaza plan, as presented to them by his Board of Peace, which oversees its implementation. Smoke rises following an Israeli military strike in Gaza City on Tuesday. AP Photo/Jehad Alshrafi Russian Deputy Ambassador to the United Nations Anna Evstigneeva told the Security Council on Tuesday that a roadmap prepared by Trump’s Board of Peace envoy for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov, had so far failed to gain the support of Israel and Hamas, with the demilitarisation of Gaza remaining the main stumbling block. The Board of Peace declined comment on the Cairo talks earlier on Thursday. The diplomat close to the talks said the negotiations were making progress toward a roadmap that would see all heavy and light weapons in Gaza decommissioned.



The plan calls for a surge in humanitarian aid, governance by a civilian Palestinian administration, the disarmament of Hamas, the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza and the deployment of an international force to help maintain security. But progress has stalled in previous months. On Thursday, a Hamas official said the group was coming with a “positive and good” response, but did not say whether the group had agreed to fully disarm – a key sticking point in the talks over the past four months. Hamas wants Israel to commit to ending attacks on Gaza and withdrawing its forces. Sources close to Hamas said the group was willing to “confine and store” heavy weapons under a Palestinian body, not hand them over to Israel. Hamas did not comment on the matter.



It is not yet clear what will happen regarding light or personal weapons or whether the new Hamas stance will be accepted by Israel or the Board of Peace. The diplomat involved in the talks said the roadmap under discussion in Cairo would also see authority transferred in phases to the U.S.-backed National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), under the principle of “one authority, one law, one weapon”. The plan includes the elimination of tunnels, arms stockpiles and weapons production facilities, the diplomat said, adding that by the end of the process there would be no remaining militant infrastructure in Gaza. The diplomat described the roadmap as being based on reciprocal steps rather than trust. So far, the reality on the ground in Gaza remains far from this roadmap. The Israeli military has continued to expand its military occupation of Gaza, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu saying that Israel intends to expand the area under its control to 70 per cent of the enclave.



It remains unclear how many forces would be available to deploy with the planned International Stabilisation Force, and whether Israeli troops would withdraw from the enclave. Related Article Graphic content

Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israel investigating after photo of stripped and bound detainee is shared In Cairo, two Egyptian sources said Hamas had agreed to several contentious points, including the handover of weapons, but had requested changes regarding the definition of the infrastructure to be dismantled, adding more talks were underway. The truce halted full-scale fighting, but has not ended near-daily Israeli strikes. Health officials said separate Israeli strikes had killed at least two children, a woman and three men in Gaza on Thursday. The Israeli military said it struck Hamas militants in the enclave.



The latest deaths add to a toll of more than 1200 Palestinians, mostly civilians, killed by Israeli attacks since the ceasefire took effect, according to Gaza health officials. Four Israeli soldiers have been killed by militants in Gaza since the ceasefire. Hamas does not usually disclose its losses. Expanding marine parks around Lord Howe and Norfolk Island would mean Australia reaches its goal to protect 30 per cent of its oceans well before 2030.

The plan was announced by Environment Minister Murray Watt today alongside the 10-year review of how existing marine parks are working.

The proposed expansions would bring an additional 671,500 square kilometres of Australia’s waters under protection, protecting the areas’ high biodiversity of migratory seabirds, cetaceans, fish and sharks.

The review will include six new management plans for 44 Australian Marine Parks, which cover 2.37 million square kilometres of ocean – an area larger than Queensland and NSW combined.

Public consultation on the preparation of new management plans, and the proposed changes to Norfolk and Lord Howe marine parks, is open until 4pm AEST on September 30 through the Have Your Say portal.

The fishing industry will also be consulted directly, the government said.

World.title: This five-star production is Macbeth as you’ve never seen it before
World.content:
Key points THEATRE: Mackenzie is Yve Blake’s original, freewheeling adaptation of Macbeth

MUSICAL: After 48 years Ned Kelly: The Musical finally has its Melbourne premiere

MUSIC: Jeane’s songs are good on record, but live, they explode

THEATRE: Steel Magnolias is ultimately a paean to the camaraderie between women

is ultimately a paean to the camaraderie between women DANCE: Vista deploys a narrative device that doesn’t quite work

THEATRE

Mackenzie ★★★★★

Bell Shakespeare, Arts Centre Melbourne, until August 9 Bring me a bucket of water, would you? I’m writing a five-star review of a Bell Shakespeare show, and my hair might catch fire. (Five stars! Bell Shakespeare?) A scene from the Bell Shakespeare production of Mackenzie, a reimagining of Macbeth. Brett Boardman Australia’s most prominent Shakespeare company has been, for significant stretches of its history, bedevilled by incestuousness and mediocrity. No point denying it. I’ve followed Bell for decades now and its most reliable fare, oddly enough, tends to lie outside the Shakespearean canon. Over the years, it has done everything from Molière to Eugene O’Neill, and it usually rises to the occasion. But there’s never been anything half so funny and alive as Mackenzie. Yve Blake’s original, freewheeling adaptation of Macbeth relocates the action from the blasted heaths of medieval Scotland to a cutthroat realm behind the scenes of a children’s TV show. It’s comedic and dramatic genius – a pop girl transformation of the Scottish play that does for Shakespeare what Six did for the wives of Henry VIII.



In this version, King Duncan becomes tween TV star Dahlia (Anusha Thomas) – think Hannah Montana or a young Britney Spears, and you’ll get the idea – and the Macbeth-figure, Mackenzie (Kimberley Hodgson), is an overlooked child actor with a horrific bowl cut who plays Dahlia’s ugly duckling sidekick. Lady Macbeth is converted into Mackenzie’s manipulative stage mum, Ruth (Nikki Britton), while Banquo is Mackenzie’s best friend and fellow child star Beau (Ryan González). Ryan González and Kimberley Hodgson play best friends who have a wedge driven between them. Brett Boardman The witches? An eccentric make-up artist (Jane Watt) prone to strange prophetic “episodes”. Macduff? A butch lesbian and head of catering at the studio (Billie Palin) with more than enough reason for vengeance. Even telling you this much feels like a slight spoiler, given how much delight Shakespeare lovers will take in Blake’s inspired tweaks to the Bard’s dramatic architecture, and the hilarious Easter eggs and in-jokes sprinkled throughout the show.



Director Virginia Gay is one of the funniest women in Australian theatre, and the acting is brilliant across the board. Every single member of the cast achieves an exquisite level of clowning, and the energy and commitment and berserk stylisation of the performances take Mackenzie to another level as a satire of both showbiz and adolescence. Related Article Stage shows ‘What if my writing is terrible?’: The six-week sprint to opening night Credibly reversing gender in relation to Macbeth’s violence and paranoia is a masterstroke, and a deeply feminist one, that mocks misogyny and exploitation in the entertainment industry, while giving a broad licence to comedy that’s just plain wrong – and a springboard from which to vault into Mackenzie’s nihilistic acceptance of her fate. Genuine pathos attends Hodgson’s marvellous metamorphosis from an awkward 13-year-old to the beautiful child tyrant Mackenzie becomes, and even Britton’s overwhelming caricature of a stage mother wrenches tragedy from its opposite. The play isn’t a fully fledged musical, but – between all the intrigue and silliness that erupts the moment the cameras stop rolling – it is buoyed by slick street choreography and catchy pop songs. It’s also flamboyantly costumed and lit, with all the glam outfits and faddish accessories a teen pop princess could want.



Mackenzie should prove a winner with almost everyone, though particularly younger audiences. It reminded me that Bell Shakespeare was the company that first gave me the theatre bug as a kid, and it’s a joy to watch a show guaranteed to spread the passion to a new generation.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead MUSICALS

Reg Livermore’s Ned Kelly: The Musical ★★★★★

Victorian Opera, Union Theatre, until July 25 Reg Livermore’s Ned Kelly: The Musical sets itself a challenge from the outset. First, which version of the much disputed Kelly story do you tell? Do you portray the famous outlaw as a folk hero or a villain? Then, once that is sorted, what tone should the whole thing have? After all, there are very real deaths and tragedies scattered throughout this story – and we all know how badly things turn out for the Kelly gang. From left: Luke London, Liam Head, Ethan Jones and Darcy Wain as the Kelly Gang. Casey Horsfield This new production by Victorian Opera navigates all of this deftly. The story firmly has its flag planted in the folk hero camp, but does not gloss over the harsher realities of the story. The crimes are grounded in their context and the scenes slip from high-energy numbers to heart-wrenching grief with deceptive ease. It’s fun without ever being glib and serious without seeming insincere.



There are many times you’ll watch a musical, have a great time, then not be able to hum a single bar the moment you get home. That’s not the case here. In Ned Kelly the music is exceptional: memorable, eclectic and highly accomplished. Conductor Simon Holt – who also provided additional music and orchestration, necessary because there was no complete score of the original – conducts the Victorian Opera Chamber Orchestra with verve. Related Article Arts Australian theatre is caught in a cancellation crisis – this obscure 1970s Ned Kelly musical offers hope Maria Mercedes as Ma Kelly uses her powerful voice to infuse every scene she is in with fierce love, rage and pride. Ethan Jones as Ned Kelly is a star on the rise; he is just as confident in a solo ballad as he is leading show highlight Gonna Rob a Bank. His Kelly is puckish while unwavering when it comes to fighting for what he feels is right. Melbourne’s opening night of Ned Kelly: The Musical was originally supposed to take place in 1978, but after premiering in Adelaide and then touring to Sydney, its season was cut short and the rest of the tour cancelled. With the recent cancellations of Waitress, Beetlejuice and Dear Evan Hansen, it’s an all-too-familiar scenario. Second chances don’t come around often, but it’s fortunate in this case that it did. It’s a very specific joy to watch a show and have it be familiar in a way so many are not; that it is built around stories you’ve heard your whole life, with settings that in some cases are almost just a stone’s throw away.



This isn’t a production that should languish in obscurity; this is a revamped homegrown musical that should be celebrated and seen widely – and far more frequently than every 48 years.

Reviewed by Elizabeth Flux MUSIC

Jeane ★★★★

The Tote, July 24 Melbourne institution The Tote has seen it all over the years, but crowd-surfing nuns might be a first. Two songs into Jeane’s launch for debut EP Sicko, a pair of the religious rebels appear on stage in prayer, before launching themselves into the sold-out crowd. Jeane perform at The Tote. Richard Clifford It’s the kind of irreverence that the Melbourne four-piece thrives on. Led by fiery frontwoman Jazz Johnston, Jeane is a shape-shifting musical enigma. Their music showcases a range of styles and moods, flitting from soft, piano-led songs – what Johnston describes on the night as “medicine” music – to short, sharp blasts with a punk rock heart.



Johnston’s magnetic presence seals the deal live: her vocals are soulful one minute, an ear-splitting yelp the next. There’s a cheeky smirk on her face as she sings, as if she’s letting the audience in on a secret. A shaky start to the male vocal harmonies irons out as the set continues; the camaraderie and synergy between the band members is palpable as they work in tandem to build to gorgeous, glorious climaxes, then simmer down again. These songs are good on record, but live, they explode. Under Johnston’s spell, the small venue feels both intimate and like a stadium. She commands the space, making use of every corner – from sitting on the edge of the stage and singing directly to punters in the front, to literally bouncing off the walls towards the end of the set, when she climbs onto tables and speaker stacks, slick with sweat as she screams into the microphone. Fizzing with energy: Jeane at The Tote. Richard Clifford The audience yells back, particularly during the chorus of propulsive single Cash, and it’s an ecstatic mess of noise and movement.



Unusually for a local act and this stage in particular, the band return for an encore and the place is fizzing with the energy of it all. Sickos, the lot of us.

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen THEATRE

Steel Magnolias ★★★★

Athenaeum Theatre, until August 16 Most people would have heard of the 1989 American movie starring a swath of Hollywood luminaries (Dolly Parton, Sally Field, Shirley MacLaine, Daryl Hannah, Olympia Dukakis, Julia Roberts), but it’s likely that not many would have realised that Steel Magnolias was a theatrical piece before it was successfully translated to screen. This production, on tour around the country, is based on the original play by Robert Harling and follows the same beats as the movie. From left: Jessica Redmayne, Belinda Giblin, Lisa McCune, Mandy Bishop, Lotte Beckett and Debra Lawrance in Steel Magnolias. Brett Boardman Director Lee Lewis eschews any drastic reinterpretation; the Southern American accents are retained (kudos to Jennifer White, dialect coach), and there are no attempts to modernise or change its location.



Once again Steel Magnolias is set inside Truvy’s (Mandy Bishop) home salon in Louisiana (motto: “There’s no such thing as natural beauty”). To the delight of nostalgics of the era, 1980s fashion and styles are in abundant display thanks to designer Simone Romaniuk – think stiff bouffant hair and soft pastel tones in the set dressing and wardrobe, with pink as the accent colour. It’s a busy thoroughfare: a site of information exchange, barbs, advice and laughter amid the hooded hair dryers, nail polish and hair rollers. There’s Annelle (Lotte Beckett), a newcomer to the town and recently hired hair stylist; M’Lynn (Lisa McCune) and her daughter Shelby (Jessica Redmayne), a young bride; Clairee (Tracy Mann), a widow rediscovering independence; and Ouiser (Belinda Giblin), the neighbourhood grouch. Steel Magnolias is ultimately a paean to the camaraderie between women. Brett Boardman All the big moments are dramatised in this cosy salon that spans a couple of years, including births, marriages, heartbreak, divorce, disease, sacrifice and illness. The salon acts as a safe space for confession and solace, and in between the divulging of secrets and gossip, the play explores the bond between mother and daughter and the support of community.



The collective’s emotional strength is to be sorely tested because these steel magnolias, with their metaphorical mix of floral charms and gritty centres, must rally around when death eventually comes for one in their fold. Related Article Visual art ‘I’ve seen a lot of Monet’s water lilies. Do I really need to see any more?’ It’s a character-driven narrative that focuses on the personal stories and interrelationships between the six women; the men – their partners and sons – are referred to but never seen, relegated offstage. As an ensemble, the actors work well together – the wisecracks and hard-won wisdom that bounce off each other feel authentic. It’s impossible to single out any for individual praise, as they all acquit themselves with the ease and professionalism that can only exist after decades in the business. The play teeters between comedy and tragedy; every time it veers toward melodrama or is at risk of appearing too mawkish, a snappy quip manages to bring some light relief.



Steel Magnolias is ultimately a paean to the camaraderie between women, and this production sizzles with the energy of a megawatt hairdryer as it navigates life’s big and small moments. Go see it with your posse of girlfriends.

Reviewed by Thuy On DANCE

Vista ★★

Stephanie Lake Company, Malthouse, until August 1 The first half of Stephanie Lake’s Vista is a glib imitation of dance theatre, a succession of predictable shapes and transitions and opaque fragments of drama, each section falling away to reveal another just the same – like slices of a grey sausage. Vista by Stephanie Lake Company at the Malthouse Theatre. Pippa Samaya Or perhaps, more poetically, like the fluttering of an empty sleeve. Movement without bodied substance. Profluent sameness. An impersonal exercise composed for a camera-like gaze rather than the shared space of live performance.



And what is our reward for all this smoothness? A colourful burlesque. In part two, the first half is reperformed as a hectic carousel: scenes run backwards and dancers mock their former reserve with extravagant weeping, while others loudly commentate on the movements. There are two problems with this device. First, the opening really is a bore: plausible convolutions ornamented with undulations; affectless attitudinising amounting to a necropolitan chic. It’s the choreographic equivalent of a monotone recitation. Editor's pick Melbourne live reviews Pretty Woman the movie is beloved. Does it work as a musical? Second, part two is actually not much better. Yes, the constant swapping of partners and the increased energy and messiness create the impression of spontaneity, but it’s the same drab material. The improvement is largely a matter of speed and effort. There is more colour and more dash and more enthusiasm. But beneath the structural gimmickry, the choreographic language remains unchanged, mechanical and lacking any strong organising subjectivity. Lake has inherited the miscellaneous contemporary dance legacy of those choreographers with whom she once danced. Yet, sometimes, her work can seem curtailed by that inheritance, neither tracing it to its sources nor looking elsewhere. It is, in other words, oddly featureless.



Of course, I should resist such sweeping statements but, really, I wish this piece had a third part: another turn of the carousel, carrying us into a genuinely new and improbable vista, introducing more than a clever replay of something that we’ve seen before.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: A sprint finish and a rare double: How Australia’s new middle distance sensation toppled a champion
World.content:
SportAthleticsCommonwealth Games A sprint finish and a rare double: How Australia’s new middle distance sensation toppled a champion Michael Gleeson July 31, 2026 — 9:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“Rose! Rose! Imagine Alan! He’ll be so excited.” Alan is the groundskeeper at the Newcastle athletics track where Rose Davies and Jess Hull train. Davies was in the media zone, a second Commonwealth gold medal won in the 5000m, a flag on her shoulders, finishing a video interview. She turned excitedly to Hull, her Australian teammate and Olympic silver medallist. An elated Rose Davies wins gold in the 5000m at the Commonwealth Games ahead of Jess Hull in Glasgow. AP Photo/Alastair Grant “He’ll have been watching. He’ll be so happy,” Davies beamed.



Related Article Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games 2026 as it happened: Historic gold for Australia at the track, sprint stars win through to 200m final; Aussie cyclist sets world record For years Hull has been the mentor, pushing Davies along. In the home straight of the 5000m in Glasgow, Hull might have preferred she didn’t do quite so much pushing. Hull knew with 150 metres to go that Australia were going to win silver and gold. Davies didn’t think that. She didn’t let herself think anything; she had Jess Hull on her shoulder and had the sick realisation she had to try to beat an Olympic silver medallist in a sprint to the line. Davies doesn’t yet grasp that Hull was thinking the same thing, that she would have to go stride for stride with Rose Davies, the woman who only nights ago won the 10km race and was able to elevate herself into history.



On Monday night Davies surprised herself when she won gold in the 10,000m. On Thursday night after holding out Hull in that sprint down the home straight she added the 5000m gold. No woman in the history of the Commonwealth Games had ever won the double. Davies now has. Don’t lightly move on from that. The middle distances races at the Commonwealth Games have fielded greats of the sport. Davies leads Hull to the line. Getty Images “Oh my God! Oh my gosh! I can’t believe it. I’m so so happy. To win in the 10k was a dream, and then I knew I had to refocus. And yeah, to win in the 5k is just crazy, yeah?” she said.



“I can’t believe it. It means the world to me. I mean, as a little girl you watch the Commonwealth Games and you see your idols on the screen and you want that to be you and I just can’t believe that I’ve achieved that.” With four laps to go Scotland’s Megan Keith broke for the lead. The crowd in the stands went with her but not the crowd behind her on the track. The field gave her short a leash. The crowd gave her another leg. Rose Davies and Jess Hull celebrate after winning gold and silver in the women’s 5000m. AP Photo/Alastair Grant It is a small track at Scotstoun, a boutique stadium, but the stands shook as the Scot counted down the laps and held her lead. With three laps to go Davies made her move and tightened the gap on Keith. Hull tied her caravan to Davies and stayed with her. With two laps to go Keith still had the lead but Davies was on her shoulder. Hull was sweating on Davies. Uganda’s Esther Chebet, England’s Hannah Nuttall and Kenya’s Carolin Nyaga were all clinging on but you sensed they were flagging.



Related Article Commonwealth Games Five years ago, this Aussie had never tried cycling. She’s now a gold medallist With one lap to go Keith had the lead. Just. Davies and Hull looked stronger and poised to kick up a gear. The other three faded. At the 150-metre mark Keith flagged. Davies pushed around her and Hull followed. “With 150 to go, I realised we were going to go 1-2 and that was pretty incredible,” said Hull who ran the mile heat on Wednesday and will run the final of that event on Saturday night. “Then I was already sort of thinking, ‘I wish this was only a mile’. Kicking at the end of the five is a different beast [to the mile] and I think my tactics were quite raw out there. I think a few times I found myself not really quite knowing what to do, which doesn’t happen in the 15 [1500m], but in the five it was a little bit of foreign territory.



“I think I might have played some cards very early in that first two to three [km] when there was just a few shifts, and I realised at the top of that straight I was like, oh, I might be one card short for what Rose is going to throw at me.” By the top of that straight Keith had been cut, Australia were going to double. Hull had the reputation, the experience and the medals from world championships and Olympics, but Davies had the legs. She was relentless in that final straight. She crossed in 14:44.53, 0.48 seconds ahead of Hull. The pair embraced and cried and smiled and hugged. All at once. They jogged another lap in celebration. “Jess is obviously a massive inspiration to me. She’s done so much, and she’s such a good role model for the sport. To be in a sprint finish with her is crazy. We both train at the same track in Newcastle, and I see her like week to week. To have two Newcastle girls gunning for the line in a Commonwealth Games, and to come first and second is insane and so good for Newcastle.” Hull felt banking a silver medal would help her try to win the mile on Saturday.



“It almost just takes the pressure off for the mile now. I think a lot of why I wanted to do the 5000 was I didn’t have a Commonwealth medal, so even if you look back at world indoors, I ran two events because I almost wanted to go into the 1500 final having already won a medal. Because then it’s just like I can breathe a bit,“ she said. (Hull’s pet event is the 1500 but the distance is adjusted to 1600m (a mile) at these Games.) “I don’t know too many people that would have said Australia 1-2 in the 5000 12 months ago, two years ago. So for us to do it is very special. There’s so much pride there for being two Aussies, going 1-2, but also just for what Rose and just what she has done.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

Strike action that stopped Brisbane’s ferry network on Friday has concluded, with CityCats gradually churning back into service from 10am.

The strike, which cancelled all services for two hours, was part of wider industrial action that will run for the week – through to Friday, August 7 – and will include cancelled services and ticketing equipment not being available.

CityCats stopped running at whichever stop they were closest to at 8am. Julius Dennis

Unionists had claimed they were forced to take action after negotiations between the Australian Maritime Union and the boats’ operator, RiverCity Ferries, fell over.

Signs posted by the council at terminals across the city warned ferries would stop running at whichever stop they were closest to at 8am.

World.title: Labor ignored internal report revealing toll of scrapping Baby Boomer health rebate
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAged care Labor ignored internal report revealing toll of scrapping Baby Boomer health rebate Brittany Busch July 31, 2026 — 10:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Labor was warned that scrapping the private health rebate for over-65s meant some pensioners would have to cut back on spending or go without cover, according to documents released to the Coalition under freedom of information laws. Opposition health and aged care spokeswoman Anne Ruston said on Friday the documents revealed that the Department of Health had used fictional case studies to demonstrate the effects of Labor’s budget change on older Australians, showing that some would rein in already strained budgets and others would drop their private health insurance altogether. Coalition aged care spokeswoman Anne Ruston vowed to fight the changes. Alex Ellinghausen Labor announced in April it would scrap the Howard-era bonus for seniors as it wrangles with the $47 billion aged care sector plagued by workforce and resource challenges. Health and Ageing Minister Mark Butler said the change would free up funding for under-pressure aged care services. Ruston has vowed to fight the changes in the Senate, saying older Australians on fixed retirement incomes were the least able to respond to price shocks such as the hundreds of dollars extra per year they can expect to pay without the rebate.



Older Australians receive a rebate up to 8 per cent higher than younger people on a similar income. Related Article Aged care Labor’s reforms harm the people they’re supposed to help: aged care watchdog The upper house, where the Coalition, Greens and crossbenchers can join forces to block government legislation, has proven a minefield for Labor on aged care reform. The government has twice in the past year caved to Senate pressure, first agreeing to fast-track the release of 20,000 home care packages and then to guarantee a new layer of human oversight for the algorithm that assesses care package needs. “We will do everything we can in the parliament to block these changes and have called for a Senate inquiry to pursue the truth about who will be most affected by this new tax,” Ruston said in a statement. “Mark Butler has badly underestimated the damage his own policy will do.” Ruston also pointed to polling commissioned by Private Healthcare Australia that showed more than a third of over-65s with private health said they were more likely to drop their cover without the premium rebate.



Treasury has forecast only 44,000 of the 3 million over-65s with private health insurance would be pushed into the public health system because of the changes. Responding to reports first published by News Ltd, Butler on Friday said he was confident in the department modelling and took a swipe at the Queensland, NSW and Tasmanian governments, which have rebelled against the change and argued it would increase the burden carried by their state health services. “I’m a little surprised, frankly, that the state governments have swallowed the rather self-serving modelling that the insurance industry itself is putting out there,” he told Seven’s Sunrise program. Butler said every dollar saved on the premium rebate would go back into supporting older Australians in other ways, such as funding more aged care beds. Health and Ageing Minister Mark Butler is overseeing sweeping reforms to aged care and the NDIS. Alex Ellinghausen



“We’ve put an eye-watering amount of extra money into aged care over the last few years to get it out of the position that the royal commission described it, out of neglect. And to fund the extra demand that’s coming from the ageing and the Baby Boomer generation … that sometimes involves difficult decisions in a budget,” he said. Butler said older Australians would still get a rebate on private health insurance, but it would be based on their income like everyone else. “Two households next to each other, for example, on $50,000, one of them over 65, the other household in their 40s or in their 50s with kids, they’ll now both receive the same subsidy from ... taxpayers to pay for their private health insurance.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: ASX jumps after Wall Street rally; HSBC sells $36b Australian home loan portfolio to US giant
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX jumps after Wall Street rally; HSBC sells $36b Australian home loan portfolio to US giant Stan Choe Updated July 31, 2026 — 10:04am ,first published July 31, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has jumped at the open after a monster day for Microsoft’s stock led a powerful rebound on Wall Street, while computer-chip companies regained some of their sharp recent losses. The S&P/ASX 200 surged 85.8 points, or 1 per cent, to 9053.5 in early trade. The bourse lost 0.8 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.35¢. Technology stocks continue to drive the direction of Wall Street. Bloomberg Global bank HSBC is selling its $36 billion Australian home loan portfolio to private equity giant Blackstone, and it will wind down the rest of its local retail banking business over the next 18 months. The banking group on Friday said it was quitting retail banking in Australia to focus on banking commercial and corporate clients, as part of a simplification push. Overnight, the S&P 500 rallied 1.7 per cent and more than recovered its drop from the day before, which was its worst in seven weeks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 613 points, or 1.2 per cent. The Nasdaq composite, which is full of artificial-intelligence stocks, rallied 2.8 per cent a day after it fell 9.8 per cent below its record set last month.



On Wall Street, Microsoft led the way and leaped 15.5 per cent for its best day in nearly 18 years after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Growth was strong for its Azure cloud business, and CEO Satya Nadella said it reflects how customers are using Microsoft to move into AI. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates As the Fed sits tight on interest rates, investors take action Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Perhaps just as importantly for Wall Street, Microsoft did not announce a big increase in how much it plans to spend on AI investments, something that several other Big Tech rivals have done. Worries are high that such spending is eating into companies’ cash flows and may not ultimately be worth it if AI does not produce as much productivity and profits as promised. Apple released its results after the closing bell, with sales and profits beating Wall Street expectations, fuelled by its customers snapping up iPhones and MacBooks amid price increases across the consumer electronics sector. Driving Apple’s results was a 21.7 per cent increase in iPhone sales to $US54.25 billion ($77.2 billion), above analyst estimates of $US53.86 billion, according to LSEG data. Those iPhone sales were Apple’s best-ever for a third quarter, when phone sales typically begin to slow as customers anticipate new models during the fall. Apple shares are 3.3 per cent lower in after-hours trade.



Amazon said it will be increasing this year’s capital spending on technology, mostly artificial intelligence, by an additional 10 per cent after the tech and e-commerce giant delivered strong profits and net sales during for fiscal second quarter, helped by surging growth in its prominent cloud computing unit. Amazon shares surged 9.4 per cent in after-hours trade. The company said that sales in its cloud computing unit called AWS rose 37 per cent during the April-June period, faster than the 28 per cent clip in the previous quarter and marking the fastest rate of growth in 18 quarters. CEO and President Andy Jassy disclosed to investors on the call that Amazon now expects capital spending to total $US220 billion, which also includes outlays on robots, semiconductors and satellites. That’s up from the $US200 billion investment plan that was announced in February and well above the $US128 billion in capital spending for all of last year Meta Platforms fell 8 per cent. The parent company of Facebook and Instagram reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though it made slightly more in revenue than expected. It also raised the lower end of its forecasted range for spending on investments this year. Companies involved in the making of the computer memory and processors that such “hyperscalers” are buying to power their AI efforts rose, recovering some of the big losses they’ve taken on worries their stock prices shot too high in the euphoria around AI.



Micron Technology jumped 18.4 per cent, for example, to trim its loss for the week to 5 per cent. It was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500 after Microsoft. Lam Research, a supplier to the semiconductor industry, soared 18 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Chip giant Advanced Micro Devices rallied 13 per cent. On the losing end of Wall Street was Jersey Mike’s Subs. The sandwich chain’s stock fell 6 per cent in its first day of trading on the New York Stock Exchange. In the bond market, longer-term Treasury yields held steadier following their sharp accelerations Wednesday. They had jumped after the chairman of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, gave few clues about what the central bank will do with interest rates to combat the painfully high inflation that continues to hurt the country. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they can also slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury was 4.67 per cent, the same as late Wednesday. The 30-year Treasury yield ticked up to 5.22 per cent from 5.20 per cent, a day after it shot up from 5.09 per cent. Those yields move with investors’ expectations for inflation and economic growth in upcoming years. Warsh reaffirmed on Wednesday the Fed wants to get inflation back to 2 per cent, even though the central bank decided not to raise interest rates despite inflation remaining higher than that. He also implied the bond market may already be doing some of the Fed’s work to restrain inflation, and he pointed to how yields have climbed since the central bank’s last meeting six weeks earlier. That leaves investors questioning whether the Fed is prepared to act if inflation worsens, or whether it is relying on financial markets to achieve the same outcome, according to Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management. “If investors conclude that the latter is true, the credibility of the Fed’s inflation-fighting commitment could come under increasing scrutiny. Arguably, it already is.” President Donald Trump, who nominated Warsh to lead the Fed, has lobbied for lower interest rates even though they could cause inflation to accelerate.



Reports released Thursday suggested the US economy’s growth slowed by more during the spring than economists expected. A measure of Inflation, meanwhile, remained worse last month than the Federal Reserve’s target, but it slowed from May’s level. Related Article Opinion

Home loans Buckle up for the banks’ mortgage war! Home loans have fallen off a cliff Elizabeth Knight Business columnist In the oil market, prices eased. Brent crude, the international standard, fell 1.4 per cent to settle at $US86.88 per barrel. It had swung as low as $US72 early this month and as high as $US102 last week on uncertainty about whether the United States and Iran could reach a deal to allow oil tankers to move freely again from the Middle East to customers worldwide. In stock markets worldwide, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.2 per cent, and France’s CAC 40 rose 0.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves.



Seoul’s market has been at the centre of AI’s huge swings because it’s dominated by two tech titans, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. After more than doubling through this year’s first six months, the Kospi has plunged 34 per cent so far in July. Its drop on Thursday came as Samsung Electronics dipped 0.7 per cent. The tech giant reported a record profit for the spring and said demand for its chips continues to outpace supply, but its earnings nevertheless fell shy of analysts’ high expectations. World.title: Anthropic’s Claude AI hacked three real companies during testing
World.content:

Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic has revealed its Claude models broke into the live systems of three organisations during cybersecurity testing, days after rival OpenAI disclosed a similar issue.

The company said a misconfiguration left its testing environments connected to the internet, despite Claude being told in its prompt that it was in a sealed simulation. Believing the real companies it found were part of the exercise, Claude compromised them using basic techniques including weak passwords and unauthenticated endpoints.

On June 13, Anthropic suspended worldwide access to its two most powerful AI models. Bloomberg

More to come.
