World.title: Trump says Hamas will disarm under deal for Gaza to get new government
World.content:
Breaking WorldMiddle EastIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Trump says Hamas will disarm under deal for Gaza to get new government Nidal al-Mughrabi and Bo Erickson Updated July 31, 2026 — 9:45am ,first published 9:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cairo/washington: US President Donald Trump said Cairo talks between mediators and Hamas leaders had led to a “historic agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas” in what he described as structured phases. Sources close to the talks told Reuters earlier on Thursday that progress had been made, but it was uncertain if the agreement would hold, as an Israeli official had said the proposed terms were not satisfactory. US President Donald Trump at the White House on Thursday. AP Photo/Alex Brandon “This agreement is a critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government that will work closely with the Board of Peace to help the Palestinian people,” Trump said in a social media post late on Thursday (Washington time) as he thanked mediators Egypt, Qatar and Turkey. “At the same time, Israel will have the security it deserves, with Gaza no longer used as a base for terror attacks.”



The Israeli embassy in Washington and Hamas did not immediately respond to requests for comment about Trump’s post. Earlier, Israeli strikes killed at least six Palestinians in Gaza on Thursday, including two children, medics said. Palestinians inspect damage on Thursday, a day after an Israeli airstrike hit Gaza City. Bloomberg A Hamas official and a diplomat close to the Cairo talks said the progress would be tested by Israel’s response and whether this allowed a broad accord to be reached. However, the Israeli official earlier on Thursday, who declined to be identified, said Israel had rejected a proposal. “Israel demands the complete disarmament of Hamas, including the removal of weapons from Gaza and the complete demilitarisation of the Strip as a precondition for any process,” the official said.



“The 15-point document in question does not provide a satisfactory response to these demands and Israel conveyed its objections.” Hamas leaders are holding talks with mediators from Egypt, Qatar and Turkey on the second phase of Trump’s Gaza plan, as presented to them by his Board of Peace, which oversees its implementation. Smoke rises following an Israeli military strike in Gaza City on Tuesday. AP Photo/Jehad Alshrafi Russian Deputy Ambassador to the United Nations Anna Evstigneeva told the Security Council on Tuesday that a roadmap prepared by Trump’s Board of Peace envoy for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov, had so far failed to gain the support of Israel and Hamas, with the demilitarisation of Gaza remaining the main stumbling block. The Board of Peace declined comment on the Cairo talks earlier on Thursday. The diplomat close to the talks said the negotiations were making progress toward a roadmap that would see all heavy and light weapons in Gaza decommissioned.



The plan calls for a surge in humanitarian aid, governance by a civilian Palestinian administration, the disarmament of Hamas, the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza and the deployment of an international force to help maintain security. But progress has stalled in previous months. On Thursday, a Hamas official said the group was coming with a “positive and good” response, but did not say whether the group had agreed to fully disarm – a key sticking point in the talks over the past four months. Hamas wants Israel to commit to ending attacks on Gaza and withdrawing its forces. Sources close to Hamas said the group was willing to “confine and store” heavy weapons under a Palestinian body, not hand them over to Israel. Hamas did not comment on the matter.



It is not yet clear what will happen regarding light or personal weapons or whether the new Hamas stance will be accepted by Israel or the Board of Peace. The diplomat involved in the talks said the roadmap under discussion in Cairo would also see authority transferred in phases to the U.S.-backed National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), under the principle of “one authority, one law, one weapon”. The plan includes the elimination of tunnels, arms stockpiles and weapons production facilities, the diplomat said, adding that by the end of the process there would be no remaining militant infrastructure in Gaza. The diplomat described the roadmap as being based on reciprocal steps rather than trust. So far, the reality on the ground in Gaza remains far from this roadmap. The Israeli military has continued to expand its military occupation of Gaza, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu saying that Israel intends to expand the area under its control to 70 per cent of the enclave.



It remains unclear how many forces would be available to deploy with the planned International Stabilisation Force, and whether Israeli troops would withdraw from the enclave. Related Article Graphic content

Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israel investigating after photo of stripped and bound detainee is shared In Cairo, two Egyptian sources said Hamas had agreed to several contentious points, including the handover of weapons, but had requested changes regarding the definition of the infrastructure to be dismantled, adding more talks were underway. The truce halted full-scale fighting, but has not ended near-daily Israeli strikes. Health officials said separate Israeli strikes had killed at least two children, a woman and three men in Gaza on Thursday. The Israeli military said it struck Hamas militants in the enclave.



The latest deaths add to a toll of more than 1200 Palestinians, mostly civilians, killed by Israeli attacks since the ceasefire took effect, according to Gaza health officials. Four Israeli soldiers have been killed by militants in Gaza since the ceasefire. Hamas does not usually disclose its losses. Expanding marine parks around Lord Howe and Norfolk Island would mean Australia reaches its goal to protect 30 per cent of its oceans well before 2030.

The plan was announced by Environment Minister Murray Watt today alongside the 10-year review of how existing marine parks are working.

The proposed expansions would bring an additional 671,500 square kilometres of Australia’s waters under protection, protecting the areas’ high biodiversity of migratory seabirds, cetaceans, fish and sharks.

The review will include six new management plans for 44 Australian Marine Parks, which cover 2.37 million square kilometres of ocean – an area larger than Queensland and NSW combined.

Public consultation on the preparation of new management plans, and the proposed changes to Norfolk and Lord Howe marine parks, is open until 4pm AEST on September 30 through the Have Your Say portal.

The fishing industry will also be consulted directly, the government said.

World.title: This five-star production is Macbeth as you’ve never seen it before
World.content:
Key points THEATRE: Mackenzie is Yve Blake’s original, freewheeling adaptation of Macbeth

MUSICAL: After 48 years Ned Kelly: The Musical finally has its Melbourne premiere

MUSIC: Jeane’s songs are good on record, but live, they explode

THEATRE: Steel Magnolias is ultimately a paean to the camaraderie between women

is ultimately a paean to the camaraderie between women DANCE: Vista deploys a narrative device that doesn’t quite work

THEATRE

Mackenzie ★★★★★

Bell Shakespeare, Arts Centre Melbourne, until August 9 Bring me a bucket of water, would you? I’m writing a five-star review of a Bell Shakespeare show, and my hair might catch fire. (Five stars! Bell Shakespeare?) A scene from the Bell Shakespeare production of Mackenzie, a reimagining of Macbeth. Brett Boardman Australia’s most prominent Shakespeare company has been, for significant stretches of its history, bedevilled by incestuousness and mediocrity. No point denying it. I’ve followed Bell for decades now and its most reliable fare, oddly enough, tends to lie outside the Shakespearean canon. Over the years, it has done everything from Molière to Eugene O’Neill, and it usually rises to the occasion. But there’s never been anything half so funny and alive as Mackenzie. Yve Blake’s original, freewheeling adaptation of Macbeth relocates the action from the blasted heaths of medieval Scotland to a cutthroat realm behind the scenes of a children’s TV show. It’s comedic and dramatic genius – a pop girl transformation of the Scottish play that does for Shakespeare what Six did for the wives of Henry VIII.



In this version, King Duncan becomes tween TV star Dahlia (Anusha Thomas) – think Hannah Montana or a young Britney Spears, and you’ll get the idea – and the Macbeth-figure, Mackenzie (Kimberley Hodgson), is an overlooked child actor with a horrific bowl cut who plays Dahlia’s ugly duckling sidekick. Lady Macbeth is converted into Mackenzie’s manipulative stage mum, Ruth (Nikki Britton), while Banquo is Mackenzie’s best friend and fellow child star Beau (Ryan González). Ryan González and Kimberley Hodgson play best friends who have a wedge driven between them. Brett Boardman The witches? An eccentric make-up artist (Jane Watt) prone to strange prophetic “episodes”. Macduff? A butch lesbian and head of catering at the studio (Billie Palin) with more than enough reason for vengeance. Even telling you this much feels like a slight spoiler, given how much delight Shakespeare lovers will take in Blake’s inspired tweaks to the Bard’s dramatic architecture, and the hilarious Easter eggs and in-jokes sprinkled throughout the show.



Director Virginia Gay is one of the funniest women in Australian theatre, and the acting is brilliant across the board. Every single member of the cast achieves an exquisite level of clowning, and the energy and commitment and berserk stylisation of the performances take Mackenzie to another level as a satire of both showbiz and adolescence. Related Article Stage shows ‘What if my writing is terrible?’: The six-week sprint to opening night Credibly reversing gender in relation to Macbeth’s violence and paranoia is a masterstroke, and a deeply feminist one, that mocks misogyny and exploitation in the entertainment industry, while giving a broad licence to comedy that’s just plain wrong – and a springboard from which to vault into Mackenzie’s nihilistic acceptance of her fate. Genuine pathos attends Hodgson’s marvellous metamorphosis from an awkward 13-year-old to the beautiful child tyrant Mackenzie becomes, and even Britton’s overwhelming caricature of a stage mother wrenches tragedy from its opposite. The play isn’t a fully fledged musical, but – between all the intrigue and silliness that erupts the moment the cameras stop rolling – it is buoyed by slick street choreography and catchy pop songs. It’s also flamboyantly costumed and lit, with all the glam outfits and faddish accessories a teen pop princess could want.



Mackenzie should prove a winner with almost everyone, though particularly younger audiences. It reminded me that Bell Shakespeare was the company that first gave me the theatre bug as a kid, and it’s a joy to watch a show guaranteed to spread the passion to a new generation.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead MUSICALS

Reg Livermore’s Ned Kelly: The Musical ★★★★★

Victorian Opera, Union Theatre, until July 25 Reg Livermore’s Ned Kelly: The Musical sets itself a challenge from the outset. First, which version of the much disputed Kelly story do you tell? Do you portray the famous outlaw as a folk hero or a villain? Then, once that is sorted, what tone should the whole thing have? After all, there are very real deaths and tragedies scattered throughout this story – and we all know how badly things turn out for the Kelly gang. From left: Luke London, Liam Head, Ethan Jones and Darcy Wain as the Kelly Gang. Casey Horsfield This new production by Victorian Opera navigates all of this deftly. The story firmly has its flag planted in the folk hero camp, but does not gloss over the harsher realities of the story. The crimes are grounded in their context and the scenes slip from high-energy numbers to heart-wrenching grief with deceptive ease. It’s fun without ever being glib and serious without seeming insincere.



There are many times you’ll watch a musical, have a great time, then not be able to hum a single bar the moment you get home. That’s not the case here. In Ned Kelly the music is exceptional: memorable, eclectic and highly accomplished. Conductor Simon Holt – who also provided additional music and orchestration, necessary because there was no complete score of the original – conducts the Victorian Opera Chamber Orchestra with verve. Related Article Arts Australian theatre is caught in a cancellation crisis – this obscure 1970s Ned Kelly musical offers hope Maria Mercedes as Ma Kelly uses her powerful voice to infuse every scene she is in with fierce love, rage and pride. Ethan Jones as Ned Kelly is a star on the rise; he is just as confident in a solo ballad as he is leading show highlight Gonna Rob a Bank. His Kelly is puckish while unwavering when it comes to fighting for what he feels is right. Melbourne’s opening night of Ned Kelly: The Musical was originally supposed to take place in 1978, but after premiering in Adelaide and then touring to Sydney, its season was cut short and the rest of the tour cancelled. With the recent cancellations of Waitress, Beetlejuice and Dear Evan Hansen, it’s an all-too-familiar scenario. Second chances don’t come around often, but it’s fortunate in this case that it did. It’s a very specific joy to watch a show and have it be familiar in a way so many are not; that it is built around stories you’ve heard your whole life, with settings that in some cases are almost just a stone’s throw away.



This isn’t a production that should languish in obscurity; this is a revamped homegrown musical that should be celebrated and seen widely – and far more frequently than every 48 years.

Reviewed by Elizabeth Flux MUSIC

Jeane ★★★★

The Tote, July 24 Melbourne institution The Tote has seen it all over the years, but crowd-surfing nuns might be a first. Two songs into Jeane’s launch for debut EP Sicko, a pair of the religious rebels appear on stage in prayer, before launching themselves into the sold-out crowd. Jeane perform at The Tote. Richard Clifford It’s the kind of irreverence that the Melbourne four-piece thrives on. Led by fiery frontwoman Jazz Johnston, Jeane is a shape-shifting musical enigma. Their music showcases a range of styles and moods, flitting from soft, piano-led songs – what Johnston describes on the night as “medicine” music – to short, sharp blasts with a punk rock heart.



Johnston’s magnetic presence seals the deal live: her vocals are soulful one minute, an ear-splitting yelp the next. There’s a cheeky smirk on her face as she sings, as if she’s letting the audience in on a secret. A shaky start to the male vocal harmonies irons out as the set continues; the camaraderie and synergy between the band members is palpable as they work in tandem to build to gorgeous, glorious climaxes, then simmer down again. These songs are good on record, but live, they explode. Under Johnston’s spell, the small venue feels both intimate and like a stadium. She commands the space, making use of every corner – from sitting on the edge of the stage and singing directly to punters in the front, to literally bouncing off the walls towards the end of the set, when she climbs onto tables and speaker stacks, slick with sweat as she screams into the microphone. Fizzing with energy: Jeane at The Tote. Richard Clifford The audience yells back, particularly during the chorus of propulsive single Cash, and it’s an ecstatic mess of noise and movement.



Unusually for a local act and this stage in particular, the band return for an encore and the place is fizzing with the energy of it all. Sickos, the lot of us.

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen THEATRE

Steel Magnolias ★★★★

Athenaeum Theatre, until August 16 Most people would have heard of the 1989 American movie starring a swath of Hollywood luminaries (Dolly Parton, Sally Field, Shirley MacLaine, Daryl Hannah, Olympia Dukakis, Julia Roberts), but it’s likely that not many would have realised that Steel Magnolias was a theatrical piece before it was successfully translated to screen. This production, on tour around the country, is based on the original play by Robert Harling and follows the same beats as the movie. From left: Jessica Redmayne, Belinda Giblin, Lisa McCune, Mandy Bishop, Lotte Beckett and Debra Lawrance in Steel Magnolias. Brett Boardman Director Lee Lewis eschews any drastic reinterpretation; the Southern American accents are retained (kudos to Jennifer White, dialect coach), and there are no attempts to modernise or change its location.



Once again Steel Magnolias is set inside Truvy’s (Mandy Bishop) home salon in Louisiana (motto: “There’s no such thing as natural beauty”). To the delight of nostalgics of the era, 1980s fashion and styles are in abundant display thanks to designer Simone Romaniuk – think stiff bouffant hair and soft pastel tones in the set dressing and wardrobe, with pink as the accent colour. It’s a busy thoroughfare: a site of information exchange, barbs, advice and laughter amid the hooded hair dryers, nail polish and hair rollers. There’s Annelle (Lotte Beckett), a newcomer to the town and recently hired hair stylist; M’Lynn (Lisa McCune) and her daughter Shelby (Jessica Redmayne), a young bride; Clairee (Tracy Mann), a widow rediscovering independence; and Ouiser (Belinda Giblin), the neighbourhood grouch. Steel Magnolias is ultimately a paean to the camaraderie between women. Brett Boardman All the big moments are dramatised in this cosy salon that spans a couple of years, including births, marriages, heartbreak, divorce, disease, sacrifice and illness. The salon acts as a safe space for confession and solace, and in between the divulging of secrets and gossip, the play explores the bond between mother and daughter and the support of community.



The collective’s emotional strength is to be sorely tested because these steel magnolias, with their metaphorical mix of floral charms and gritty centres, must rally around when death eventually comes for one in their fold. Related Article Visual art ‘I’ve seen a lot of Monet’s water lilies. Do I really need to see any more?’ It’s a character-driven narrative that focuses on the personal stories and interrelationships between the six women; the men – their partners and sons – are referred to but never seen, relegated offstage. As an ensemble, the actors work well together – the wisecracks and hard-won wisdom that bounce off each other feel authentic. It’s impossible to single out any for individual praise, as they all acquit themselves with the ease and professionalism that can only exist after decades in the business. The play teeters between comedy and tragedy; every time it veers toward melodrama or is at risk of appearing too mawkish, a snappy quip manages to bring some light relief.



Steel Magnolias is ultimately a paean to the camaraderie between women, and this production sizzles with the energy of a megawatt hairdryer as it navigates life’s big and small moments. Go see it with your posse of girlfriends.

Reviewed by Thuy On DANCE

Vista ★★

Stephanie Lake Company, Malthouse, until August 1 The first half of Stephanie Lake’s Vista is a glib imitation of dance theatre, a succession of predictable shapes and transitions and opaque fragments of drama, each section falling away to reveal another just the same – like slices of a grey sausage. Vista by Stephanie Lake Company at the Malthouse Theatre. Pippa Samaya Or perhaps, more poetically, like the fluttering of an empty sleeve. Movement without bodied substance. Profluent sameness. An impersonal exercise composed for a camera-like gaze rather than the shared space of live performance.



And what is our reward for all this smoothness? A colourful burlesque. In part two, the first half is reperformed as a hectic carousel: scenes run backwards and dancers mock their former reserve with extravagant weeping, while others loudly commentate on the movements. There are two problems with this device. First, the opening really is a bore: plausible convolutions ornamented with undulations; affectless attitudinising amounting to a necropolitan chic. It’s the choreographic equivalent of a monotone recitation. Editor's pick Melbourne live reviews Pretty Woman the movie is beloved. Does it work as a musical? Second, part two is actually not much better. Yes, the constant swapping of partners and the increased energy and messiness create the impression of spontaneity, but it’s the same drab material. The improvement is largely a matter of speed and effort. There is more colour and more dash and more enthusiasm. But beneath the structural gimmickry, the choreographic language remains unchanged, mechanical and lacking any strong organising subjectivity. Lake has inherited the miscellaneous contemporary dance legacy of those choreographers with whom she once danced. Yet, sometimes, her work can seem curtailed by that inheritance, neither tracing it to its sources nor looking elsewhere. It is, in other words, oddly featureless.



Of course, I should resist such sweeping statements but, really, I wish this piece had a third part: another turn of the carousel, carrying us into a genuinely new and improbable vista, introducing more than a clever replay of something that we’ve seen before.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: A sprint finish and a rare double: How Australia’s new middle distance sensation toppled a champion
World.content:
SportAthleticsCommonwealth Games A sprint finish and a rare double: How Australia’s new middle distance sensation toppled a champion Michael Gleeson July 31, 2026 — 9:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“Rose! Rose! Imagine Alan! He’ll be so excited.” Alan is the groundskeeper at the Newcastle athletics track where Rose Davies and Jess Hull train. Davies was in the media zone, a second Commonwealth gold medal won in the 5000m, a flag on her shoulders, finishing a video interview. She turned excitedly to Hull, her Australian teammate and Olympic silver medallist. An elated Rose Davies wins gold in the 5000m at the Commonwealth Games ahead of Jess Hull in Glasgow. AP Photo/Alastair Grant “He’ll have been watching. He’ll be so happy,” Davies beamed.



Related Article Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games 2026 as it happened: Historic gold for Australia at the track, sprint stars win through to 200m final; Aussie cyclist sets world record For years Hull has been the mentor, pushing Davies along. In the home straight of the 5000m in Glasgow, Hull might have preferred she didn’t do quite so much pushing. Hull knew with 150 metres to go that Australia were going to win silver and gold. Davies didn’t think that. She didn’t let herself think anything; she had Jess Hull on her shoulder and had the sick realisation she had to try to beat an Olympic silver medallist in a sprint to the line. Davies doesn’t yet grasp that Hull was thinking the same thing, that she would have to go stride for stride with Rose Davies, the woman who only nights ago won the 10km race and was able to elevate herself into history.



On Monday night Davies surprised herself when she won gold in the 10,000m. On Thursday night after holding out Hull in that sprint down the home straight she added the 5000m gold. No woman in the history of the Commonwealth Games had ever won the double. Davies now has. Don’t lightly move on from that. The middle distances races at the Commonwealth Games have fielded greats of the sport. Davies leads Hull to the line. Getty Images “Oh my God! Oh my gosh! I can’t believe it. I’m so so happy. To win in the 10k was a dream, and then I knew I had to refocus. And yeah, to win in the 5k is just crazy, yeah?” she said.



“I can’t believe it. It means the world to me. I mean, as a little girl you watch the Commonwealth Games and you see your idols on the screen and you want that to be you and I just can’t believe that I’ve achieved that.” With four laps to go Scotland’s Megan Keith broke for the lead. The crowd in the stands went with her but not the crowd behind her on the track. The field gave her short a leash. The crowd gave her another leg. Rose Davies and Jess Hull celebrate after winning gold and silver in the women’s 5000m. AP Photo/Alastair Grant It is a small track at Scotstoun, a boutique stadium, but the stands shook as the Scot counted down the laps and held her lead. With three laps to go Davies made her move and tightened the gap on Keith. Hull tied her caravan to Davies and stayed with her. With two laps to go Keith still had the lead but Davies was on her shoulder. Hull was sweating on Davies. Uganda’s Esther Chebet, England’s Hannah Nuttall and Kenya’s Carolin Nyaga were all clinging on but you sensed they were flagging.



Related Article Commonwealth Games Five years ago, this Aussie had never tried cycling. She’s now a gold medallist With one lap to go Keith had the lead. Just. Davies and Hull looked stronger and poised to kick up a gear. The other three faded. At the 150-metre mark Keith flagged. Davies pushed around her and Hull followed. “With 150 to go, I realised we were going to go 1-2 and that was pretty incredible,” said Hull who ran the mile heat on Wednesday and will run the final of that event on Saturday night. “Then I was already sort of thinking, ‘I wish this was only a mile’. Kicking at the end of the five is a different beast [to the mile] and I think my tactics were quite raw out there. I think a few times I found myself not really quite knowing what to do, which doesn’t happen in the 15 [1500m], but in the five it was a little bit of foreign territory.



“I think I might have played some cards very early in that first two to three [km] when there was just a few shifts, and I realised at the top of that straight I was like, oh, I might be one card short for what Rose is going to throw at me.” By the top of that straight Keith had been cut, Australia were going to double. Hull had the reputation, the experience and the medals from world championships and Olympics, but Davies had the legs. She was relentless in that final straight. She crossed in 14:44.53, 0.48 seconds ahead of Hull. The pair embraced and cried and smiled and hugged. All at once. They jogged another lap in celebration. “Jess is obviously a massive inspiration to me. She’s done so much, and she’s such a good role model for the sport. To be in a sprint finish with her is crazy. We both train at the same track in Newcastle, and I see her like week to week. To have two Newcastle girls gunning for the line in a Commonwealth Games, and to come first and second is insane and so good for Newcastle.” Hull felt banking a silver medal would help her try to win the mile on Saturday.



“It almost just takes the pressure off for the mile now. I think a lot of why I wanted to do the 5000 was I didn’t have a Commonwealth medal, so even if you look back at world indoors, I ran two events because I almost wanted to go into the 1500 final having already won a medal. Because then it’s just like I can breathe a bit,“ she said. (Hull’s pet event is the 1500 but the distance is adjusted to 1600m (a mile) at these Games.) “I don’t know too many people that would have said Australia 1-2 in the 5000 12 months ago, two years ago. So for us to do it is very special. There’s so much pride there for being two Aussies, going 1-2, but also just for what Rose and just what she has done.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: Brad Olsen steps down as chief executive at Infometrics
World.content:
High-profile economist Brad Olsen is stepping down from his role as chief executive at Infometrics, to focus on his principal economist role.

Chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan will move into an acting managing director role.

"I'm wanting to better focus my time on ensuring as many people as possible - Infometrics clients, decision makers and the public at large - are better informed and that economics is put simply," Olsen said,

"That remains the mission at Infometrics, and I'm stoked Gareth is stepping into the managing director role to keep the business moving forward. Moving back to the principal economist role means I can best dedicate my time to getting out and interacting with our clients, and seeing the economy up close and personal."

Olsen said it felt like the right time to make the change.

"I have spent a third of my career, before 30, as chief executive and it's a lot of energy on top of the economist role flying around the country."

Kiernan joined Infometrics in 1999, and was previously managing director in 2006, before moving to become operations director in 2014.

"I'm excited about the opportunity to build on the great work done by Brad leading Infometrics, and I look forward to driving further growth in the business," Kiernan said.

World.title: Opportunity Party reveals candidates for 40 electorates
World.content:
The Opportunity Party has unveiled its party list for the election, with 40 candidates all contesting electorate seats.

Making the announcement at WQ Hotel in Wellington, leader Qiulae Wong said the team were standing because they expected "better than the current political parties are delivering".

The latest RNZ-Reid Research poll put the party at 4.7 percent, on the cusp of making it over the 5 percent threshold that would get the party into Parliament even without winning an electorate.

Securing 5 percent of the vote would net the party six MPs.

Second on the list was Wong's deputy Daniel Eb, standing in Kaipara ki Mahurangi, who previously founded an 'open farm day' initiative and handles the party's communications.

Kayla Kingdon-Bebb, Daniel Eb and Jodie Kuntzsch. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Running for Wellington North, third-ranked Jessica Hammond has been a candidate for the party in every election it has contested and works in policy.

Fourth is Dr Kayla Kingdon-Bebb, also in Wellington, who is the former chief executive of WWF New Zealand and Department of Conservation policy director with expertise in Treaty law and resource management.

Fifth is Ngāi Tahu leader Eden Skipper, standing in Christchurch, who the party said has researched "alternative economic futures".

And sixth was Jodie Kuntzsch, in Nelson, who led the establishment of Moananui - a group that partners fishing, aquaculture and research groups - and has 20 years' experience in the seafood industry.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Mt Albert the target

Wong told reporters the party was only looking to win the Mt Albert seat - her electorate - and everywhere else candidates were campaigning for the party vote.

"Our support is spread across the country, and we believe that there are certainly at least 150,000 New Zealanders out there that are committed to this mission with us," she said.

Wong was confident the candidates had the policy expertise required to make a difference in government.

"People that have worked in the public service, in our full list, we have both central and local government experience, so I think we we do possess a lot of that knowledge of how things work," she said.

Eden Skipper and Jessica Hammond. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"But I think importantly, we also bring a fresh perspective that can challenge the status quo because that has not been delivering what New Zealanders need, and that's why we are bringing this new perspective to politics."

Opportunity's flagship policies include: establishing a universal basic income of up to $370 a week, and a 1.75 percent annual tax on the value or urban land and 0.5 percent on rural land.

Wong acknowledged those were unlikely to be supported by major parties, but she said it was important to show New Zealanders the direction Opportunity would be pursuing.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Opportunity has been open to working with any party - whether that be a coalition, confidence and supply agreement or from the cross-benches - and Wong said its door remained open to National, even after leader Christopher Luxon ruled out working with them.

She was not worried that rule-out would dissuade centre-right voters from supporting Opportunity.

"We've actually had the opposite. I've had numerous emails and messages from former National voters that were disappointed in Christopher Luxon's comments and say that they want to see us working with them."

World.title: 'Not acceptable': 33 percent Watercare payrises knocked back by councillors
World.content:
Pay rises knocked back by Auckland Council committee Nine To Noon Download MP3 17m

A proposal to give Watercare board members a 33 percent payrise has been knocked back by an Auckland Council committee.

A paper from staff to the Appointment and Performance Committee detailed Watercare's governance responsibilities had increased following water reform and balance sheet separation, and as such it was appropriate to increase board remuneration.

An 18 per cent pay rise for board members of Auckland Transport and Tataki Unlimited was also proposed.

Appointment and performance committee chairperson Daniel Newman told Nine to Noon reviews of pay were done once a term, but he was expecting to see a "modest increase".

"The quantum of fees proposed is not acceptable to me or my colleagues," he said.

Newman said the 33 percent increase was a "surprise" and the council needed to be mindful of the public perception around this.

"I accept people need to be remunerated but... the amounts go well beyond what is reasonable to the people of Auckland.

"[We] don't expect Aucklanders would've accepted those figures."

Newman expected the next step would be a further paper with different options on increases, but ultimately, he said it would be up to shareholders to make a call and "politicians will decide this".

The money needed for paying salary increases to the organisations would come from within the budget envelopes of the organisations themselves, Newman said. But these were ultimately council-controlled, so ratepayers were the backstop.

"My constituents in Manurewa and Papakura include some of the poorest people in Auckland, so I'm mindful of how they will see this."

During Thursday's discussions, Newman said there was support for the paper to be withdrawn.

World.title: Tom Walsh settles for Commonwealth Games silver as three-peat bid falls short
World.content:
Tom Walsh was chasing his third straight Commonwealth Games title in Glasgow. Simon Stacpoole / www.photosport.nz

Tom Walsh admits he let the occasion get the better of him as his bid for a historic third straight Commonwealth Games shot put title ended in silver on Friday - a disappointment the veteran says has only sharpened his focus on the Los Angeles Olympics.

The veteran shotputter had to settle for silver in Glasgow after Nigeria's Chukwuebuka Enekwechi snatched gold with a fifth-round throw of 21.07m.

"I'm not here to get second. Between me and my team, we want to achieve some things in the next two years and today wasn't up to that standard," Walsh said.

The 33-year-old admitted he had let the occasion get the better of him despite arriving in outstanding physical shape.

"Physically, I'm in great shape. Just mentally I didn't quite put it together today. I let the occasion get the better of me, which is very disappointing, but it also gives us some room to improve."

Despite the frustration, Walsh said the result had not shaken his confidence and was already looking towards the Diamond League finals before building to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

"LA is my goal at the moment, and we'll see what comes after that. If I'm still loving it and still enjoying it, I'll keep going if I can make it work."

Asked whether that could include a fifth Commonwealth Games appearance, Walsh joked "I mightn't have a marriage if I do a fifth".

The two-time Commonwealth champion looked on track to make history after opening with 21.03m, to lead through the first three rounds.

But after fouling in the third and fourth rounds, Enekwechi edged ahead in the fifth. Walsh's response landed outside the sector - taking out a television microphone - before his final throw failed to reclaim the lead.

While silver was a bitter pill to swallow, Walsh said experience had helped him appreciate the achievement.

"One thing with age is I understand how rare these things can be, so having the weight of a medal around my neck is a pretty cool feeling.

"With age and having a young family it does bring perspective ... obviously I'm disappointed with how I threw and not getting the job done, but I don't think I'm going to be as hard on myself as I was earlier in my career."

Anna Grimaldi (NZL) wins bronze in the Para 100m T47 Final on Day 7 of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland on Thursday 30 July 2026. (Photo: Simon Stacpoole / www.photosport.nz) Simon Stacpoole / www.photosport.nz

Earlier, three-time Paralympic champion Anna Grimaldi marked her Commonwealth Games debut with bronze in the women's T47 100m.

Despite having competed at international level for more than a decade, Glasgow is the first time Grimaldi has competed in a Commonwealth Games as part of an integrated New Zealand Team.

The 28-year-old said it was remarkable to still be experiencing new milestones after 13 years in the sport.

"This is my 10th time representing New Zealand in the black singlet... it's kind of crazy that far in to be having these new opportunities."

Despite being disappointed with how she ran, Grimaldi said competing at her first Commonwealth Games had been "really special", describing the chance to race "in a new team, in a new environment, in a new country, at a new event" as one she had long anticipated.

World.title: Winston Peters ‘inviting a sacking’ with attack on Chinese-born MP, Helen Clark says
World.content:
Helen Clark discusses Peters’ comments to Lawrence Xu-Nan Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Former Prime Minister Helen Clark says Winston Peters' comments about a Chinese-born Green MP appears to be "inviting a sacking".

On Wednesday, Peters told Lawrence Xu-Nan to "go back to your own country" during a debate in Parliament.

"That's where they lie like a flatfish, but they don't lie like that here, all right?" Peters said.

China has expressed its concerns about the remarks, which have been reported by the South China Morning Post.

Clark on Friday told Morning Report they were "very concerning" on two levels.

"Obviously on the level of an MP who came to New Zealand as a child, who's been here for 32 years ... I mean, this is quite extraordinary and I think sends a chill right around our migrant communities as to whether people are ever actually going to feel part of, and be welcomed in, New Zealand," she said.

"But then to add to that, you have the line around 'go back to your own country, where they lie like flatfish'. Now that country, of course, is a very great power, it's our largest trading partner - that is no way to speak about it.

"And you're left with this big concern of, can the foreign minister now manage the relationship with that key strategic partner? And the answer has to be, not really."

Clark believed a lot of different considerations would be going through Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's mind.

"Firstly, it seems to me that the behaviour of New Zealand First and of their leader, and of Shane Jones, has for some time been inviting a sacking, inviting a breakup of the coalition, and frankly, so close to an election campaign, that's probably, you know, neither here nor there.

"But there's also a point of view which says he's not only inviting sacking, he's inviting attention, so don't give it to him. But actually, in the end if you say nothing you seem complicit.

"When you're speaking in parliament you may think you have a hat on as New Zealand First leader but actually offshore you are going to be seen as the foreign minister and the statements that you make will either give credit to your country or they won't, and we know what the case is here.

"It's extremely difficult but I think that it does invite a sacking and the consequences that flow from that. In the end, you know, others have to be seen to stand for something and not for nothing, and to let this go I think is many steps too far."

However, comments from the Chinese Foreign Ministry's daily media briefing added further context to the Chinese Embassy's statement.

"Parliamentary debates in New Zealand are New Zealand's internal affairs. China will not comment on that," spokesperson Mao Ning said in the translated comments.

She said China had noted the criticism of Peters' remarks, "including [by] Prime Minister Christopher Luxon", and said China hoped Peters would avoid bringing the country into domestic politics in future.

"China respects the development paths, systems and models independently chosen by the people of all countries, and opposes all forms of discrimination and prejudice.

"It is hoped that relevant individual in New Zealand will do more things that contribute to the friendship between our two countries, and refrain from making China an issue in domestic politics."

Brash backs sacking call

Don Brash RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Former National and ACT leader Don Brash said Peters' comments were a blow to a very important relationship, which carried a "serious prospect" that Peters should be sacked as Foreign Minister.

However, doing so would come with risks.

"It's one thing to make a comment in the house about a flippant remark, but to go on about the China government itself, there's a serious prospect I think the prime minister should sack him as minister of foreign affairs ... it's a serious blow to a very important relationship.

"Of course, if he does, the government is over and we have an election. And he may be counting on there being enough racist New Zealanders to persevere."

Brash said it almost looked like a deliberate move, saying Peters was a wily politician and it was "hard to believe he's done it by accident".

Peters has been approached for comment.

In a social media post, Peters earlier said the outrage over his comments proved his point.

World.title: Silver Ferns to meet England in Commonwealth Games semi-finals
World.content:
The Silver Ferns will have to beat England in the semi-finals in Glasgow if they are to make their first Commonwealth Games gold medal match since 2014.

England will have their tails up after putting up their best performance in Glasgow by far with a 58-54 win over the fifth-ranked South Africa on Friday morning.

Anticipation was high that South Africa would pull off an upset over the third ranked England Roses in the last pool match of the tournament.

Earlier in the week, the Diamonds posted a 19-goal win over England, before beating South Africa by a 10-goal margin.

With South Africa beating England 2-1 in a series earlier in the year, Pool A was always considered the 'Pool of Death'.

The Silver Ferns topped Pool B earlier in the day after demolishing Trinidad and Tobago 83-23 to make it five straight wins.

Australia went through Pool A unbeaten, and will meet Jamaica in the first semi-final on Saturday evening. The Silver Ferns and England will meet at midnight on Saturday New Zealand time.

The New Zealanders were reduced to 10 players for their final pool match with young defender Catherine Hall awaiting a MRI scan to determine the extent of a knee injury suffered in the previous match against Wales.

Shooter Georgia Heffernan was also left off the team sheet after suffering an ankle knock in the same match but coach Dame Noeline Taurua said Heffernan would be available for selection for the semi-final.

At the 2023 Netball World Cup, the Silver Ferns suffered a massive blow when strike shooter Grace Nweke suffered a tournament ending injury in pool play. The Ferns finished outside of the medals in fourth.

Taurua said selectors picked a versatile squad.

"We're always looking at the depth and making sure that if an injury happens or people can't take the court, we've already got the depth and we knew that in each position we've got three deep," Taurua said.

"The positive is that we're in towards the business end. We're not at the beginning, so we've got fresh legs and that's why those combinations and the changes that we've made earlier in the tournament, we've got something in our back pocket."

The 10 players were rotated throughout the match as New Zealand went on to post their highest score and biggest winning margin in 24 outings against a poor Trinidad & Tobago.

The Silver Ferns went through pool play unbeaten, with earlier wins over Scotland, Jamaica, Uganda, and Wales.

The Proteas boast one of the best shooters in the world in Elmeré van der Berg, who scored the most goals in her debut season in Australia's Suncorp Super Netball competition this year.

South Africa came out strong to win the first quarter 17-11 but a defensive change for England saw them mount a fight-back in the second spell.

Coming on at goal keep Halimat Adio applied all kinds of pressure on van der Berg and put doubt into the feeders minds.

At half-time, South Africa held a slim 29-28 goal lead.

South Africa lost their starting wing attack to a head knock in the third quarter, which disrupted the Proteas attacking end.

England ramped up their efforts in the third quarter, to lead by four going into the final turn.

Liv Tchine and Lois Pearson combined brilliantly in the England shooting end.

Pearson has stepped up brilliantly into the goal attack position, with the England Roses missing the experienced Helen Housby through injury.

The Roses also lost impressive defender Jaz Brown in the lead-up to the event to injury but Adio's efforts against South Africa show what she is capable of.

The Silver Ferns and England have played out some tight matches in recent years.

England beat New Zealand on their way to finishing runners up at the 2023 World Cup to Australia.

World.title: Body found in search for woman missing in Auckland
World.content:
Police looking for a woman reported missing from Birkenhead in Auckland last week have found a body.

Police said earlier they had serious concerns for Maree Jennins who was reported missing from a complex on Roseberry Rd on Tuesday night last week and was last seen a week ago.

Detective Senior Sergeant Mike Williams, of the Waitematā East CIB, said a body was located off Piha Road on Thursday afternoon by Search and Rescue personnel.

"While formal identification is ongoing, it is believed to be the body of the 69-year-old reported missing," he said.

"Police's thoughts are with her family, and they are being offered any required support."

World.title: As it happened: Kiwi gold for David Liti, Emma Foy at Glasgow Commonwealth Games
World.content:
Leonard Powell live from Commonwealth Games Morning Report Download MP3 1m 43s

Another successful day for New Zealand at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, with gold medals to weightlifter David Liti and para-cyclist Emma Foy.

Both had to overcome the odds for victory, with Liti trailling his Indian rival by 10kg after the snatch and need a personal best 223kg clean and jerk to overcome the deficit. He had two attempts available, but he needed only one.

Foy and pilot Jessie Hodges fell behind Australia in the best-of-three sprint format at the velodrome, and were then involved in a crash with their rivals at the start of the second race.

After medical checks and track inspection, the Kiwis won the re-race and then commanded the deciding race for gold.

Shot putter Tom Walsh narrowly missed his attempt at a shot put hattrick, after winning at Gold Coast 2018 and Birmingham 2022, pipped in the penultimate round by Nigerian Chukwuebuka Enekwechi.

The women's team pursuit took silver behind Australia, while para-cyclist Nicole Murray and the men's pursuiters and para sprinter Anna Grimaldi all took bronze.

Murray briefly held the world record for the newly introduced 4000m individual pursuit for her C5 classification, but lost it within minutes to an Australian rival.

Another big day of medal prospects in store tonight, with our women's pole vaulters in action and more track cycling.

World.title: 'Never for sale': European nations vow World Cup boycott over FIFA plan
World.content:
European nations have agreed to boycott the World Cup and all other FIFA competitions in protest over president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in soccer's biggest tournament to private equity investors.

"UEFA and its national associations will not participate in FIFA competitions," the European soccer body said after an urgent online meeting of its 55 member nations.

On a seismic day in soccer politics, support in Asia and CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) for FIFA and Infantino was also shaken.

The next scheduled FIFA tournament is in weeks in Europe — the Women's Under-20 World Cup hosted by Poland from September 5 — and the four British federations comprise FIFA's only bidder to host the 2035 Women's World Cup. That decision is due on November 23.

"Some things are simply too important to sell," UEFA said in a statement. "The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale."

The strategy meeting was called to counter Infantino's offer of $US20 million ($28.45 million) to each of FIFA's 211 global members, which has to be accepted by mid-September.

Infantino's secret project to spin off its commercial operations in a new $US20 billion ($28.45 billion) subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), 20 per cent owned by private investors was revealed on Tuesday.

The core investor would be a New York investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

Infantino wrote to the 211 members — already the effective owners of FIFA as a non-profit association under Swiss law — that if they approved FFE, their promised $US10 million basic funding for the next four years would double to $US20 million. He projected their FIFA funding through 2038 would be $US86 million ($122 million) each, instead of about $US36 million ($51 million).

A breakdown of FIFA's bid to sell the World Cup Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in FIFA's events and competitions arm to investors would grant them control over the World Cup.

"This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA's duty as the custodian of world football," said UEFA, where Infantino was a staffer and its CEO-like general secretary when he was first elected to lead FIFA in 2016.

Infantino's high-stakes gambit now could threaten his previously secure 11-year presidency of FIFA as anger and frustration with him rise among soccer stakeholders, including three of the six continental bodies.

FIFA has set a November 18 deadline for potential candidates to declare in a presidential vote of the 211 members scheduled next March in Rabat, Morocco.

Infantino had seemed after the World Cup to have a clear path to being re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term in office until 2031, despite a furore over letting United States forward Folarin Balogun play against Belgium after a red card in his previous game.

"Game over, Gianni #InfantinOUT," the Football Supporters Europe group, which advises UEFA on fan issues such as ticket prices, posted after the boycott threat.

UEFA detailed why soccer officials fear external investors owning a stake in the global game's biggest events, including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women.

"The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever," UEFA said. "Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure."

Infantino has presented the private equity offer as a chance to "turbocharge" funding development of soccer across the world, where a majority of the 211 FIFA members rely on its funding.

Officials from about 40 UEFA members spoke at the urgent meeting, with anger expressed that FIFA is not using some of its multi-billion-dollar reserves to fund extra development programs.

"As a result of today's discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive," the European soccer body said, "unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership."

CONCACAF also released a statement saying its organisation was built on service, "transparent governance, and the long-term stewardship of football".

"History has shown FIFA and the football family what happens when the custodians of the game lose sight of these values," it said.

Deep concerns were raised about the lack of due process, the short deadline imposed, the lack of review or approval by relevant bodies, and the need for private investment to fund programs.

"For these reasons, CONCACAF and its 41 Member Associations have rejected the proposal," it said.

The associations called on their FIFA Council Members to engage FIFA to determine how existing reserves could be used to increase FIFA Forward funding for football development across the region, and urged that all matters follow proper governance processes.

CONCACAF did not threaten a boycott of FIFA competitions. However, Europe's 55 associations and CONCACAF's 41 would make nearly half of the 211 total votes available.

"FIFA's unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football," the Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said in a letter to its 46 members of FIFA, warning of risks to their own competitions.

Sheikh Salman, an ally of Infantino since losing the FIFA presidential election to him in 2016, wrote: "Such an initiative will not succeed without the support of all the confederations, which is not the case now."

In a video message published Wednesday by FIFA, Infantino insisted spinning off its money-making operations was "an offer, not an obligation."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

A FIFA presentation for its members, co-written with its banking advisors from J.P. Morgan and seen by the AP, set a goal for FFE as "commercial rigour and expertise to better capitalise on broadcast rights, sponsorships and a growing tournament portfolio."

That growing portfolio would likely include adding more teams to FIFA competitions like the World Cup and Club World Cup for men and women, and potentially staging them more often than every four years, including in the US.

FIFA adding teams, games and competitions would squeeze the value, status and space in the congested global fixture calendar for those that fund and are organised by the six continental soccer bodies like UEFA and the AFC.

A threatened World Cup boycott from Europe helped derail Infantino's 2021 plan to stage World Cups every two years instead of four.

AP/ABC

World.title: Australia's old friend wasn't at the Glasgow velodrome, but the old enemy was
World.content:
The crowds at the 2026 Commonwealth Games have varied in size and spirit.

Particularly at the Scottish Event Campus, not far from the city centre, casual fans will wander down and get a taste of the action if they've got time on their weekend.

It's school holiday time in Glasgow too, so plenty of families looking for a way to occupy the kids have made their way into the various arenas.

You may never get the chance to watch again, so a spot of 3x3 basketball or bowls, accompanied by some frankly excellent tunes and an overpriced carton of chips, is a decent way to spend four hours.

Aussie sprint stars through to 200m finals, gold rush at the velodrome Australia's track cycling squad claims three golds on the first day of competition at the velodrome, as Lachie Kennedy and Torrie Lewis fly into their second finals of the week.

That's especially true when the weather has been so dreary to start the Games.

But on a day when it dried out at last, thousands made a decidedly purposeful pilgrimage to the velodrome at the Glasgow International Arena, just next to the home ground of Celtic Football Club.

This was not something you happen upon. This was something you go to. This was the moment Scotland had been waiting for at the arena named for one of their favourite sons, Sir Chris Hoy.

Ironically, before every race it was a pre-recorded Sir Chris (the real thing might have caused a riot) and fellow Scottish icon Duncan Scott telling the crowd to quiet down — or "haud yer wheesht", as Scott said — for the starter's buzzer.

But even Sir Chris — the six-time Olympic, 11-time world and two-time Commonwealth cycling champion — couldn't have contained his house when it was Scotland's Neil Fache (along with pilot Aaron Pope) who won the first gold of the track cycling program for these Games in the men's tandem B 1,000m time trial.

Scots Neil Fachie MBE (left) and pilot Aaron Pope won the first gold medal of the cycling program in Glasgow. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

Australian Kane Perris won Australia's first medal in that event alongside pilot Luke Zaccaria, and earlier in the day, Tara Neyland had picked up Australia's first world record in any event at these Games when she clocked 4:49.648 in qualifying for the C4-5 4,000m individual pursuit.

She later went on to win gold, but only after the women's team pursuit squad started what the cycling team hopes will be a gold rush in Glasgow.

Trailing New Zealand at the halfway mark of the gold medal race against New Zealand, the team of Georgia Baker, Claudia Marcks, Alyssa Polites and Felicity Wilson-Haffenden put away their schedule and just started racing.

"That's my happy place. When we start racing, that's when I'm happiest. When the board goes away, and the hand signals come out, that's when I come into my own," 21-year-old gun Wilson-Haffenden said.

Women's team pursuit gold marked the start of what promises to be a big Games for Australian cycling. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"Just pedal. I was riding 50-cent coins by the end; the pedals weren't going around smooth but giving as much power as I had, grit the teeth, and get to the finish line."

England pipped their men's counterparts, and Jessica Gallagher was unable to defend her Birmingham gold in the tandem B sprint final after a tyre failure caused a nasty crash with the New Zealanders in the second race.

But, as pilot Jacqui Mengler-Mohr put it: "It's not how many times you fall, it's how many times you get back up."

Silver medallists Jessica Gallagher (right) and Jacqueline Mengler-Mohr had a nasty fall as they won tandem B sprint silver. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

And getting back up was exactly what the men's team sprinters did, going one better than the women's team and taking down their English rivals in the final.

They never looked like getting caught over the 1,000m race as Leigh Hoffman won a title as the leader of a new-look team with 23-year-old Danny Barber and 22-year-old Ryan Elliott.

The revamp came after the defection of Olympic gold medallist and sprint superstar Matthew Richardson, whose name Elliott wouldn't even utter when talking about the rivalry with Team England.

"I think it's definitely grown a lot since the swap and defection," he said.

"Between the GB guys maybe a bit less so but definitely between the defector himself."

Australian defector Richardson out of Games after fall Matt Richardson, a three-time Olympic medallist in Paris for Australia before he sensationally defected to the land of his birth, has been ruled out of the Commonwealth Games.

He wasn't the only departure after the team's gold medal at the Paris Olympics, with Matthew Glaetzer retiring and Tom Cornish pivoting to endurance events, making way for Elliott and Barber.

"There's a big change in the roster after Paris, and everyone's question then is: how well can our system back up? What's their depth?" he said.

"Us as the younger guys coming through wanted to prove we have depth in Australia and we're here because we're hungry."

Hoffman said he enjoyed riding with teammates who were 100 per cent in it for Australia.

Ryan Elliott (left), Danny Barber and Leigh Hoffman won team sprint gold in their new formation. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"It would've been great if he stayed with Australia but his heart was obviously never always in it, so good riddance," he said.

Richardson is no longer coming to Glasgow after an ugly fall during a keirin race in Japan just days ago, and Hoffman is disappointed he and Barber won't get a crack at him in the individual event.

"I would have loved for him to come here and race and see how I and Danny stack up against him," Hoffman said.

"I'm upset he's not here, but that is what it is. … I've got plenty of other fish to worry about."

England, Wales, Scotland, Australia and New Zealand are some of the world's strongest track cycling nations, with Malaysia's Azizul Awang and Nicholas Paul from Trinidad and Tobago threats for Hoffman and Barber.

But the good news is Hoffman isn't going anywhere.

"We checked his passport and his lineage," Elliott said.

"So he's good."

World.title: Ex-MAFS star Ridge Barredo sticking to weightlifting despite ugly injury
World.content:
Ridge Barredo's description of the knee injury that ended his Commonwealth Games weightlifting campaign is enough to turn most of us off even watching the sport for good.

"I heard it pop on the third attempt, I tried to give it my all and I heard it pop [out] and pop back in," he said of his failed third snatch attempt in the men's 110kg class.

"Just to feel it was a little bit scary. Initial pain was an eight or nine out of 10."

Barredo said it was the first time he had ever experienced an injury like that, sustained as he tried to throw 162 kilograms over his head.

Loading Instagram content

By the time he spoke to media, having been helped off the Armadillo stage, he said he was just "a little bit uncomfortable" and described the pain as down to a six or seven out of 10.

This was his third Commonwealth Games and the 30-year-old vowed to be back at Amdavad in four years.

"It's not the end. I'm still relatively young, still hungry for it, still want to be the best in Australia," he said.

"I'm not done yet, no way. Not a chance. I'll be back for sure. Four times, watch, mark my words."

And he said this difficult and painful journey is still preferable to a return to the scene that made his descriptor on Google not "athlete" or "weightlifter", but "internet personality".

That's thanks to his turn on reality TV show Married At First Sight three years ago.

One of only a handful of successful couples from the program, Barredo and wife Jade are still together.

Loading Instagram content

Jade and daughter Victoria were in the crowd watching as he suffered his injury.

And while the program worked out for him, Barredo says his TV days are over.

"My TV career is definitely done, I've found my partner. I'm off reality TV. Wouldn't recommend it," he said.

"If you want to have some fun in a toxic environment, go for it, but personally I wouldn't be going back."

He's not the only Games athlete shunning the reality TV scene (for now) with Scottish swimmer Katie Shanahan revealing she had to make a choice to continue swimming or go on Love Island last year.

'If you've got a lane, you've got a chance' An unexpected source kicks off another record-breaking night for Australian swimming as we get implicit and explicit reminders that we shouldn't take this for granted.

Shanahan opted not to enter the villa, ultimately winning silver in the women's 200m backstroke on the first night of the Glasgow swimming program.

"I'm the biggest Love Island fan ever. I've watched every season," Shanahan told BBC Scotland.

"Last year the producers asked me and [English swimmer] Abbie Wood if we would be interested in doing it.

"I couldn't go on, though, because [I was] focusing on the swimming, but who knows in the future?

"I was a bit tempted but the swimming had to come first."

World.title: 'Try not to die': Why Glasgow's gales hit different for hurdlers
World.content:
After rain blighted the first six days of the Commonwealth Games, Glasgow dialled up the dimmer on Thursday morning.

But a gorgeous, sunny, slightly brisk morning turned blustery and bleak by the time athletics competition was in full swing at Scotstoun Stadium.

It mercifully stayed dry as day seven's heats and qualifiers kicked off, but the wind was wreaking havoc across the track and field.

Australian javelin thrower Cameron McEntyre was launching into a mighty headwind that saw none of the 17 throwers reach the qualification standard of 84 metres.

The temperature plummeted as clouds rolled over Scotstoun. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

McEntyre got through on his 78.91m effort, but Kenya's Julius Yego, boasting the fourth longest throw in the Commonwealth this year, missed out on qualifying for the final as he finished in 13th spot.

"Everyone struggled with the wind and the temperature as well. Hopefully better conditions tomorrow and then push for a podium [but] everyone's in the same boat," McEntyre said, crediting his thorough preparation at training for keeping him ready for a day like today.

"If it's pissing down with rain or huge headwinds, whatever the conditions are, we just deal with it because we know one day there's gonna be a competition that's exactly the same."

And while hurling a spear into a breeze that's trying to throw it back at you might sound like the more dangerous prospect, Michelle Jenneke said her 100m hurdles with the wind at her back is a frightening experience.

Michelle Jenneke said the tailwind can mess up hurdlers' all-important stride patterns. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"I get pretty jealous when I see the sprinters because you get a tailwind and you run fast, we get a tailwind and we're like 'let's try not to die today'. The hurdles were really coming at us," Jenneke said.

"I am just really really grateful we knew that was going to be a possibility and we really trained for it. It was tough today, towards the end I was really struggling to make sure I was hitting my stride pattern. But I think I did it really well, I did really safe and still managed to run quite fast."

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

Jenneke clocked a time of 12.72 seconds, 0.05 of a second outside her personal best from two years ago, but this time with an illegal +4.3 metres per second tailwind.

"The wind was really pushing us onto the hurdles, it was a good time, though," she said after progressing to the evening's final as the sixth-fastest qualifier.

"Hopefully a little less windy [in the final] but I did really prepare for that tailwind and I think I handled it better than some of the other athletes."

Adeyah Brewster (background) went down at the final hurdle. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

She certainly did, with Barbados's Adeyah Brewster clipping the final hurdle and falling flat on her belly barely 6 metres short of the finish line.

National 400m champion Reece Holder experienced both sides of the coin in his single-lap semifinal, saying it was exactly what they expected when coming to Glasgow.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

"Everyone's running in the same conditions, so can't really complain because everyone's showing up to show out," he said.

Holder, who suffered a hamstring injury in mid-May, missed the 400m final while teammate Tom Reynolds won his semifinal to progress.

"I actually only just put spikes on two weeks ago from May," he said.

"So to come out here and run 45s, just be thankful for that and push forward for the future.

"I just don't think I'm race fit. Big ups to everyone else out there putting on a show for everyone in these conditions, but I just don't think I was there."

World.title: Roosters put up 82 points for highest NRL score in 91 years
World.content:
Sydney Roosters sent a warning to the rest of the NRL about their premiership credentials with a 82-12 whipping of North Queensland in Townsville, the most points by a winning team in 91 years.

Halfback Sam Walker, in the midst of a multi-million dollar contract negotiation, showed why Roosters supremo Nick Politis wants to keep him at the club for life in a masterclass display.

This was a muscle flex of epic proportions as the visitors scored the equal most first half points in premiership history to lead 48-6 after 40 minutes.

The Roosters scored eight first half tries with fullback James Tedesco and Walker both crossing twice. Walker's 24 points in the first half, including eight goals from as many attempts, was also the equal most points by an individual in an opening 40 minutes.

The team total of 82 was the most by a team since the Roosters beat Canterbury 87-7 in 1935. It was also the third-highest in premiership history.

Walker finished with 36 individual points and a hat-trick of tries, as did unstoppable winger Mark Nawaqanitawase.

Tedesco left the field at halftime with an ankle injury in a concern for the Tricolours.

North Queensland were helpless before the Tricolour onslaught. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock )

The Roosters temporarily joined Penrith on 34 competition points at the top of the table in their most complete performance of the season.

It was their sixth win in a row and a sign that come September they will be in prime position to challenge their bogey team Penrith.

The Cowboys are hanging on in eighth position but will drop back to ninth if Canterbury beat Melbourne away on Friday night.

The nature of the thrashing will test Cowboys coach Todd Payten's ability to get an appropriate response

Captain Tedesco, fresh from a hat-trick of tries last week, started and finished the opening try and it was carnage from that moment.

Roosters forwards Naufahu Whyte and Salesi Foketi monstered the hosts early and the spine of Tedesco, Daly Cherry-Evans, Walker and Reece Robson ran riot.

Tedesco, also the NSW custodian, is making a compelling case to oust Reece Walsh from the fullback position for Australia at the World Cup later in the year.

The Cowboys levelled at six-all when halves Jake Clifford and Jaxon Purdue combined to put Braidon Burns over but that was the only moment the match was in the balance.

A brilliant interchange of passing between halfback Walker and Tedesco led to the No.7 slicing over.

Tedesco then laid on a try for centre Hugo Savala with a left-foot grubber and it was clear which way the match was heading. . Walker's left foot step on the last tackle to score his second was elite.

The dazzling half set up runaway Foketi for a 40m rampage to the line.

The last try of the match, scored by replacement fullback Cody Ramsey, featured Walker grubbering and then kicking the ball over the head of the last dismal line of Cowboys defence.

AAP

World.title: Cats hold off Magpies comeback for critical MCG win
World.content:
Geelong burst out of the gates and then held off Collingwood's fightback to record a critical 25-point win at the MCG.

The Cats got out to a 49-point lead before the Magpies started to whittle the lead down, but never got closer than three-goals as Geelong saw the game out professionally.

Collingwood also lost Jeremy Howe to a broken arm in the third quarter and Harry Perryman to a hamstring strain earlier in the match.

World.title: Women's 5,000m turns into all-Australian classic as Davies, Hull fire for medals
World.content:
Australian Rose Davies has made Commonwealth Games track history with her second gold medal in Glasgow.

Davies roared to a landmark track triumph, becoming the first woman ever to complete the 5,000m and 10,000m double.

The Newcastle-born 26-year-old dropped to her knees in joy after winning the shorter distance at Scotstoun Stadium on Friday morning after a battle royale with her Australian teammate, Jessica Hull.

In a glorious finale, the two Australians took control of the race in a last-lap dust-up, with Olympic 1,500m silver medallist Hull looking poised to strike gold with her superior sprint power off the final bend.

But Davies, who had been a sensational winner of the 10,000m on the opening day of the athletics program, showed extraordinary resolve to kick again and prevail over the final few metres.

The third Australian home was Linden Hall, who finished seventh.

Gold medalist Australia's Rose Davies and silver medalist Jessica Hull were all smiles after the race. (Reuters: Isabel Infantes)

Also on the track, Lachie Kennedy and Torrie Lewis are dreaming of multiple individual Commonwealth Games medals in Glasgow after the red-hot sprinters surged into their respective 200m finals.

Kennedy ran 20.12 seconds in the outside lane, finishing third in his heat and missing an automatic qualifying spot.

But the 22-year-old was also one of the two fastest losers — and third-fastest across all heats — which was enough to progress to the final.

Before the Games, Kennedy declared the 100m was his biggest priority, freely admitting he was "not as invested" in his other sprint events.

Lachlan Kennedy turned in a strong run from an outside lane to qualify for the 200m final. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

But the man who has won Australia's first Commonwealth men's sprint medal since 1962 is now eyeing more hardware, with a 200m final and 4x100m relay ahead on the program.

"It all depends on the conditions, but I definitely think I can win. That's for sure," Kennedy said.

"I don't know about times. Like, time is so dependent on conditions, but I think I've got what it takes to win.

"But there's some good guys up there, man. So I'm going to have to be at my best."

Lewis qualified automatically for the women's final in a dead heat with Jamaica's Alana Reid, running 20.64 (+4.7m/s) in windy conditions.

The pair were involved in a three-way photo finish with England's Success Eduan, who qualified as one of the two fastest losers.

Cyclists claim three gold for Australia

Leigh Hoffman has bid former teammate Matt Richardson good riddance after Australia's gold medal in the team sprint on day one of the Commonwealth Games track cycling program.

Teammate Ryan Elliott also joked they had cleared Hoffman as their leader, checking his passport to make sure he will stay in the Australian program.

While expressing sympathy for Richardson after a recent nasty race crash in Japan, his former teammates finally spoke freely about the shock defection.

Their big win over England was one of Australia's three cycling gold medals at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome on Friday morning, along with the women's team pursuit and para-cyclist Tara Neyland.

Leigh Hoffman of Team Australia celebrates after winning the gold medal during the Men's Team Sprint finals. (Getty: Molly Darlington)

Soon after the Paris Olympics, Richardson stunned the sport by switching allegiances to Great Britain.

The ex-Australian was to be one of the biggest stories of the Glasgow Games, taking on former teammates in the match sprint. But there was more drama on the eve of the track program when Richardson pulled out because of injuries from the Japan crash, when a rival cyclist sideswiped him.

Hoffman was sympathetic, to an extent. After largely keeping their counsel over the past two years, the Australians made their feelings about the defection clear.

"It was horrible. I've seen video of the crash. It's pretty serious. I would have loved for him to come here and race and see how [teammate] Danny [Barber] and I stack up," Hoffman said.

" It would have been great if he stayed in Australia, but his heart was obviously never always in it, so good riddance. "

Elliott was also asked about Hoffman stepping up since Paris as the leader of the sprint squad.

"We checked his passport for his lineage, so he's good," Elliott joked, in reference to Richardson's dual citizenship.

Australia won three of the seven gold medals on offer during day one at the velodrome.

The Australian women successfully defended their team pursuit Games title, overhauling New Zealand and breaking their own Commonwealth Games record.

Sophie Edwards came out of the pursuit quartet who qualified fastest, with three-time Games gold medallist Georgia Baker taking her place.

Felicity Wilson-Haffenden, Claudia Marcks and Alyssa Polites joined Baker in comfortably beating New Zealand for the gold medal.

Sophie Edwards, Claudia Marcks, Alyssa Polites and Felicity Wilson-Haffenden compete in the Women's 4,000m Team Pursuit. (Getty: Patrick Khachfe)

Australia rode 4:10.658, while New Zealand clocked 4:12.775.

"Bloody awesome. I couldn't ask for much more. We came in here wanting to win gold, but it's easier said than done," said women's coach Ash Ankudinoff, a former team pursuit world champion.

"It's an exciting bunch. I never cracked an Olympic medal, but we have a good bunch.

" It's just a step in the right direction. Look out, LA. "

Kane Perris and his pilot Luke Zaccaria won bronze in the men's tandem B 1km time trial, while Scotland delighted the crowd by winning the first gold of the track program in the event ahead of Wales.

Para-sport veteran Jess Gallagher, with Jacqui Mengler-Mohr piloting, took silver behind New Zealand in the women's tandem B sprint.

Molly McGill, Kristina Clonan and Alessia McCaig were fourth-fastest qualifiers in the women's team sprint and lost their bronze ride-off to Scotland, as Wales beat England for gold.

World.title: Rinehart lobbied Qld government to move Olympic events to Rockhampton
World.content:
Billionaire mining magnate Gina Rinehart wrote to Queensland's deputy premier advocating for Olympic rowing and canoeing to be held in Rockhampton prior to the beef capital being awarded the event.

The state government has consistently dismissed criticism of the croc-infested Fitzoy River hosting the 2032 Games events.

A letter from Mrs Rinehart to Jarrod Bleijie, obtained under right to information laws, asked the government to consider Rockhampton before the LNP's Games Delivery Plan release in March 2025.

"As a supporter of Australian rowing for more than a decade, I am aware that the Australian team often trains on the Fitzroy River and that Rockhampton annually hosts the Queensland state school championships," the letter said.

"This rowing facility is world-class and is already close to major infrastructure, so it offers the potential to save taxpayer money."

School rowers training on the Fitzroy River. (Supplied: Rockhampton Grammar School)
